module handshake_deadline (
    input  wire       clk,
    input  wire       i_ce,      // global enable / idle condition
    input  wire       start,     // upstream wants a parse burst
    input  wire       done,      // target signals completion early
    output wire       req,
    output wire       ack,
    output wire       busy_o,
    output wire       timeout
);
    // four-phase handshake: IDLE -> REQ (req rises) -> ACK (ack rises)
    //                       -> DROP (req drops) -> IDLE (ack drops)
    localparam [1:0] P_IDLE = 2'd0,
                     P_REQ  = 2'd1,
                     P_ACK  = 2'd2,
                     P_DROP = 2'd3;

    reg [1:0] phase = P_IDLE;   // handshake phase
    reg       busy  = 1'b0;     // mirrors the phase by construction
    reg [2:0] cnt   = 3'd4;     // completion deadline countdown

    assign req    = (phase == P_REQ)  || (phase == P_ACK);
    assign ack    = (phase == P_ACK)  || (phase == P_DROP);
    assign busy_o = busy;

    // the deadline has expired while the engine is still engaged
    assign timeout = busy && (cnt == 3'd0);

    always @(posedge clk) begin
        if (i_ce) begin
            case (phase)
                P_IDLE: begin
                    if (start) begin
                        phase <= P_REQ;   // req rises
                        busy  <= 1'b1;
                    end
                end
                P_REQ: begin
                    // req may not drop here; the target must raise ack first.
                    // the deadline forces the ack phase on the last tick,
                    // so the countdown can never run through zero.
                    if (done || cnt <= 3'd1)
                        phase <= P_ACK;   // ack rises
                    else
                        cnt   <= cnt - 3'd1;
                end
                P_ACK: begin
                    phase <= P_DROP;      // req drops, ack still high
                end
                P_DROP: begin
                    phase <= P_IDLE;      // ack drops
                    busy  <= 1'b0;
                    cnt   <= 3'd4;        // rearm the deadline
                end
            endcase
        end
    end

    // P1: the completion deadline never expires while the engine is engaged
    always @(posedge clk)
        assert (!timeout);

    // P2: while a request is outstanding the deadline is a live value
    always @(posedge clk)
        if (phase == 2'd1)
            assert (cnt >= 3'd1 && cnt <= 3'd4);
endmodule

module lefdef_parse_fsm (
    input  wire       clk,
    input  wire       rst,
    input  wire       ce,
    input  wire [1:0] tok,
    output reg  [2:0] state,
    output reg        hdr_seen,
    output reg  [3:0] macro_cnt
);
    // binary-encoded parser FSM; encodings 3'd6 and 3'd7 are never entered
    localparam S_IDLE   = 3'd0;  // waiting for a file
    localparam S_HEADER = 3'd1;  // VERSION / UNITS block
    localparam S_MACRO  = 3'd2;  // MACRO record
    localparam S_PINS   = 3'd3;  // PIN records of current macro
    localparam S_LAYER  = 3'd4;  // LAYER / PORT geometry
    localparam S_END    = 3'd5;  // END LIBRARY

    initial state     = S_IDLE;
    initial hdr_seen  = 1'b0;    // shadow register: header block was parsed
    initial macro_cnt = 4'd0;

    always @(posedge clk) begin
        if (rst) begin
            state     <= S_IDLE;
            hdr_seen  <= 1'b0;
            macro_cnt <= 4'd0;
        end else if (ce) begin
            case (state)
                S_IDLE: begin
                    if (tok == 2'd1)
                        state <= S_HEADER;
                end
                S_HEADER: begin
                    if (tok == 2'd2) begin
                        hdr_seen <= 1'b1;   // header fully consumed
                        state    <= S_MACRO;
                    end
                end
                S_MACRO: begin
                    if (tok == 2'd3)
                        state <= S_PINS;
                    else if (tok == 2'd0)
                        state <= S_END;
                end
                S_PINS: begin
                    if (tok == 2'd3)
                        state <= S_LAYER;
                end
                S_LAYER: begin
                    if (tok == 2'd0) begin
                        state     <= S_MACRO;
                        macro_cnt <= macro_cnt + 4'd1;
                    end
                end
                S_END: begin
                    if (tok == 2'd1)
                        state <= S_IDLE;
                end
                default: begin
                    // illegal encoding recovery path (never taken in practice)
                    state <= S_PINS;
                end
            endcase
        end
    end

    // Precedence: pin records can only be seen after the header was parsed.
    always @(posedge clk)
        if (state == S_PINS)
            assert (hdr_seen);
endmodule

module handshake_deadline (
    input  wire       clk,
    input  wire       i_ce,      // global enable / idle condition
    input  wire       start,     // upstream wants a parse burst
    input  wire       done,      // target signals completion early
    output wire       req,
    output wire       ack,
    output wire       busy_o,
    output wire       timeout
);
    // four-phase handshake: IDLE -> REQ (req rises) -> ACK (ack rises)
    //                       -> DROP (req drops) -> IDLE (ack drops)
    localparam [1:0] P_IDLE = 2'd0,
                     P_REQ  = 2'd1,
                     P_ACK  = 2'd2,
                     P_DROP = 2'd3;

    reg [1:0] phase = P_IDLE;   // handshake phase
    reg       busy  = 1'b0;     // mirrors the phase by construction
    reg [2:0] cnt   = 3'd4;     // completion deadline countdown
    reg [2:0] used  = 3'd0;     // enabled cycles this burst has been engaged
    reg       drain = 1'b0;     // extra busy cycle after a full-budget burst

    assign req    = (phase == P_REQ)  || (phase == P_ACK);
    assign ack    = (phase == P_ACK)  || (phase == P_DROP);
    assign busy_o = busy || drain;  // hold busy one cycle longer after a slow burst

    // the deadline has expired while the engine is still engaged
    assign timeout = busy && (cnt == 3'd0);

    always @(posedge clk) begin
        if (i_ce) begin
            case (phase)
                P_IDLE: begin
                    drain <= 1'b0;
                    if (start) begin
                        phase <= P_REQ;   // req rises
                        busy  <= 1'b1;
                    end
                end
                P_REQ: begin
                    // req may not drop here; the target must raise ack first.
                    // the deadline forces the ack phase on the last tick,
                    // so the countdown can never run through zero.
                    if (done || cnt <= 3'd1)
                        phase <= P_ACK;   // ack rises
                    else
                        cnt   <= cnt - 3'd1;
                    used  <= used + 3'd1;   // charge the latency counter
                end
                P_ACK: begin
                    phase <= P_DROP;      // req drops, ack still high
                    used  <= used + 3'd1;
                end
                P_DROP: begin
                    phase <= P_IDLE;      // ack drops
                    busy  <= 1'b0;
                    cnt   <= 3'd4;        // rearm the deadline
                    used  <= 3'd0;
                    drain <= (used >= 3'd5); // burst ate the whole budget
                end
            endcase
        end
    end

    // P1: the completion deadline never expires while the engine is engaged
    always @(posedge clk)
        assert (!timeout);

    // P2: while a request is outstanding the deadline is a live value
    always @(posedge clk)
        if (phase == 2'd1)
            assert (cnt >= 3'd1 && cnt <= 3'd4);

    // P3: a burst never stays engaged longer than the budget plus the ack tail
    always @(posedge clk)
        if (busy)
            assert (used <= 3'd5);
endmodule

prompt.content:
You write SystemVerilog modules for a formal verification dataset.

Each module is a "planted triple": a design containing an internal structural
relation R that holds by construction, plus a property P that is true of the design
but CANNOT be proven by k-induction unless the prover is also given R.

## The criterion

Three conditions, all required.

(1) P is true of the design.

(2) P is NOT inductive on its own. Concretely, there exists a state S such that:
      - S satisfies P
      - S violates R  (so S is unreachable in real operation, but a solver
        performing induction may start there)
      - S transitions in ONE step to a state that VIOLATES P

    S must also be a state the design can IDLE IN — one it can remain in for
    arbitrarily many cycles by holding the enable low. This matters: a one-step
    CTI only shows P is not 1-inductive, but the prover uses a 20-state window.
    If the design can stall in S, the solver builds a window of 20 copies of S and
    then takes the violating transition, so the property fails induction at ANY
    depth rather than only at depth 1. Without a stall, P may survive 20-induction
    and the triple is rejected.

    Condition (2) is the whole task. A property that is merely "weaker than R" is
    not enough. If every state satisfying P steps to another state satisfying P,
    then P is inductive by itself and the module is worthless for this dataset.

    Counterexample to avoid: if `count` is a 3-bit register, `count <= 7` is a
    consequence of any relation involving count, but it is trivially inductive
    because the register cannot hold anything larger. Rejected.

(3) P AND R TOGETHER ARE INDUCTIVE. R must be strong enough to exclude S and every
    state like it. It is not enough that R is true and P is weak — R must actually
    close the proof.

    R may be a conjunction of several clauses. The individual clauses do NOT each
    need to be inductive on their own; the requirement is that the conjunction,
    together with P, closes induction. Multi-clause relations are welcome and often
    necessary.

## Hard constraints on the Verilog

- These assertion forms are supported and all of them are welcome:
      always @(posedge clk) assert (expr);
      always @(*)           assert (expr);
      assert property (expr);                    // module level, NO clock inside
      always @(posedge clk) assert property (expr);
  `$past`, `$rose`, `$fell` and `$stable` work inside a clocked always block.
  Gate any `$past` check with a past-valid register so cycle zero is not judged:
      reg pv = 0;
      always @(posedge clk) pv <= 1;
      always @(posedge clk) if (pv) assert (out == $past(in));
- Do NOT put a clock inside the property: `assert property (@(posedge clk) ...)`,
  `disable iff`, `|->`, `|=>`, `##N`, `property ... endproperty`, `s_eventually`,
  sequences and `bind` are REJECTED by the toolchain — the module fails to parse
  and is never graded. Do not nest these functions either: `$past($rose(x))`
  fails to elaborate.
- Give every state register an `initial` value, so counterexamples are genuine
  from-reset traces rather than artifacts of an unconstrained start state.
- The design MUST have an enable or idle condition — an input that, when low, leaves
  all state unchanged (e.g. `i_ce`, `step`, or push and pop both low). Condition (2)
  depends on it: the state S must be one the design can sit in indefinitely.
- One property per module, unless the property style below asks for two.
- Never write `assume`. Assumptions are not checked and would let a false premise
  carry the proof.
- Never write `->` as logical implication in an expression — the toolchain rejects
  it. Write `!a || b` instead.
- If a register's declared width admits values it can never reach (e.g. a counter
  that saturates at 8 in a 4-bit reg), include an invariant bounding it — induction
  otherwise starts from an impossible value and fails on a phantom CTI.

## Output format

Your output is emitted through the API's structured-output mode — the schema is
enforced. Field order is deliberate: the reasoning fields come FIRST. Work out the
state S that breaks induction BEFORE writing the design, then write a design in
which that state is reachable-under-induction and the transition is real.

Field notes:

- `cti_reasoning`: one or two sentences: why this state satisfies P, why it
  violates R, and what its successor does that breaks P.

- `cti_state`: the state S from condition (2), as a list of {signal, value}
  pairs with concrete values. Every signal needed to evaluate both P and R must
  appear. Vague answers are rejected: "pointers disagree" is not acceptable;
  [{"signal": "count", "value": "3'd1"}, {"signal": "wptr", "value": "2'd2"},
  {"signal": "rptr", "value": "2'd0"}] is.

  Self-check before you answer: evaluate R at cti_state. It MUST come out false.
  If your named state does not violate your own invariant, you have contradicted
  yourself — fix one or the other.

- `invariants` is R. Supplied SEPARATELY from the Verilog — it must NOT appear as
  an assertion in the source. One string per clause.

- `verilog` is the full module source with the property assertion inline.

- `top_module` must match `module <name>` in the source. `clock` is the clock
  signal name.

- `antecedents` is the guard of P. If P is `if (count == 3'd0) assert (wptr == rptr);`
  the antecedent is `"count == 3'd0"`. If P is unconditional, use [].
  Prefer writing P with a guard, because real hardware properties are overwhelmingly
  conditional — an assertion about what must hold *when something happens*.

- `sanity_covers` must be genuinely reachable, e.g. `"count == 3'd2"` for a counter
  that gets there. Only checked when the property has an antecedent.

## Design idea

Module smbus_pec_mon: an SMBus monitor for a 128-bit SoC prototyping bus bridge. It tracks SCL-low timeouts and folds 128-bit transfer words into a CRC-8 PEC (poly 0x07). Inputs: clk, rst_n, en (all state holds when en=0), scl_low, wvalid, wdata[127:0]. Every register below updates only when en=1.

State registers:
- low_cnt[5:0]: counts consecutive scl_low cycles and clears when SCL goes high. It saturates at TMAX=50.
- timeout_flag (1 bit): set when low_cnt==TMAX-1 && scl_low.
- before_to (1 bit): reset to 1 and cleared the first time timeout_flag rises. This is the scope register.
- wbuf[127:0]: latched input word.
- pend (1 bit): set on wvalid, cleared on fold. It feeds the PEC path.
- pend_cnt (1 bit): a duplicate pending flag, set and cleared identically to pend. It feeds the count path.
- pec_acc[7:0]: PEC accumulator. When pend=1 it takes pec_acc <= crc8_128(pec_acc, wbuf).
- wcnt[6:0]: folded-word counter, incremented mod 128 when pend_cnt=1. An increment always changes its value.
- pec_snap[7:0]: precedence shadow. When pend_cnt=1 it takes pec_snap <= crc8_128(pec_acc, wbuf), recording the PEC value produced by the most recent counted fold.

Relation R (holds by construction): pend == pend_cnt && pec_snap == pec_acc.

Property P (precedence, before-timeout scope, $stable style). P captures that a PEC change must be preceded by, and coincide with, a counted word fold:
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff(!rst_n) before_to && $past(before_to) && $stable(wcnt) |-> $stable(pec_acc));
In words: if the word counter did not move, the PEC accumulator did not move either. Antecedents are before_to and $past(before_to).

P is true on reachable states. pec_acc changes only when pend=1, and by R pend_cnt=1 at the same moment, so wcnt changes too. Therefore $stable(wcnt) implies no fold, which implies $stable(pec_acc).

Counter-example to induction (P holds, R is violated):
- State: before_to=1, timeout_flag=0, low_cnt=0, pend=1, pend_cnt=0, pec_acc=8'h00, wbuf=128'h1, pec_snap=8'h00, wcnt=7'd5.
- This satisfies P now, and it violates R because pend != pend_cnt.
- With en=0 the state is frozen for any number of cycles. Every register is $stable, so P holds vacuously, and a k-induction run of any depth fails to reach a contradiction.
- On the first cycle with en=1 and scl_low=0, pec_acc becomes crc8(0x00, 128'h1)=0x07 while wcnt stays 5. Then $stable(wcnt) holds but pec_acc changed, which violates P while before_to is still 1.

Supplying R as a lemma excludes the pend/pend_cnt mismatch, and P becomes 1-inductive.

## Size

Make the design's data words 128-bit, with counters and pointers only as wide as they need to be; if it stores several items, give that storage 128 entries.

Declare the design's registers and storage at this size, and size every
constant to match.

## Worked example

With step low the design idles here indefinitely; one rotate-left step then yields 4'b0101, where bits 0 and 2 are both set, breaking the property.",

    {
      "signal": "state",
      "value": "4'b1010"
    }

Each module is a "planted triple": a design containing an internal structural
relation R that holds by construction, plus a property P that is true of the design
but CANNOT be proven by k-induction unless the prover is also given R.

## The criterion

Three conditions, all required.

(1) P is true of the design.

(2) P is NOT inductive on its own. Concretely, there exists a state S such that:
      - S satisfies P

        performing induction may start there)
      - S transitions in ONE step to a state that VIOLATES P

    arbitrarily many cycles by holding the enable low. This matters: a one-step
    CTI only shows P is not 1-inductive, but the prover uses a 20-state window.

    then takes the violating transition, so the property fails induction at ANY
    depth rather than only at depth 1. Without a stall, P may survive 20-induction
    and the triple is rejected.

    Condition (2) is the whole task. A property that is merely "weaker than R" is
    not enough. If every state satisfying P steps to another state satisfying P,
    then P is inductive by itself and the module is worthless for this dataset.

    Counterexample to avoid: if `count` is a 3-bit register, `count <= 7` is a
    consequence of any relation involving count, but it is trivially inductive
    because the register cannot hold anything larger. Rejected.

(3) P AND R TOGETHER ARE INDUCTIVE. R must be strong enough to exclude S and every
    state like it. It is not enough that R is true and P is weak — R must actually
    close the proof.

    R may be a conjunction of several clauses. The individual clauses do NOT each
    need to be inductive on their own; the requirement is that the conjunction,
    together with P, closes induction. Multi-clause relations are welcome and often
    necessary.

## Hard constraints on the Verilog

- These assertion forms are supported and all of them are welcome:
      always @(posedge clk) assert (expr);
      always @(*)           assert (expr);
      assert property (expr);                    // module level, NO clock inside
      always @(posedge clk) assert property (expr);
  `$past`, `$rose`, `$fell` and `$stable` work inside a clocked always block.
  Gate any `$past` check with a past-valid register so cycle zero is not judged:
      reg pv = 0;
      always @(posedge clk) pv <= 1;
      always @(posedge clk) if (pv) assert (out == $past(in));
- Do NOT put a clock inside the property: `assert property (@(posedge clk) ...)`,

  sequences and `bind` are REJECTED by the toolchain — the module fails to parse
  and is never graded. Do not nest these functions either: `$past($rose(x))`
  fails to elaborate.
- Give every state register an `initial` value, so counterexamples are genuine
  from-reset traces rather than artifacts of an unconstrained start state.

  all state unchanged (e.g. `i_ce`, `step`, or push and pop both low). Condition (2)

  carry the proof.

enforced. Field order is deliberate: the reasoning fields come FIRST. Work out the
state S that breaks induction BEFORE writing the design, then write a design in

Inputs: clk, rst, en (when low, every register holds), arm, start, clr, sel_add (add vs double), and wr_addr/wr_data (operand load while not running).

State registers:
- armed (1)
- started (1)
- done (1)
- pre_clr (1): starts at 1, cleared the first cycle en && clr.
- step [31:0]: micro-op index; 0 means not running.
- acc [31:0]: field multiply/add result.
- rf (16 x 32)

Behaviour when en is high:
- arm sets armed.
- If start && armed && step==0, then step<=1 and started<=1.
- While step != 0, each cycle performs micro-op number step from a fixed 11-op schedule, for example T6=Y1*Y1, T7=X1*T6, T8=X1*X1 and so on. Each op reads two rf entries, writes acc into a temporary, and does step<=step+1.

- started -> armed
- done -> started

- pre_clr=1, armed=1, started=0, done=0, step=10, en=0.
- P holds because done=0.
- R is violated because step != 0 while started=0.
- With en low the state is frozen indefinitely, so arbitrarily long stuttering prefixes all satisfy P. Plain k-induction therefore cannot exclude it for any k.

On the next en=1 cycle with clr=0:
- step goes 10 -> 11.
- One more cycle sets done=1 with started=0, violating P.

Supplying R as a lemma makes P 1-inductive. step==0 is guaranteed whenever started is 0, so done can only be set after the start event, which itself required armed.

## Size

Make the design's counters and data words 32-bit (wider only where a count needs more); if it stores several items, give that storage 16 entries.

Declare the design's registers and storage at this size, and size every
constant to match.

prompt.content:
You write SystemVerilog modules for a formal verification dataset.

Each module is a "planted triple": a design containing an internal structural
relation R that holds by construction, plus a property P that is true of the design
but CANNOT be proven by k-induction unless the prover is also given R.

## The criterion

Three conditions, all required.

(1) P is true of the design.

(2) P is NOT inductive on its own. Concretely, there exists a state S such that:
      - S satisfies P
      - S violates R  (so S is unreachable in real operation, but a solver
        performing induction may start there)
      - S transitions in ONE step to a state that VIOLATES P

    S must also be a state the design can IDLE IN — one it can remain in for
    arbitrarily many cycles by holding the enable low. This matters: a one-step
    CTI only shows P is not 1-inductive, but the prover uses a 20-state window.
    If the design can stall in S, the solver builds a window of 20 copies of S and
    then takes the violating transition, so the property fails induction at ANY
    depth rather than only at depth 1. Without a stall, P may survive 20-induction
    and the triple is rejected.

    Condition (2) is the whole task. A property that is merely "weaker than R" is
    not enough. If every state satisfying P steps to another state satisfying P,
    then P is inductive by itself and the module is worthless for this dataset.

    Counterexample to avoid: if `count` is a 3-bit register, `count <= 7` is a
    consequence of any relation involving count, but it is trivially inductive
    because the register cannot hold anything larger. Rejected.

(3) P AND R TOGETHER ARE INDUCTIVE. R must be strong enough to exclude S and every
    state like it. It is not enough that R is true and P is weak — R must actually
    close the proof.

    R may be a conjunction of several clauses. The individual clauses do NOT each
    need to be inductive on their own; the requirement is that the conjunction,
    together with P, closes induction. Multi-clause relations are welcome and often
    necessary.

## Hard constraints on the Verilog

- These assertion forms are supported and all of them are welcome:
      always @(posedge clk) assert (expr);
      always @(*)           assert (expr);
      assert property (expr);                    // module level, NO clock inside
      always @(posedge clk) assert property (expr);
  `$past`, `$rose`, `$fell` and `$stable` work inside a clocked always block.
  Gate any `$past` check with a past-valid register so cycle zero is not judged:
      reg pv = 0;
      always @(posedge clk) pv <= 1;
      always @(posedge clk) if (pv) assert (out == $past(in));
- Do NOT put a clock inside the property: `assert property (@(posedge clk) ...)`,
  `disable iff`, `|->`, `|=>`, `##N`, `property ... endproperty`, `s_eventually`,
  sequences and `bind` are REJECTED by the toolchain — the module fails to parse
  and is never graded. Do not nest these functions either: `$past($rose(x))`
  fails to elaborate.
- Give every state register an `initial` value, so counterexamples are genuine
  from-reset traces rather than artifacts of an unconstrained start state.
- The design MUST have an enable or idle condition — an input that, when low, leaves
  all state unchanged (e.g. `i_ce`, `step`, or push and pop both low). Condition (2)
  depends on it: the state S must be one the design can sit in indefinitely.
- One property per module, unless the property style below asks for two.
- Never write `assume`. Assumptions are not checked and would let a false premise
  carry the proof.
- Never write `->` as logical implication in an expression — the toolchain rejects
  it. Write `!a || b` instead.
- If a register's declared width admits values it can never reach (e.g. a counter
  that saturates at 8 in a 4-bit reg), include an invariant bounding it — induction
  otherwise starts from an impossible value and fails on a phantom CTI.

## Output format

Your output is emitted through the API's structured-output mode — the schema is
enforced. Field order is deliberate: the reasoning fields come FIRST. Work out the
state S that breaks induction BEFORE writing the design, then write a design in
which that state is reachable-under-induction and the transition is real.

Field notes:

- `cti_reasoning`: one or two sentences: why this state satisfies P, why it
  violates R, and what its successor does that breaks P.

- `cti_state`: the state S from condition (2), as a list of {signal, value}
  pairs with concrete values. Every signal needed to evaluate both P and R must
  appear. Vague answers are rejected: "pointers disagree" is not acceptable;
  [{"signal": "count", "value": "3'd1"}, {"signal": "wptr", "value": "2'd2"},
  {"signal": "rptr", "value": "2'd0"}] is.

  Self-check before you answer: evaluate R at cti_state. It MUST come out false.
  If your named state does not violate your own invariant, you have contradicted
  yourself — fix one or the other.

- `invariants` is R. Supplied SEPARATELY from the Verilog — it must NOT appear as
  an assertion in the source. One string per clause.

- `verilog` is the full module source with the property assertion inline.

- `top_module` must match `module <name>` in the source. `clock` is the clock
  signal name.

- `antecedents` is the guard of P. If P is `if (count == 3'd0) assert (wptr == rptr);`
  the antecedent is `"count == 3'd0"`. If P is unconditional, use [].
  Prefer writing P with a guard, because real hardware properties are overwhelmingly
  conditional — an assertion about what must hold *when something happens*.

- `sanity_covers` must be genuinely reachable, e.g. `"count == 3'd2"` for a counter
  that gets there. Only checked when the property has an antecedent.

## Design idea

GPU core scan-dump unit built from LSSD L1/L2 latch pairs. A debug host requests a scan dump of a 2-entry, 64-bit warp-register snapshot. Each bit position is an LSSD pair: an L1 latch with a system clock and a scan A-clock feeds an L2 latch clocked by B. The latches are modeled as registers updated on internal A/B pulse phases.

State (all held when en=0):
- l1[0:1], l2[0:1]: 64-bit each, the latch pairs.
- busy: 1 bit.
- ph: 1 bit; 0 means an A pulse is due, 1 means a B pulse is due.
- sc: 7-bit shift count.
- cd: 8-bit countdown.

Behaviour when en=1:
- Idle, !scan_req: system capture into l1 is allowed and B copies l1 into l2. busy, sc, ph and cd are unchanged.
- Accept, !busy && scan_req: busy<=1, cd<=128, sc<=0, ph<=0.
- While busy, every cycle cd<=cd-1.
- When busy and ph==0 (A pulse): l1[i] <= {l2[i][62:0], scan_in_i}, where entry 1's scan_in is entry 0's l2 MSB and entry 0's is tdi. ph<=1.
- When busy and ph==1 (B pulse): l2<=l1, ph<=0, sc<=sc+1.
- Completion is triggered by the shift counter, not the countdown: when busy && ph==1 && sc==63, busy<=0 and sc<=0. cd decrements on that cycle as usual, from 1 to 0.
- tdo = l2[1][63].

Relation R (by construction):
- busy -> (cd == 128 - 2*sc - ph) && sc <= 63
- !busy -> (cd == 0 && sc == 0 && ph == 0)

Property P (global, two assertions, no arming):
- A1 (bounded response, safety form): busy -> cd != 0. The countdown never expires while the dump is outstanding.
- A2: !busy -> cd == 0. An idle unit never holds a stale countdown.

Neither assertion is inductive alone:
- A1 counterexample: busy=1, cd=1, sc=10, ph=0 satisfies A1 and A2 but violates R. One enabled cycle gives busy=1, cd=0, which violates A1.
- A2 counterexample: busy=1, cd=5, sc=63, ph=1 satisfies A1, and A2 vacuously, but violates R. It steps to busy=0, cd=4, which violates A2.

Either state can be held indefinitely with en=0, since all registers freeze. Adding R closes both assertions:
- Under R, busy && sc==63 && ph==1 forces cd==1, so completion lands exactly on cd==0.
- Under R, any other busy state has cd >= 2, so cd-1 stays nonzero.
- Idle with cd==0 is preserved, and accept loads cd=128 with sc=0, ph=0, which re-establishes R.

k = 128 cycles is the response bound.

## Size

Make the design's counters and data words 64-bit (wider only where a count needs more); if it stores several items, give that storage 2 entries.

Declare the design's registers and storage at this size, and size every
constant to match.

    "state == 4'b0100"
  ]

You write SystemVerilog modules for a formal verification dataset.

Each module is a "planted triple": a design containing an internal structural
relation R that holds by construction, plus a property P that is true of the design
but CANNOT be proven by k-induction unless the prover is also given R.

## The criterion

Three conditions, all required.

(1) P is true of the design.

(2) P is NOT inductive on its own. Concretely, there exists a state S such that:
      - S satisfies P
      - S violates R  (so S is unreachable in real operation, but a solver
        performing induction may start there)
      - S transitions in ONE step to a state that VIOLATES P

    S must also be a state the design can IDLE IN — one it can remain in for
    arbitrarily many cycles by holding the enable low. This matters: a one-step
    CTI only shows P is not 1-inductive, but the prover uses a 20-state window.
    If the design can stall in S, the solver builds a window of 20 copies of S and
    then takes the violating transition, so the property fails induction at ANY
    depth rather than only at depth 1. Without a stall, P may survive 20-induction
    and the triple is rejected.

    Condition (2) is the whole task. A property that is merely "weaker than R" is
    not enough. If every state satisfying P steps to another state satisfying P,
    then P is inductive by itself and the module is worthless for this dataset.

    Counterexample to avoid: if `count` is a 3-bit register, `count <= 7` is a
    consequence of any relation involving count, but it is trivially inductive
    because the register cannot hold anything larger. Rejected.

(3) P AND R TOGETHER ARE INDUCTIVE. R must be strong enough to exclude S and every
    state like it. It is not enough that R is true and P is weak — R must actually
    close the proof.

    R may be a conjunction of several clauses. The individual clauses do NOT each
    need to be inductive on their own; the requirement is that the conjunction,
    together with P, closes induction. Multi-clause relations are welcome and often
    necessary.

## Hard constraints on the Verilog

- These assertion forms are supported and all of them are welcome:
      always @(posedge clk) assert (expr);
      always @(*)           assert (expr);
      assert property (expr);                    // module level, NO clock inside
      always @(posedge clk) assert property (expr);

  Gate any `$past` check with a past-valid register so cycle zero is not judged:
      reg pv = 0;
      always @(posedge clk) pv <= 1;
      always @(posedge clk) if (pv) assert (out == $past(in));

  `disable iff`, `|->`, `|=>`, `##N`, `property ... endproperty`, `s_eventually`,
  sequences and `bind` are REJECTED by the toolchain — the module fails to parse
  and is never graded. Do not nest these functions either: `$past($rose(x))`
  fails to elaborate.
- Give every state register an `initial` value, so counterexamples are genuine
  from-reset traces rather than artifacts of an unconstrained start state.
- The design MUST have an enable or idle condition — an input that, when low, leaves
  all state unchanged (e.g. `i_ce`, `step`, or push and pop both low). Condition (2)
  depends on it: the state S must be one the design can sit in indefinitely.

- Never write `assume`. Assumptions are not checked and would let a false premise
  carry the proof.
- Never write `->` as logical implication in an expression — the toolchain rejects
  it. Write `!a || b` instead.
- If a register's declared width admits values it can never reach (e.g. a counter
  that saturates at 8 in a 4-bit reg), include an invariant bounding it — induction

Your output is emitted through the API's structured-output mode — the schema is
enforced. Field order is deliberate: the reasoning fields come FIRST. Work out the
state S that breaks induction BEFORE writing the design, then write a design in
which that state is reachable-under-induction and the transition is real.

  violates R, and what its successor does that breaks P.

- clk, rst.
- en: the idle input. When en is low, every register holds.
- in_valid; in_data[8][64]; in_sel[7:0], which picks the table entry.
- cfg_we, cfg_addr[7:0], cfg_bits[19:0]: table write port.

State registers:
- cfg_tab[256][20]: permutation table.
- stage_cfg[5][4]: settings latched per stage for the beat in flight.
- data_pipe[5][8][64]: words held between stages.
- valid_pipe[4:0]: one valid bit per stage.
- inflight[63:0]: number of beats currently in the network.
- beats_done[63:0]: retired-beat counter, not used in P.
- armed (1 bit): sticky; set the first time cfg_we is high while en is high, never cleared.

Behaviour when en is high:
- cfg_we writes cfg_tab[cfg_addr].
- valid_pipe shifts left: valid_pipe <= {valid_pipe[3:0], in_valid}.
- data_pipe and stage_cfg advance one stage. Each stage swaps or passes its lane pairs according to its 4 bits, wired as a Benes network (butterfly, then inverse butterfly).

- Reset clears everything.

- R fails because popcount(valid_pipe) = 0 but inflight = 5.

Make the design's counters and data words 64-bit (wider only where a count needs more); if it stores several items, give that storage 256 entries.

Declare the design's registers and storage at this size, and size every
constant to match.

With tick low the design idles here indefinitely; one tick then takes remaining to 0 while elapsed becomes 6, so the property fails in the next state.",

      "value": "64'd1"
    }

  "clock": "clk",

    "remaining == 64'd0"
  ],
  "sanity_covers": [
    "remaining == 64'd40"
  ]
}

prompt.content:
You write SystemVerilog modules for a formal verification dataset.

Each module is a "planted triple": a design containing an internal structural
relation R that holds by construction, plus a property P that is true of the design
but CANNOT be proven by k-induction unless the prover is also given R.

## The criterion

Three conditions, all required.

(1) P is true of the design.

(2) P is NOT inductive on its own. Concretely, there exists a state S such that:
      - S satisfies P
      - S violates R  (so S is unreachable in real operation, but a solver
        performing induction may start there)
      - S transitions in ONE step to a state that VIOLATES P

    S must also be a state the design can IDLE IN — one it can remain in for
    arbitrarily many cycles by holding the enable low. This matters: a one-step
    CTI only shows P is not 1-inductive, but the prover uses a 20-state window.
    If the design can stall in S, the solver builds a window of 20 copies of S and
    then takes the violating transition, so the property fails induction at ANY
    depth rather than only at depth 1. Without a stall, P may survive 20-induction
    and the triple is rejected.

    Condition (2) is the whole task. A property that is merely "weaker than R" is
    not enough. If every state satisfying P steps to another state satisfying P,
    then P is inductive by itself and the module is worthless for this dataset.

    Counterexample to avoid: if `count` is a 3-bit register, `count <= 7` is a
    consequence of any relation involving count, but it is trivially inductive
    because the register cannot hold anything larger. Rejected.

(3) P AND R TOGETHER ARE INDUCTIVE. R must be strong enough to exclude S and every
    state like it. It is not enough that R is true and P is weak — R must actually
    close the proof.

    R may be a conjunction of several clauses. The individual clauses do NOT each
    need to be inductive on their own; the requirement is that the conjunction,
    together with P, closes induction. Multi-clause relations are welcome and often
    necessary.

## Hard constraints on the Verilog

- These assertion forms are supported and all of them are welcome:
      always @(posedge clk) assert (expr);
      always @(*)           assert (expr);
      assert property (expr);                    // module level, NO clock inside
      always @(posedge clk) assert property (expr);
  `$past`, `$rose`, `$fell` and `$stable` work inside a clocked always block.
  Gate any `$past` check with a past-valid register so cycle zero is not judged:
      reg pv = 0;
      always @(posedge clk) pv <= 1;
      always @(posedge clk) if (pv) assert (out == $past(in));
- Do NOT put a clock inside the property: `assert property (@(posedge clk) ...)`,
  `disable iff`, `|->`, `|=>`, `##N`, `property ... endproperty`, `s_eventually`,
  sequences and `bind` are REJECTED by the toolchain — the module fails to parse
  and is never graded. Do not nest these functions either: `$past($rose(x))`
  fails to elaborate.
- Give every state register an `initial` value, so counterexamples are genuine
  from-reset traces rather than artifacts of an unconstrained start state.
- The design MUST have an enable or idle condition — an input that, when low, leaves
  all state unchanged (e.g. `i_ce`, `step`, or push and pop both low). Condition (2)
  depends on it: the state S must be one the design can sit in indefinitely.
- One property per module, unless the property style below asks for two.
- Never write `assume`. Assumptions are not checked and would let a false premise
  carry the proof.
- Never write `->` as logical implication in an expression — the toolchain rejects
  it. Write `!a || b` instead.
- If a register's declared width admits values it can never reach (e.g. a counter
  that saturates at 8 in a 4-bit reg), include an invariant bounding it — induction
  otherwise starts from an impossible value and fails on a phantom CTI.

## Output format

Your output is emitted through the API's structured-output mode — the schema is
enforced. Field order is deliberate: the reasoning fields come FIRST. Work out the
state S that breaks induction BEFORE writing the design, then write a design in
which that state is reachable-under-induction and the transition is real.

Field notes:

- `cti_reasoning`: one or two sentences: why this state satisfies P, why it
  violates R, and what its successor does that breaks P.

- `cti_state`: the state S from condition (2), as a list of {signal, value}
  pairs with concrete values. Every signal needed to evaluate both P and R must
  appear. Vague answers are rejected: "pointers disagree" is not acceptable;
  [{"signal": "count", "value": "3'd1"}, {"signal": "wptr", "value": "2'd2"},
  {"signal": "rptr", "value": "2'd0"}] is.

  Self-check before you answer: evaluate R at cti_state. It MUST come out false.
  If your named state does not violate your own invariant, you have contradicted
  yourself — fix one or the other.

- `invariants` is R. Supplied SEPARATELY from the Verilog — it must NOT appear as
  an assertion in the source. One string per clause.

- `verilog` is the full module source with the property assertion inline.

- `top_module` must match `module <name>` in the source. `clock` is the clock
  signal name.

- `antecedents` is the guard of P. If P is `if (count == 3'd0) assert (wptr == rptr);`
  the antecedent is `"count == 3'd0"`. If P is unconditional, use [].
  Prefer writing P with a guard, because real hardware properties are overwhelmingly
  conditional — an assertion about what must hold *when something happens*.

- `sanity_covers` must be genuinely reachable, e.g. `"count == 3'd2"` for a counter
  that gets there. Only checked when the property has an antecedent.

## Design idea

Tensil-style TCU microcode sequencer (module tcu_useq). It picks the next control-store address for the accelerator's instruction decoder (MatMul / DataMove / SIMD microroutines).

Inputs:
- clk, rst.
- en: idle/enable. When low, every state register holds.
- op[2:0]: INC=0, JMP=1, BR=2, CALL=3, RET=4.
- cond: branch condition.
- sel[1:0]: picks a jump-table entry.
- tw_en, tw_idx[1:0], tw_data[15:0]: write port for the jump table.

State registers (reset values in brackets):
- upc[15:0]: microprogram counter [0].
- jt[0:3][15:0]: 4-entry jump/branch target table, written through the tw_* port when en is high [0].
- ret_reg[15:0]: microsubroutine return register [0].
- ret_valid (1 bit): set means a return is pending [0].
- shadow_ret[15:0]: verification shadow holding the link address captured at the most recent CALL [0].
- pv (1 bit): past-valid flag, set to 1 after the first cycle.

Next-state rules (all apply only when en=1):
- INC: upc <= upc+1.
- JMP: upc <= jt[sel].
- BR: upc <= cond ? jt[sel] : upc+1.
- CALL: ret_reg <= upc+1, shadow_ret <= upc+1, ret_valid <= 1, upc <= jt[sel].
- RET with ret_valid=1: upc <= ret_reg, ret_valid <= 0.
- RET with ret_valid=0: upc <= upc+1.
The outputs are upc and ret_valid.

Relation R (holds by construction): ret_reg == shadow_ret. Both are written only on CALL, from the same upc+1 value, and both reset to 0.

Property P (precedence, global, $past style): a return-target address seen in upc must have been recorded earlier by a CALL.
  always @(posedge clk) if (pv && $past(en) && $past(op)==4 && $past(ret_valid)) assert (upc == $past(shadow_ret));

Why k-induction fails without R. Take this induction state:
- pv=1, ret_valid=1, ret_reg=16'h0040, shadow_ret=16'h0013.
- upc and jt arbitrary.
- The past-cycle registers record en=0.

It satisfies P, because the previous cycle was idle, so the antecedent is false. It violates R, since 0x0040 != 0x0013.

Holding en=0 for any number of cycles keeps all state frozen, and P stays vacuously true at each step. That yields an arbitrarily long P-satisfying prefix, so no depth k rules it out.

The next step is en=1, op=RET. Then upc becomes 0x0040 while $past(shadow_ret)=0x0013, so P fails.

With R supplied as a lemma, the RET step gives upc = old ret_reg = old shadow_ret. P then becomes 1-inductive.

## Size

Make the design's counters and data words 16-bit (wider only where a count needs more); if it stores several items, give that storage 4 entries.

Declare the design's registers and storage at this size, and size every
constant to match.

You write SystemVerilog modules for a formal verification dataset.

Each module is a "planted triple": a design containing an internal structural
relation R that holds by construction, plus a property P that is true of the design
but CANNOT be proven by k-induction unless the prover is also given R.

## The criterion

Three conditions, all required.

(1) P is true of the design.

(2) P is NOT inductive on its own. Concretely, there exists a state S such that:
      - S satisfies P
      - S violates R  (so S is unreachable in real operation, but a solver
        performing induction may start there)
      - S transitions in ONE step to a state that VIOLATES P

    S must also be a state the design can IDLE IN — one it can remain in for
    arbitrarily many cycles by holding the enable low. This matters: a one-step
    CTI only shows P is not 1-inductive, but the prover uses a 20-state window.
    If the design can stall in S, the solver builds a window of 20 copies of S and
    then takes the violating transition, so the property fails induction at ANY
    depth rather than only at depth 1. Without a stall, P may survive 20-induction
    and the triple is rejected.

    Condition (2) is the whole task. A property that is merely "weaker than R" is
    not enough. If every state satisfying P steps to another state satisfying P,
    then P is inductive by itself and the module is worthless for this dataset.

    Counterexample to avoid: if `count` is a 3-bit register, `count <= 7` is a
    consequence of any relation involving count, but it is trivially inductive
    because the register cannot hold anything larger. Rejected.

(3) P AND R TOGETHER ARE INDUCTIVE. R must be strong enough to exclude S and every
    state like it. It is not enough that R is true and P is weak — R must actually
    close the proof.

    R may be a conjunction of several clauses. The individual clauses do NOT each
    need to be inductive on their own; the requirement is that the conjunction,
    together with P, closes induction. Multi-clause relations are welcome and often
    necessary.

## Hard constraints on the Verilog

- These assertion forms are supported and all of them are welcome:
      always @(posedge clk) assert (expr);
      always @(*)           assert (expr);
      assert property (expr);                    // module level, NO clock inside
      always @(posedge clk) assert property (expr);
  `$past`, `$rose`, `$fell` and `$stable` work inside a clocked always block.
  Gate any `$past` check with a past-valid register so cycle zero is not judged:
      reg pv = 0;
      always @(posedge clk) pv <= 1;
      always @(posedge clk) if (pv) assert (out == $past(in));
- Do NOT put a clock inside the property: `assert property (@(posedge clk) ...)`,
  `disable iff`, `|->`, `|=>`, `##N`, `property ... endproperty`, `s_eventually`,
  sequences and `bind` are REJECTED by the toolchain — the module fails to parse
  and is never graded. Do not nest these functions either: `$past($rose(x))`
  fails to elaborate.
- Give every state register an `initial` value, so counterexamples are genuine
  from-reset traces rather than artifacts of an unconstrained start state.
- The design MUST have an enable or idle condition — an input that, when low, leaves
  all state unchanged (e.g. `i_ce`, `step`, or push and pop both low). Condition (2)
  depends on it: the state S must be one the design can sit in indefinitely.
- One property per module, unless the property style below asks for two.
- Never write `assume`. Assumptions are not checked and would let a false premise
  carry the proof.
- Never write `->` as logical implication in an expression — the toolchain rejects
  it. Write `!a || b` instead.
- If a register's declared width admits values it can never reach (e.g. a counter
  that saturates at 8 in a 4-bit reg), include an invariant bounding it — induction
  otherwise starts from an impossible value and fails on a phantom CTI.

## Output format

Your output is emitted through the API's structured-output mode — the schema is
enforced. Field order is deliberate: the reasoning fields come FIRST. Work out the
state S that breaks induction BEFORE writing the design, then write a design in
which that state is reachable-under-induction and the transition is real.

Field notes:

- `cti_reasoning`: one or two sentences: why this state satisfies P, why it
  violates R, and what its successor does that breaks P.

- `cti_state`: the state S from condition (2), as a list of {signal, value}
  pairs with concrete values. Every signal needed to evaluate both P and R must
  appear. Vague answers are rejected: "pointers disagree" is not acceptable;
  [{"signal": "count", "value": "3'd1"}, {"signal": "wptr", "value": "2'd2"},
  {"signal": "rptr", "value": "2'd0"}] is.

  Self-check before you answer: evaluate R at cti_state. It MUST come out false.
  If your named state does not violate your own invariant, you have contradicted
  yourself — fix one or the other.

- `invariants` is R. Supplied SEPARATELY from the Verilog — it must NOT appear as
  an assertion in the source. One string per clause.

- `verilog` is the full module source with the property assertion inline.

- `top_module` must match `module <name>` in the source. `clock` is the clock
  signal name.

- `antecedents` is the guard of P. If P is `if (count == 3'd0) assert (wptr == rptr);`
  the antecedent is `"count == 3'd0"`. If P is unconditional, use [].
  Prefer writing P with a guard, because real hardware properties are overwhelmingly
  conditional — an assertion about what must hold *when something happens*.

- `sanity_covers` must be genuinely reachable, e.g. `"count == 3'd2"` for a counter
  that gets there. Only checked when the property has an antecedent.

## Design idea

Module vcd_mac_learn: a 12-entry L2 learning table. Its reinterpreted VCD theme is a capture window restricted to a timestamp range, like the VCD time-range cut.

Inputs: clk, rst, en (when low, every register holds), learn_v, src_mac[31:0], src_port[3:0], look_v, dst_mac[31:0], age_tick, win_open (Q), win_close (R).

State registers:
- key[0:11][31:0]
- port[0:11][3:0]
- valid[0:11] (1 bit each)
- age[0:11] (1 bit each)
- rr_ptr[3:0], wraps 0..11
- learn_cnt[31:0]: the shadow register, a saturating count of learn events
- hit_q (1 bit): registered lookup hit
- out_port[3:0]
- win (1 bit): window register

Behaviour when en=1:
- Learn: if src_mac matches a valid entry, update its port and set its age bit. Otherwise write to the lowest invalid entry, or to entry rr_ptr if all are full, then advance rr_ptr. Set valid and age. learn_cnt increments, saturating at 32'hFFFFFFFF.
- Lookup: dst_mac is compared against all 12 valid keys in parallel. hit_q<=any match, and out_port<=the matching entry's port. A hit sets that entry's age bit.
- age_tick: entries with age=0 have valid cleared; all other age bits are cleared.
- Window: win<=1 on win_open and win<=0 on win_close (close wins on a tie). It can open and close any number of times.
- rst clears everything.

Relation R (holds by construction):
- for all i: valid[i] -> learn_cnt!=0
- hit_q -> learn_cnt!=0
It holds because valid bits are only ever set by a learn, the learn increments learn_cnt in the same cycle, and the saturating count never returns to 0.

Property P (precedence between Q and R, written as an edge check):
 assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (rst) (win && $rose(hit_q)) |-> (learn_cnt != 0));
In words: whenever a lookup hit rises inside the open window, some learn must have happened earlier.

State that satisfies P but violates R:
- valid[5]=1, key[5]=32'hA5A5_0001, port[5]=3
- learn_cnt=0, hit_q=0, win=1
- all other valid bits 0
P holds here because hit_q is not rising. With en=0 this state is frozen indefinitely, so arbitrarily long P-satisfying prefixes exist and k-induction cannot rule it out.

Step to violation: raise en with look_v=1 and dst_mac=32'hA5A5_0001 (no learn, no age_tick, no close). Next cycle hit_q rises while win=1 and learn_cnt==0, so P fails.

Why R is needed: P alone says nothing about valid bits, so the inductive step admits this unreachable state. Adding R as a strengthening invariant excludes it, because any valid entry forces learn_cnt!=0, and P becomes 1-inductive.

## Size

Make the design's counters and data words 32-bit (wider only where a count needs more); if it stores several items, give that storage 12 entries.

Declare the design's registers and storage at this size, and size every
constant to match.

The RISC-V architecture, an open-source ISA licensed under the Berkeley Software Distribution (BSD), has been gaining global recognition both in academic circles and in the market. - replay_ptr[4:0]: next slot to re-issue.

- log_cnt[63:0]: commands logged; a redundant shadow of issue_cnt.
- err_status[63:0]: error status register. Bit0 is a sticky counter-mismatch flag, bit1 is a sticky parity-alert flag, bits[63:32] hold the replay count.

You write SystemVerilog modules for a formal verification dataset.

Each module is a "planted triple": a design containing an internal structural
relation R that holds by construction, plus a property P that is true of the design
but CANNOT be proven by k-induction unless the prover is also given R.

## The criterion

Three conditions, all required.

(1) P is true of the design.

(2) P is NOT inductive on its own. Concretely, there exists a state S such that:
      - S satisfies P
      - S violates R  (so S is unreachable in real operation, but a solver
        performing induction may start there)
      - S transitions in ONE step to a state that VIOLATES P

    S must also be a state the design can IDLE IN — one it can remain in for
    arbitrarily many cycles by holding the enable low. This matters: a one-step
    CTI only shows P is not 1-inductive, but the prover uses a 20-state window.
    If the design can stall in S, the solver builds a window of 20 copies of S and
    then takes the violating transition, so the property fails induction at ANY
    depth rather than only at depth 1. Without a stall, P may survive 20-induction
    and the triple is rejected.

    Condition (2) is the whole task. A property that is merely "weaker than R" is
    not enough. If every state satisfying P steps to another state satisfying P,
    then P is inductive by itself and the module is worthless for this dataset.

    Counterexample to avoid: if `count` is a 3-bit register, `count <= 7` is a
    consequence of any relation involving count, but it is trivially inductive
    because the register cannot hold anything larger. Rejected.

(3) P AND R TOGETHER ARE INDUCTIVE. R must be strong enough to exclude S and every
    state like it. It is not enough that R is true and P is weak — R must actually
    close the proof.

    R may be a conjunction of several clauses. The individual clauses do NOT each
    need to be inductive on their own; the requirement is that the conjunction,
    together with P, closes induction. Multi-clause relations are welcome and often
    necessary.

## Hard constraints on the Verilog

- These assertion forms are supported and all of them are welcome:
      always @(posedge clk) assert (expr);
      always @(*)           assert (expr);
      assert property (expr);                    // module level, NO clock inside
      always @(posedge clk) assert property (expr);

  Gate any `$past` check with a past-valid register so cycle zero is not judged:
      reg pv = 0;
      always @(posedge clk) pv <= 1;
      always @(posedge clk) if (pv) assert (out == $past(in));

  sequences and `bind` are REJECTED by the toolchain — the module fails to parse
  and is never graded. Do not nest these functions either: `$past($rose(x))`
  fails to elaborate.
- Give every state register an `initial` value, so counterexamples are genuine
  from-reset traces rather than artifacts of an unconstrained start state.
- The design MUST have an enable or idle condition — an input that, when low, leaves
  all state unchanged (e.g. `i_ce`, `step`, or push and pop both low). Condition (2)
  depends on it: the state S must be one the design can sit in indefinitely.

  carry the proof.

  it. Write `!a || b` instead.
- If a register's declared width admits values it can never reach (e.g. a counter
  that saturates at 8 in a 4-bit reg), include an invariant bounding it — induction

Your output is emitted through the API's structured-output mode — the schema is
enforced. Field order is deliberate: the reasoning fields come FIRST. Work out the
state S that breaks induction BEFORE writing the design, then write a design in
which that state is reachable-under-induction and the transition is real.

  violates R, and what its successor does that breaks P.

  yourself — fix one or the other.

  an assertion in the source. One string per clause.

Stochastic parking-load estimator (sc_park_alu). It estimates combined car-park load from random bitstreams. - arm_seen (1 bit) and start_seen (1 bit): sticky flags.
- done_seen (1 bit).
- len_cnt[15:0]: stream-length counter.
- ones_cnt[15:0]: output-ones counter.
- log_q[0:7][15:0]: an 8-entry result log.
- log_ptr[2:0].

Behaviour when en=1:
- IDLE with arm_req: go to ARMED and set arm_seen.
- ARMED with start_req: go to RUN, set start_seen, and clear len_cnt and ones_cnt.

- (phase==RUN || phase==DONE) -> start_seen
- (len_cnt!=0) -> start_seen
- start_seen -> arm_seen
- done_seen -> start_seen
- ones_cnt <= len_cnt
- len_cnt <= 700

Make the design's counters and data words 16-bit (wider only where a count needs more); if it stores several items, give that storage 8 entries.

Declare the design's registers and storage at this size, and size every
constant to match.

  visitor budget on the boundary:

  |---|---|

  | 13:00 – 16:00 | 500 |

You write SystemVerilog modules for a formal verification dataset.

Each module is a "planted triple": a design containing an internal structural
relation R that holds by construction, plus a property P that is true of the design
but CANNOT be proven by k-induction unless the prover is also given R.

## The criterion

Three conditions, all required.

(1) P is true of the design.

(2) P is NOT inductive on its own. Concretely, there exists a state S such that:
      - S satisfies P
      - S violates R  (so S is unreachable in real operation, but a solver
        performing induction may start there)
      - S transitions in ONE step to a state that VIOLATES P

    S must also be a state the design can IDLE IN — one it can remain in for
    arbitrarily many cycles by holding the enable low. This matters: a one-step
    CTI only shows P is not 1-inductive, but the prover uses a 20-state window.
    If the design can stall in S, the solver builds a window of 20 copies of S and
    then takes the violating transition, so the property fails induction at ANY
    depth rather than only at depth 1. Without a stall, P may survive 20-induction
    and the triple is rejected.

    Condition (2) is the whole task. A property that is merely "weaker than R" is
    not enough. If every state satisfying P steps to another state satisfying P,
    then P is inductive by itself and the module is worthless for this dataset.

    Counterexample to avoid: if `count` is a 3-bit register, `count <= 7` is a
    consequence of any relation involving count, but it is trivially inductive
    because the register cannot hold anything larger. Rejected.

(3) P AND R TOGETHER ARE INDUCTIVE. R must be strong enough to exclude S and every
    state like it. It is not enough that R is true and P is weak — R must actually
    close the proof.

    R may be a conjunction of several clauses. The individual clauses do NOT each
    need to be inductive on their own; the requirement is that the conjunction,
    together with P, closes induction. Multi-clause relations are welcome and often
    necessary.

## Hard constraints on the Verilog

- These assertion forms are supported and all of them are welcome:
      always @(posedge clk) assert (expr);
      always @(*)           assert (expr);
      assert property (expr);                    // module level, NO clock inside
      always @(posedge clk) assert property (expr);
  `$past`, `$rose`, `$fell` and `$stable` work inside a clocked always block.
  Gate any `$past` check with a past-valid register so cycle zero is not judged:
      reg pv = 0;
      always @(posedge clk) pv <= 1;
      always @(posedge clk) if (pv) assert (out == $past(in));

Module mips_i2c_deglitch: a spike-filter front end for the I2C controller peripheral of a NaiveMIPS-style SoC. State registers:
- sh_scl[3:0], sh_sda[3:0]: 4-entry sample shift registers. Each cycle the line's input shifts in, and the line's sample is sh_x[3].
- st_scl, st_sda (1 bit each): stable-output registers, driven out as scl_o and sda_o.
- cnt_scl[7:0], cnt_sda[7:0]: per-line glitch-width counters.
- flen[7:0]: filter-length configuration register. Reset value is 3.
- armed (1 bit): sticky register.
- pv (1 bit): past-valid register.

Behaviour when en is high:
- Configuration write: if cfg_we, then flen <= (cfg_din > 12 ? 12 : cfg_din), and both counters are cleared.
- Line update otherwise, per line x:
  - If sh_x[3] differs from st_x and cnt_x >= flen, then st_x <= sh_x[3] and cnt_x <= 0.

- It satisfies P, since cnt_scl=12 <= 12.
- It violates R, since flen > 12.
- It can be held indefinitely with en=0, which supplies an arbitrarily long P-satisfying prefix for any induction depth k.

- started_seen (1 bit).

- sumA[15:0] and sumB[15:0]: Fletcher running sums.

- ARMED with in_valid: go to RUN, set started_seen<=1 and cnt<=1, and fold the word.

relation R that holds by construction, plus a property P that is true of the design
but CANNOT be proven by k-induction unless the prover is also given R.

## The criterion

Three conditions, all required.

(1) P is true of the design.

(2) P is NOT inductive on its own. Concretely, there exists a state S such that:
      - S satisfies P
      - S violates R  (so S is unreachable in real operation, but a solver
        performing induction may start there)
      - S transitions in ONE step to a state that VIOLATES P

    arbitrarily many cycles by holding the enable low. This matters: a one-step
    CTI only shows P is not 1-inductive, but the prover uses a 20-state window.
    If the design can stall in S, the solver builds a window of 20 copies of S and
    then takes the violating transition, so the property fails induction at ANY
    depth rather than only at depth 1. Without a stall, P may survive 20-induction
    and the triple is rejected.

    Condition (2) is the whole task. A property that is merely "weaker than R" is
    not enough. If every state satisfying P steps to another state satisfying P,
    then P is inductive by itself and the module is worthless for this dataset.

    Counterexample to avoid: if `count` is a 3-bit register, `count <= 7` is a
    consequence of any relation involving count, but it is trivially inductive
    because the register cannot hold anything larger. Rejected.

(3) P AND R TOGETHER ARE INDUCTIVE. R must be strong enough to exclude S and every
    state like it. It is not enough that R is true and P is weak — R must actually
    close the proof.

    R may be a conjunction of several clauses. The individual clauses do NOT each
    need to be inductive on their own; the requirement is that the conjunction,
    together with P, closes induction. Multi-clause relations are welcome and often
    necessary.

## Hard constraints on the Verilog

- These assertion forms are supported and all of them are welcome:
      always @(posedge clk) assert (expr);
      always @(*)           assert (expr);

      reg pv = 0;

  all state unchanged (e.g. `i_ce`, `step`, or push and pop both low). Condition (2)

prompt.content:
You write SystemVerilog modules for a formal verification dataset.

Each module is a "planted triple": a design containing an internal structural
relation R that holds by construction, plus a property P that is true of the design
but CANNOT be proven by k-induction unless the prover is also given R.

## The criterion

Three conditions, all required.

(1) P is true of the design.

(2) P is NOT inductive on its own. Concretely, there exists a state S such that:
      - S satisfies P
      - S violates R  (so S is unreachable in real operation, but a solver
        performing induction may start there)
      - S transitions in ONE step to a state that VIOLATES P

    S must also be a state the design can IDLE IN — one it can remain in for
    arbitrarily many cycles by holding the enable low. This matters: a one-step
    CTI only shows P is not 1-inductive, but the prover uses a 20-state window.
    If the design can stall in S, the solver builds a window of 20 copies of S and
    then takes the violating transition, so the property fails induction at ANY
    depth rather than only at depth 1. Without a stall, P may survive 20-induction
    and the triple is rejected.

    Condition (2) is the whole task. A property that is merely "weaker than R" is
    not enough. If every state satisfying P steps to another state satisfying P,
    then P is inductive by itself and the module is worthless for this dataset.

    Counterexample to avoid: if `count` is a 3-bit register, `count <= 7` is a
    consequence of any relation involving count, but it is trivially inductive
    because the register cannot hold anything larger. Rejected.

(3) P AND R TOGETHER ARE INDUCTIVE. R must be strong enough to exclude S and every
    state like it. It is not enough that R is true and P is weak — R must actually
    close the proof.

    R may be a conjunction of several clauses. The individual clauses do NOT each
    need to be inductive on their own; the requirement is that the conjunction,
    together with P, closes induction. Multi-clause relations are welcome and often
    necessary.

## Hard constraints on the Verilog

- These assertion forms are supported and all of them are welcome:
      always @(posedge clk) assert (expr);
      always @(*)           assert (expr);
      assert property (expr);                    // module level, NO clock inside
      always @(posedge clk) assert property (expr);
  `$past`, `$rose`, `$fell` and `$stable` work inside a clocked always block.
  Gate any `$past` check with a past-valid register so cycle zero is not judged:
      reg pv = 0;
      always @(posedge clk) pv <= 1;
      always @(posedge clk) if (pv) assert (out == $past(in));
- Do NOT put a clock inside the property: `assert property (@(posedge clk) ...)`,
  `disable iff`, `|->`, `|=>`, `##N`, `property ... endproperty`, `s_eventually`,
  sequences and `bind` are REJECTED by the toolchain — the module fails to parse
  and is never graded. Do not nest these functions either: `$past($rose(x))`
  fails to elaborate.
- Give every state register an `initial` value, so counterexamples are genuine
  from-reset traces rather than artifacts of an unconstrained start state.
- The design MUST have an enable or idle condition — an input that, when low, leaves
  all state unchanged (e.g. `i_ce`, `step`, or push and pop both low). Condition (2)
  depends on it: the state S must be one the design can sit in indefinitely.
- One property per module, unless the property style below asks for two.
- Never write `assume`. Assumptions are not checked and would let a false premise
  carry the proof.
- Never write `->` as logical implication in an expression — the toolchain rejects
  it. Write `!a || b` instead.
- If a register's declared width admits values it can never reach (e.g. a counter
  that saturates at 8 in a 4-bit reg), include an invariant bounding it — induction
  otherwise starts from an impossible value and fails on a phantom CTI.

## Output format

Your output is emitted through the API's structured-output mode — the schema is
enforced. Field order is deliberate: the reasoning fields come FIRST. Work out the
state S that breaks induction BEFORE writing the design, then write a design in
which that state is reachable-under-induction and the transition is real.

Field notes:

- `cti_reasoning`: one or two sentences: why this state satisfies P, why it
  violates R, and what its successor does that breaks P.

- `cti_state`: the state S from condition (2), as a list of {signal, value}
  pairs with concrete values. Every signal needed to evaluate both P and R must
  appear. Vague answers are rejected: "pointers disagree" is not acceptable;
  [{"signal": "count", "value": "3'd1"}, {"signal": "wptr", "value": "2'd2"},
  {"signal": "rptr", "value": "2'd0"}] is.

  Self-check before you answer: evaluate R at cti_state. It MUST come out false.
  If your named state does not violate your own invariant, you have contradicted
  yourself — fix one or the other.

- `invariants` is R. Supplied SEPARATELY from the Verilog — it must NOT appear as
  an assertion in the source. One string per clause.

- `verilog` is the full module source with the property assertion inline.

- `top_module` must match `module <name>` in the source. `clock` is the clock
  signal name.

- `antecedents` is the guard of P. If P is `if (count == 3'd0) assert (wptr == rptr);`
  the antecedent is `"count == 3'd0"`. If P is unconditional, use [].
  Prefer writing P with a guard, because real hardware properties are overwhelmingly
  conditional — an assertion about what must hold *when something happens*.

- `sanity_covers` must be genuinely reachable, e.g. `"count == 3'd2"` for a counter
  that gets there. Only checked when the property has an antecedent.

## Design idea

Module hls_pixclk_swallow: a pulse-swallow clock divider that generates the line-buffer pixel strobe for a Halide-HLS stencil pipeline. It combines a dual-modulus 8/9 prescaler, a program counter and a swallow counter, giving an overall ratio of N*8+S per output strobe.

Inputs: clk, rst, en (when low, every register holds), load, N[7:0], S[7:0].

State registers:
- pre_cnt[3:0]: prescaler count.
- p_cnt[7:0]: program count.
- s_cnt[7:0]: swallow count.
- n_reg[7:0], s_reg[7:0]: latched N and S.
- phase[1:0]: IDLE=0, ARMED=1, STARTED=2, DONE=3.
- armed_seen, started_seen: 1-bit step records.
- q_seen: 1-bit sticky scope register.

Behavior (all updates only when en=1):
- Prescaler: pre_cnt counts up and reaches terminal tc at 8 when s_cnt!=0 (divide by 9). Otherwise tc is at 7 (divide by 8). pre_cnt returns to 0 on tc.
- Counters: on tc, s_cnt decrements if it is nonzero, and p_cnt decrements. When p_cnt reaches 0, the module emits strobe and reloads p_cnt=n_reg, s_cnt=s_reg.
- load:
  - latches n_reg, s_reg, p_cnt, s_cnt and clears pre_cnt;
  - sets phase=ARMED and armed_seen=1, clears started_seen;
  - sets q_seen=1, which is never cleared afterwards (event Q = first load).
- Phase steps:
  - ARMED to STARTED on the first tc; only this transition sets started_seen=1.
  - STARTED to DONE when the decrement makes p_cnt hit 0 (the strobe).
  - DONE returns to ARMED only on load.
  - IDLE ignores tc.
- rst clears everything.

Relation R (holds by construction):
- (phase==STARTED || phase==DONE) -> started_seen.
- phase!=IDLE -> armed_seen.

Property P (chain precedence arm, then start, then finish, scoped after Q):
always @(*) assert (!(q_seen && phase==2'd3) || (started_seen && armed_seen));

Why k-induction fails without R:
- Take the state q_seen=1, phase=STARTED, armed_seen=1, started_seen=0, p_cnt=1, s_cnt=0, pre_cnt=7, with load=0.
- P holds there, because phase is not DONE.
- R is violated, because the phase is STARTED while started_seen=0.
- With en=0 the state is held indefinitely, so arbitrarily long induction prefixes all satisfy P.
- One step with en=1 and load=0 fires tc (pre_cnt==7 and s_cnt==0), decrements p_cnt to 0, and moves phase to DONE.
- started_seen stays 0, since only the ARMED-to-STARTED transition sets it. P is then violated.
- Adding R as a strengthening invariant makes P 1-inductive.

## Size

Make the design's counters and data words 8-bit (wider only where a count needs more); if it stores several items, give that storage 16 entries.

Declare the design's registers and storage at this size, and size every
constant to match.

## Worked example

{

With tick low the design idles here indefinitely; one tick then takes remaining to 0 while elapsed becomes 6, so the property fails in the next state.",
  "cti_state": [
    {
      "signal": "elapsed",
      "value": "64'd5"
    },
    {
      "signal": "remaining",
      "value": "64'd1"
    }
  ],
  "invariants": [
    "elapsed + remaining == 64'd48"
  ],
  "verilog": "module timer64 (\n    input wire clk,\n    input wire rst,\n    input wire tick,\n    output wire expired,\n    output wire [63:0] o_elapsed\n);\n    localparam [63:0] PERIOD = 64'd48;\n    reg [63:0] elapsed, remaining;\n    initial begin elapsed = 64'd0; remaining = PERIOD; end\n\n    always @(posedge clk) begin\n        if (rst) begin\n            elapsed <= 64'd0;\n            remaining <= PERIOD;\n        end else if (tick && remaining != 64'd0) begin\n            elapsed <= elapsed + 64'd1;\n            remaining <= remaining - 64'd1;\n        end\n    end\n\n    assign expired = (remaining == 64'd0);\n    assign o_elapsed = elapsed;\n\n    always @(posedge clk)\n        if (expired)\n            assert (elapsed == PERIOD);\nendmodule\n",
  "top_module": "timer64",
  "clock": "clk",
  "antecedents": [
    "remaining == 64'd0"
  ],
  "sanity_covers": [
    "remaining == 64'd40"
  ]
}

Inputs: clk, rst, en (holds ALL state when low), wr, wdata[63:0], q_start, r_stop.

State registers:

- dbi_q[7:0]: per-lane DBI flags for the current beat.
- plain_q[63:0]: restored data.
- beat_cnt[63:0]: count of write beats.
- win (1 bit): observation window.

Behaviour, only when en=1:
- Lane encoding: for lane i, zeros_i = 8 - popcount(wdata[8i+:8]). The flag f_i = (zeros_i > 4). The encoded lane is wdata lane ^ {8{f_i}}.

- Window: win <= q_start ? 1 : (r_stop ? 0 : win). Set wins if both are high.
- Read output: rdata = bus_q ^ X(dbi_q), which is combinational. X(d) replicates each d[i] across byte i.

# Issie - an Interactive Schematic Simulator with Integrated Editor

Issie (Interactive Schematic Simulator with Integrated Editor) is an application for digital circuit design and simulation. It is targeted at students and hobbyists that want to get a grasp of Digital Electronics concepts in a simple and fun way. Issie is designed to be beginner-friendly and guide the users toward their goals via clear error messages and visual clues. Issie is developed and actively used in teaching at Imperial College London.

* If you are just interested in using the application, jump to the [Getting Started](#getting-started) section. 
* If you want user documentation and news go to the [web pages](https://tomcl.github.io/issie/).
* If you are interested in a more detailed description of Issie please check out the [Wiki](https://github.com/tomcl/issie/wiki).

For more technical info about the project, read on. This documentation is partly based on the excellent [VisUAL2](https://github.com/ImperialCollegeLondon/Visual2) documentation, given the similarity in the technology stack used.

## Introduction

For the Issie website go [here](https://tomcl.github.io/issie/).

The application is mostly written in F#, which gets transpiled to JavaScript via the [Fable](https://fable.io/) compiler. [Electron](https://www.electronjs.org/) is then used to convert the developed web-app to a cross-platform application. Electron provides access to platform-level APIs (such as access to the file system) which would not be available to vanilla browser web-apps.

## Property pattern

Universality: a relation between the design's registers holds in every reachable state

## Property scope

after Q until R: keep a window register set by Q and cleared by R, where R may never arrive, so the property must hold from Q onwards whether or not the window ever closes. List the window register in antecedents.

## Property style

You write SystemVerilog modules for a formal verification dataset.

Each module is a "planted triple": a design containing an internal structural
relation R that holds by construction, plus a property P that is true of the design
but CANNOT be proven by k-induction unless the prover is also given R.

## The criterion

Three conditions, all required.

(1) P is true of the design.

(2) P is NOT inductive on its own. Concretely, there exists a state S such that:
      - S satisfies P
      - S violates R  (so S is unreachable in real operation, but a solver
        performing induction may start there)
      - S transitions in ONE step to a state that VIOLATES P

    S must also be a state the design can IDLE IN — one it can remain in for
    arbitrarily many cycles by holding the enable low. This matters: a one-step
    CTI only shows P is not 1-inductive, but the prover uses a 20-state window.
    If the design can stall in S, the solver builds a window of 20 copies of S and
    then takes the violating transition, so the property fails induction at ANY
    depth rather than only at depth 1. Without a stall, P may survive 20-induction
    and the triple is rejected.

    Condition (2) is the whole task. A property that is merely "weaker than R" is
    not enough. If every state satisfying P steps to another state satisfying P,
    then P is inductive by itself and the module is worthless for this dataset.

    Counterexample to avoid: if `count` is a 3-bit register, `count <= 7` is a
    consequence of any relation involving count, but it is trivially inductive
    because the register cannot hold anything larger. Rejected.

(3) P AND R TOGETHER ARE INDUCTIVE. R must be strong enough to exclude S and every
    state like it. It is not enough that R is true and P is weak — R must actually
    close the proof.

    R may be a conjunction of several clauses. The individual clauses do NOT each
    need to be inductive on their own; the requirement is that the conjunction,
    together with P, closes induction. Multi-clause relations are welcome and often
    necessary.

## Hard constraints on the Verilog

- These assertion forms are supported and all of them are welcome:
      always @(posedge clk) assert (expr);
      always @(*)           assert (expr);
      assert property (expr);                    // module level, NO clock inside
      always @(posedge clk) assert property (expr);
  `$past`, `$rose`, `$fell` and `$stable` work inside a clocked always block.
  Gate any `$past` check with a past-valid register so cycle zero is not judged:
      reg pv = 0;
      always @(posedge clk) pv <= 1;
      always @(posedge clk) if (pv) assert (out == $past(in));

  sequences and `bind` are REJECTED by the toolchain — the module fails to parse
  and is never graded. Do not nest these functions either: `$past($rose(x))`
  fails to elaborate.
- Give every state register an `initial` value, so counterexamples are genuine
  from-reset traces rather than artifacts of an unconstrained start state.
- The design MUST have an enable or idle condition — an input that, when low, leaves
  all state unchanged (e.g. `i_ce`, `step`, or push and pop both low). Condition (2)
  depends on it: the state S must be one the design can sit in indefinitely.

- Never write `assume`. Assumptions are not checked and would let a false premise
  carry the proof.
- Never write `->` as logical implication in an expression — the toolchain rejects
  it. Write `!a || b` instead.
- If a register's declared width admits values it can never reach (e.g. a counter
  that saturates at 8 in a 4-bit reg), include an invariant bounding it — induction
  otherwise starts from an impossible value and fails on a phantom CTI.
