# A Wishbone Controlled Scope for FPGA's

This is a generic/library routine for providing a bus accessed 'scope' or
(perhaps more appropriately) a bus accessed logic analyzer for use internal to
an FPGA.  The general operation is such that this 'scope' can record and report
on any 32 bit value transiting through the FPGA that you have connected to the
scope.  Once started and reset, the
scope records a copy of the input data every time the clock ticks with the
circuit enabled.  That is, it records these values up until the trigger.  Once
the trigger goes high, the scope will record for ``bw_holdoff`` more counts
before stopping.  Values may then be read from the buffer, oldest to most
recent.  After reading, the scope may then be reset for another run.

In general, therefore, operation happens in this fashion:

1. A reset is issued.
2. Recording starts, in a circular buffer, and continues until
3. The trigger line is asserted.
  The scope registers the asserted trigger by setting the ``o_triggered`` output flag.
4. A counter then ticks until the last value is written.
  The scope registers that it has stopped recording by setting the ``o_stopped`` output flag.
5. The scope recording is then paused until the next reset.
6. While stopped, the CPU can read the data from the scope

  - oldest to most recent
  - one value per bus clock

7. Writes to the data register reset the address to the beginning of the buffer

SCAMP is my homebrew 16-bit CPU. It stands for something like "Simple Computing and Arithmetic Microcoded Processor".

# Video Filtering on Artix-7 FPGA

__Description:__

This project implements a video processing pipeline that captures video data from an OV7670 camera and applies a Gaussian lowpass filter and a Sobel edge detection filter. 

Users can use the buttons and switches on the dev board to interact with the video processing system.
- Video processing can be toggled on and off (video passthrough)
- Gaussian and Sobel filters can be enabled or disabled seperately
- Sobel filter thresholding can be changed by using the board buttons.

The project is completed; more documentation to come when I have time.

__High-level Overview:__

- The system is comprised of a camera interface block, preprocessing block, and gaussian and sobel filtering blocks.
- Processed video data is stored into a framebuffer synthesized as block memory where it is retrieved for display over HDMI.
- In RGB video passthrough mode, pixels are represented in RGB444 format and extended to RGB888 for TMDS encoding.
- In video processing modes, pixels are represented as eight-bit greyscale values. 
- Display format is 640x480 30FPS.

__Camera Interface:__

- The camera interface configures the OV7670 camera via i2c and captures pixel data (RGB444) into an asynchronous FIFO.

__Preprocessing (RGB to Greyscale):__

- The preprocessing block converts RGB444 to greyscale for filtering. It uses the algorithm ```y = 0.299*R + 0.587*G + 0.114*B```.

## Technical Report

1. [CARRV2020 Paper](https://carrv.github.io/2020/papers/CARRV2020_paper_5_MV.pdf)

## About Posit Arithmetic
Universal Numbers, or unums, are a collection of number systems which features better efficiency and mathematically correct arithmetic properties compared to the IEEE-754 floating-point standard. Unums are capable of expressing real numbers and ranges of real numbers. The newest version Unum Type-III called [Posits] is a hardware-friendly representation designed as a drop-in replacement for IEEE floats.

Posits behave much like a floating-point number of fixed size, rounding to the nearest expressible value if the result of a calculation is not expressible exactly. It offers more accuracy, and a larger dynamic range than IEEE floats with the same number of bits. Posit arithmetic tries to resolve the short-comings of IEEE floats using a dynamic representation that minimizes unusable representations and exceptional cases.

PyFPGA is an abstraction layer for working with FPGA development tools in a vendor-agnostic, programmatic way. It is a Python package that provides:

* It provides a unified API between tools/devices.

* It ensures reproducibility and repeatability.

## 简介

JSON是应用广泛的一种数据表示格式, 常用于进程间复杂数据的交互. 

多年以前我在网络上发现了某前辈发布的JSON教程, 开始接触到JSON, 后面陆续开始基于JSON开发了一些小规模工具. 作为一名验证工程师, 将验证平台真正的加入到JSON生态中, 是很久远的一个想法了, 这是JSONinSV这个项目的由来.

这个项目的目的是提供SystemVerilog实现的JSON解析库和生成库, 实现和外围组件的更有目的性的互动, 帮助使用者开发出更灵活更强大的验证应用.

此外, 本项目还提供了JSON库的单元测试, 后续可考虑将这里的单元测试框架独立出来进行项目上的应用.

## Reference

1. [ECMA-404](https://www.ecma-international.org/publications/files/ECMA-ST/ECMA-404.pdf)
1. [RFC-8259](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8259.txt)
1. [json-tutorial](https://github.com/miloyip/json-tutorial)
1. IEEE1800-IEEE Standard for SystemVerilog

## 规格介绍

JSONinSV实现的功能规格主要是三个部分:

1. JSON文本的解析, 包括从字符串解析和文本文件解析;
2. JSON文本输出, 支持JSON顶层值输出到格式化字符串以及输出到文本文件;
3. 支持JSON值的编辑;

对应JSON的值类型, JSONinSV的实现规格如下:

1. `true, false, null`只支持直接对应的小写字面值;
2. 字符串. 理论上支持任意编码格式的字符串, 但是为了EDA工具的兼容性, 用户应当尽量使用纯ASCII字符集. 结合IEEE1800 5.9节以及RFC8259的第9章, JSONinSV支持的转义字符有:
```
"\""
"\\"
"\n"
"\t"
"\f"
```
3. 数字统一解析为SystemVerilog中的real类型, 即IEEE574定义的64bit双精度浮点数. 需要支持大整数和高精度数据等超过64bit双精度浮点数表示的数据时, 建议用户使用字符串表示数值并在上层应用中实现.
4. 列表, 支持空列表.
5. 对象, 支持空对象. 对于key重复的值, 会使用后面的key-value成员进行覆盖. **需要注意的是, JSONinSV目前直接使用SystemVerilog的联合数组实现对象, 因此JSON文本中的对象成员会经过key排序存放, 不能保证存放顺序与JSON文本中成员一致.**

文本输出和对象编辑器部分, 支持如下规格:

1. 支持格式化输出, 并支持配置indent进行层级化排版输出;
2. 支持复合节点的回环检查;

# Transactron

Transactron is a library for [Amaranth HDL](https://amaranth-lang.org/) which makes designing complex digital designs easier.
It provides an abstraction for ready/valid handshake signals, automatically generates arbitration circuits, and presents an intuitive, object-oriented-like interface to the circuit designer.
The main advantages of using Transactron are:

* Abstracted handshake signalling makes it easier to design complex, latency-insensitive, pipelined circuits.
* Object-oriented-like interface allows to encapsulate complex behavior of a module and present a simple interface for its users.
  The syntax used is friendly for people coming from software development background.
* Thanks to auto-generated arbitrators and a rich library of reusable components, refactoring circuits is powerful and requires less effort.
  For example, when constructing pipelines, switching between lock-step, FIFO-coupled or combinational connection is as simple as switching a connector module.

## Design idea

Module tapeout_i2f: an 8-bit unsigned integer to 8-bit minifloat converter (4-bit exponent, 3-bit mantissa, round-to-nearest-even), styled as a tape-out flow. It is gated by a three-step chain: arm (capture the operand), then start (normalize), then finish (round into the output register). All state holds when input en is low.

Inputs: clk, en, arm, start, din[7:0], q_sess (Q, session open), r_sess (R, session close).

State registers:
- phase[1:0]: IDLE=0, ARMED=1, NORM=2, DONE=3.
- arm_f (1 bit) and start_f (1 bit): chain history flags.
- mant[7:0]: the working mantissa.
- exp[3:0]: the exponent.
- fout[7:0]: the optional output register.
- fin (1 bit): registered finish pulse.
- win (1 bit): the session window.

Behaviour when en=1:
- q_sess sets win=1, clears arm_f and start_f, sets phase=IDLE and fin=0. r_sess clears win and may never arrive.
- In IDLE, arm loads mant<=din and exp<=7, sets arm_f=1 and phase=ARMED.
- In ARMED, start sets start_f=1 and phase=NORM.
- In NORM, while mant!=0 and mant[7]==0, mant shifts left and exp decrements. Otherwise phase goes to DONE, fin<=1, and fout<={exp, rounded mant[6:4]}. Rounding uses guard bit mant[3] and sticky bits mant[2:0], and saturates on mantissa carry.
- In DONE, fin<=0 and the next arm restarts the chain. arm_f and start_f are never cleared except by q_sess.

Relation R (holds by construction):
(phase>=NORM -> start_f) && (start_f -> arm_f) && (phase!=IDLE -> arm_f).

Property P (chain precedence, scope after Q until R, $past style):

reg pv=0; always @(posedge clk) pv<=1;
always @(posedge clk) if (pv && win && $past(win) && fin) assert($past(arm_f) && $past(start_f));

In words: inside the window, an observed finish implies that arm and start both happened before it.

Why k-induction fails without R: consider the state phase=NORM, mant=8'h80, arm_f=0, start_f=0, win=1, fin=0, en=0, pv=1.
- P holds there, because fin=0.
- R is violated, because phase is NORM while start_f=0.
- The state is held indefinitely while en=0, since everything freezes. This gives an arbitrarily long P-satisfying prefix.
- Raising en=1 with no q_sess or r_sess moves the design to DONE with fin=1, because mant[7]=1. In that cycle win=1 and $past(win)=1, but $past(arm_f)=0, so P fails.

So P is true from reset only because R holds, and an inductive proof needs R as a strengthening invariant.

Each module is a "planted triple": a design containing an internal structural
relation R that holds by construction, plus a property P that is true of the design
but CANNOT be proven by k-induction unless the prover is also given R.

## The criterion

Three conditions, all required.

(1) P is true of the design.

(2) P is NOT inductive on its own. Concretely, there exists a state S such that:
      - S satisfies P
      - S violates R  (so S is unreachable in real operation, but a solver
        performing induction may start there)
      - S transitions in ONE step to a state that VIOLATES P

    arbitrarily many cycles by holding the enable low. This matters: a one-step
    CTI only shows P is not 1-inductive, but the prover uses a 20-state window.
    If the design can stall in S, the solver builds a window of 20 copies of S and
    then takes the violating transition, so the property fails induction at ANY
    depth rather than only at depth 1. Without a stall, P may survive 20-induction
    and the triple is rejected.

    Condition (2) is the whole task. A property that is merely "weaker than R" is
    not enough. If every state satisfying P steps to another state satisfying P,
    then P is inductive by itself and the module is worthless for this dataset.

    Counterexample to avoid: if `count` is a 3-bit register, `count <= 7` is a
    consequence of any relation involving count, but it is trivially inductive
    because the register cannot hold anything larger. Rejected.

(3) P AND R TOGETHER ARE INDUCTIVE. R must be strong enough to exclude S and every
    state like it. It is not enough that R is true and P is weak — R must actually
    close the proof.

    R may be a conjunction of several clauses. The individual clauses do NOT each
    need to be inductive on their own; the requirement is that the conjunction,
    together with P, closes induction. Multi-clause relations are welcome and often
    necessary.

## Hard constraints on the Verilog

- These assertion forms are supported and all of them are welcome:
      always @(posedge clk) assert (expr);
      always @(*)           assert (expr);
      assert property (expr);                    // module level, NO clock inside
      always @(posedge clk) assert property (expr);
  `$past`, `$rose`, `$fell` and `$stable` work inside a clocked always block.
  Gate any `$past` check with a past-valid register so cycle zero is not judged:
      reg pv = 0;
      always @(posedge clk) pv <= 1;
      always @(posedge clk) if (pv) assert (out == $past(in));
- Do NOT put a clock inside the property: `assert property (@(posedge clk) ...)`,
  `disable iff`, `|->`, `|=>`, `##N`, `property ... endproperty`, `s_eventually`,
  sequences and `bind` are REJECTED by the toolchain — the module fails to parse
  and is never graded. Do not nest these functions either: `$past($rose(x))`
  fails to elaborate.
- Give every state register an `initial` value, so counterexamples are genuine
  from-reset traces rather than artifacts of an unconstrained start state.
- The design MUST have an enable or idle condition — an input that, when low, leaves
  all state unchanged (e.g. `i_ce`, `step`, or push and pop both low). Condition (2)
  depends on it: the state S must be one the design can sit in indefinitely.

- Never write `assume`. Assumptions are not checked and would let a false premise
  carry the proof.
- Never write `->` as logical implication in an expression — the toolchain rejects
  it. Write `!a || b` instead.

  that saturates at 8 in a 4-bit reg), include an invariant bounding it — induction

enforced. Field order is deliberate: the reasoning fields come FIRST. Work out the
state S that breaks induction BEFORE writing the design, then write a design in
which that state is reachable-under-induction and the transition is real.

  violates R, and what its successor does that breaks P.

Ports: clk, rst, en (when low, all state holds), req, lblk[4:0]; outputs busy and done.

State registers:
- map_mem[0:31], 5-bit each (physical index)
- erase_cnt[0:31], 16-bit each
- busy, 1-bit
- scan_idx, 6-bit
- countdown, 6-bit
- best_idx, 5-bit
- best_cnt, 16-bit
- tgt, 5-bit (latched lblk)

- Reset: busy=0, scan_idx=0, countdown=0, map_mem[i]=i, erase_cnt[i]=0.
- Accept (en && req && !busy): busy=1, tgt=lblk, scan_idx=0, countdown=33, best_cnt=16'hFFFF.
- Scan step (en && busy && scan_idx<32): if erase_cnt[scan_idx] < best_cnt, set best_idx=scan_idx and best_cnt=erase_cnt[scan_idx]. Then scan_idx++ and countdown--.

- Take the state busy=1, scan_idx=5, countdown=1, with arbitrary memory contents.
- P holds, since countdown != 0.
- R is violated, since 1 != 33-5.
- With en=0 the state is held unchanged for any number of cycles, so arbitrarily long P-satisfying induction prefixes exist.

Such a state is unreachable: from reset, countdown and scan_idx move in lockstep from 33/0, so countdown reaches 1 exactly when scan_idx==32, and that commit cycle clears busy. Supplying R as a strengthening invariant makes P 1-inductive. The 32 x 16-bit erase-count memory and map memory are irrelevant to P but enlarge the state space.

Make the design's counters and data words 16-bit (wider only where a count needs more); if it stores several items, give that storage 32 entries.

Declare the design's registers and storage at this size, and size every
constant to match.

  "cti_state": [
    {
      "signal": "sa",
      "value": "32'h40000000"
    },
    {
      "signal": "sb",
      "value": "32'h00000000"
    }
  ],
  "invariants": [

  ],

  "top_module": "kitest",
  "clock": "i_clk",
  "antecedents": [],
  "sanity_covers": [
    "sa[0] == 1'b1"
  ]
}

Each module is a "planted triple": a design containing an internal structural
relation R that holds by construction, plus a property P that is true of the design
but CANNOT be proven by k-induction unless the prover is also given R.

## The criterion

Three conditions, all required.

(1) P is true of the design.

(2) P is NOT inductive on its own. Concretely, there exists a state S such that:
      - S satisfies P
      - S violates R  (so S is unreachable in real operation, but a solver
        performing induction may start there)
      - S transitions in ONE step to a state that VIOLATES P

    S must also be a state the design can IDLE IN — one it can remain in for
    arbitrarily many cycles by holding the enable low. This matters: a one-step
    CTI only shows P is not 1-inductive, but the prover uses a 20-state window.
    If the design can stall in S, the solver builds a window of 20 copies of S and
    then takes the violating transition, so the property fails induction at ANY
    depth rather than only at depth 1. Without a stall, P may survive 20-induction
    and the triple is rejected.

    Condition (2) is the whole task. A property that is merely "weaker than R" is
    not enough. If every state satisfying P steps to another state satisfying P,
    then P is inductive by itself and the module is worthless for this dataset.

    Counterexample to avoid: if `count` is a 3-bit register, `count <= 7` is a
    consequence of any relation involving count, but it is trivially inductive
    because the register cannot hold anything larger. Rejected.

(3) P AND R TOGETHER ARE INDUCTIVE. R must be strong enough to exclude S and every
    state like it. It is not enough that R is true and P is weak — R must actually
    close the proof.

    R may be a conjunction of several clauses. The individual clauses do NOT each
    need to be inductive on their own; the requirement is that the conjunction,
    together with P, closes induction. Multi-clause relations are welcome and often
    necessary.

## Hard constraints on the Verilog

- These assertion forms are supported and all of them are welcome:
      always @(posedge clk) assert (expr);
      always @(*)           assert (expr);
      assert property (expr);                    // module level, NO clock inside
      always @(posedge clk) assert property (expr);

  Gate any `$past` check with a past-valid register so cycle zero is not judged:
      reg pv = 0;
      always @(posedge clk) pv <= 1;
      always @(posedge clk) if (pv) assert (out == $past(in));

  sequences and `bind` are REJECTED by the toolchain — the module fails to parse
  and is never graded. Do not nest these functions either: `$past($rose(x))`
  fails to elaborate.
- Give every state register an `initial` value, so counterexamples are genuine
  from-reset traces rather than artifacts of an unconstrained start state.
- The design MUST have an enable or idle condition — an input that, when low, leaves
  all state unchanged (e.g. `i_ce`, `step`, or push and pop both low). Condition (2)
  depends on it: the state S must be one the design can sit in indefinitely.
- One property per module, unless the property style below asks for two.
- Never write `assume`. Assumptions are not checked and would let a false premise
  carry the proof.
- Never write `->` as logical implication in an expression — the toolchain rejects
  it. Write `!a || b` instead.
- If a register's declared width admits values it can never reach (e.g. a counter
  that saturates at 8 in a 4-bit reg), include an invariant bounding it — induction

Your output is emitted through the API's structured-output mode — the schema is
enforced. Field order is deliberate: the reasoning fields come FIRST. Work out the
state S that breaks induction BEFORE writing the design, then write a design in
which that state is reachable-under-induction and the transition is real.

  violates R, and what its successor does that breaks P.

  pairs with concrete values. Every signal needed to evaluate both P and R must
  appear. Vague answers are rejected: "pointers disagree" is not acceptable;

  {"signal": "rptr", "value": "2'd0"}] is.

  If your named state does not violate your own invariant, you have contradicted
  yourself — fix one or the other.

- `invariants` is R. Supplied SEPARATELY from the Verilog — it must NOT appear as
  an assertion in the source. One string per clause.

- `verilog` is the full module source with the property assertion inline.

- `top_module` must match `module <name>` in the source. `clock` is the clock

- `antecedents` is the guard of P. If P is `if (count == 3'd0) assert (wptr == rptr);`

  conditional — an assertion about what must hold *when something happens*.

- `sanity_covers` must be genuinely reachable, e.g. `"count == 3'd2"` for a counter

- mode_q[1:0]: 0=1x32, 1=2x16, 2=4x8.
- a_q[31:0] and b_q[31:0]: operand registers, loaded when ld.
- res_q[63:0]: lane-packed product. In 2x16 mode each lane gives a 32-bit product at bits [32i+31:32i]. In 4x8 mode each lane gives a 16-bit product at bits [16i+15:16i]. In 1x32 mode it is the full 64-bit product.
- buf_q[0:3][63:0]: the result buffer.
- valid_q[3:0]: slot-occupied mask.
- occ_q[31:0]: occupancy counter.
- win_q (1 bit): observation window.

- Pop is accepted when pop && |valid_q. It clears the lowest set valid bit and decrements occ_q.

Giving the prover R (occ_q == popcount(valid_q)) excludes this state. With R, P becomes 1-inductive.

Make the design's counters and data words 32-bit (wider only where a count needs more); if it stores several items, give that storage 4 entries.

Declare the design's registers and storage at this size, and size every
constant to match.

Each module is a "planted triple": a design containing an internal structural
relation R that holds by construction, plus a property P that is true of the design
but CANNOT be proven by k-induction unless the prover is also given R.

## The criterion

Three conditions, all required.

(1) P is true of the design.

(2) P is NOT inductive on its own. Concretely, there exists a state S such that:
      - S satisfies P
      - S violates R  (so S is unreachable in real operation, but a solver
        performing induction may start there)
      - S transitions in ONE step to a state that VIOLATES P

    S must also be a state the design can IDLE IN — one it can remain in for
    arbitrarily many cycles by holding the enable low. This matters: a one-step
    CTI only shows P is not 1-inductive, but the prover uses a 20-state window.
    If the design can stall in S, the solver builds a window of 20 copies of S and
    then takes the violating transition, so the property fails induction at ANY
    depth rather than only at depth 1. Without a stall, P may survive 20-induction
    and the triple is rejected.

    Condition (2) is the whole task. A property that is merely "weaker than R" is
    not enough. If every state satisfying P steps to another state satisfying P,
    then P is inductive by itself and the module is worthless for this dataset.

    Counterexample to avoid: if `count` is a 3-bit register, `count <= 7` is a
    consequence of any relation involving count, but it is trivially inductive
    because the register cannot hold anything larger. Rejected.

(3) P AND R TOGETHER ARE INDUCTIVE. R must be strong enough to exclude S and every
    state like it. It is not enough that R is true and P is weak — R must actually
    close the proof.

    R may be a conjunction of several clauses. The individual clauses do NOT each
    need to be inductive on their own; the requirement is that the conjunction,
    together with P, closes induction. Multi-clause relations are welcome and often
    necessary.

## Hard constraints on the Verilog

- These assertion forms are supported and all of them are welcome:
      always @(posedge clk) assert (expr);
      always @(*)           assert (expr);
      assert property (expr);                    // module level, NO clock inside
      always @(posedge clk) assert property (expr);

  Gate any `$past` check with a past-valid register so cycle zero is not judged:
      reg pv = 0;
      always @(posedge clk) pv <= 1;
      always @(posedge clk) if (pv) assert (out == $past(in));
- Do NOT put a clock inside the property: `assert property (@(posedge clk) ...)`,
  `disable iff`, `|->`, `|=>`, `##N`, `property ... endproperty`, `s_eventually`,
  sequences and `bind` are REJECTED by the toolchain — the module fails to parse
  and is never graded. Do not nest these functions either: `$past($rose(x))`
  fails to elaborate.
- Give every state register an `initial` value, so counterexamples are genuine
  from-reset traces rather than artifacts of an unconstrained start state.
- The design MUST have an enable or idle condition — an input that, when low, leaves
  all state unchanged (e.g. `i_ce`, `step`, or push and pop both low). Condition (2)

  carry the proof.

MAX = 24 is the longest run per pair, matching a 24-entry decompressor buffer.

State registers:
- cur[15:0]: current run value.
- cnt[15:0]: current run length.
- dl[15:0]: countdown of beats left before a forced flush.
- busy (1 bit): a run is outstanding.
- pre_drain (1 bit): resets to 1 and is cleared on the first enabled cycle with drain=1.
- pv (1 bit): past-valid flag.

- Start a run (idle with in_valid): cur<=in_data, cnt<=1, dl<=MAX, busy<=1.
- Busy, in_valid, in_data==cur and cnt<MAX: cnt<=cnt+1, dl<=dl-1.
- Busy, in_valid and (in_data!=cur or cnt==MAX): emit (cur, cnt) with out_valid=1, then restart the run with cnt<=1, dl<=MAX, cur<=in_data.

  reg pv = 0; always @(posedge clk) pv <= 1;

- It satisfies P, since dl != 0.
- It violates R, since cnt+dl = 11 != 25.
- It can be held for any number of cycles with en=0, which defeats k-induction for every k.
- With en=1, in_valid=1, in_data=16'h0000 and drain=0: the input matches and cnt=10 < MAX, so the next state is cnt=11, dl=0 with busy=1.
- On the following edge, $past(busy)=1 and $past(dl)=0, so P fails.
Supplying R as a lemma excludes this state and makes P 1-inductive.

## History

Back in 1992 the original [Berkeley Packet Filter (BPF)](http://www.tcpdump.org/papers/bpf-usenix93.pdf)
was designed
for capturing and filtering network packets that matched
specific rules. Filters are implemented as programs to be run
on a register-based virtual RISC machine providing a small
number of instructions inside the Linux Kernel.

Soon it became clear that extending the Kernel by
user-supplied programs proves to be useful. But the design of
the virtual machine e.g instruction set (ISA) or register
width (32-bit vs. 64-bit) couldn't keep up with the demands.

At some point [in 2014](https://lwn.net/Articles/599755/),
work to extend the existing BPF virtual machine started to
make it useful in other parts of the Linux Kernel. More,
wider registers, additional instructions and a JIT eventually
resulted in [extended BPF](https://ebpf.io/). The original
and now obsolete BPF version has been retroactively renamed
to __classic BPF (cBPF)__. Nowadays, the Linux Kernel runs
eBPF only and loaded cBPF bytecode is transparently
translated into eBPF before execution.

Further information can be found in the
[eBPF specification](https://github.com/ebpffoundation/ebpf-docs) or in the [Linux Kernel documentation](https://docs.kernel.org/bpf/index.html).

The *hBPF* project now implements most of eBPF features in
hardware (FPGA).

## The criterion

Three conditions, all required.

(1) P is true of the design.

(2) P is NOT inductive on its own. Concretely, there exists a state S such that:
      - S satisfies P
      - S violates R  (so S is unreachable in real operation, but a solver
        performing induction may start there)
      - S transitions in ONE step to a state that VIOLATES P

    arbitrarily many cycles by holding the enable low. This matters: a one-step
    CTI only shows P is not 1-inductive, but the prover uses a 20-state window.
    If the design can stall in S, the solver builds a window of 20 copies of S and
    then takes the violating transition, so the property fails induction at ANY
    depth rather than only at depth 1. Without a stall, P may survive 20-induction
    and the triple is rejected.

    Condition (2) is the whole task. A property that is merely "weaker than R" is
    not enough. If every state satisfying P steps to another state satisfying P,
    then P is inductive by itself and the module is worthless for this dataset.

    Counterexample to avoid: if `count` is a 3-bit register, `count <= 7` is a
    consequence of any relation involving count, but it is trivially inductive
    because the register cannot hold anything larger. Rejected.

    state like it. It is not enough that R is true and P is weak — R must actually
    close the proof.

    R may be a conjunction of several clauses. The individual clauses do NOT each
    need to be inductive on their own; the requirement is that the conjunction,
    together with P, closes induction. Multi-clause relations are welcome and often
    necessary.

## Hard constraints on the Verilog

- These assertion forms are supported and all of them are welcome:
      always @(posedge clk) assert (expr);
      always @(*)           assert (expr);
      assert property (expr);                    // module level, NO clock inside

Each module is a "planted triple": a design containing an internal structural
relation R that holds by construction, plus a property P that is true of the design
but CANNOT be proven by k-induction unless the prover is also given R.

## The criterion

Three conditions, all required.

(1) P is true of the design.

(2) P is NOT inductive on its own. Concretely, there exists a state S such that:
      - S satisfies P
      - S violates R  (so S is unreachable in real operation, but a solver
        performing induction may start there)
      - S transitions in ONE step to a state that VIOLATES P

    S must also be a state the design can IDLE IN — one it can remain in for
    arbitrarily many cycles by holding the enable low. This matters: a one-step
    CTI only shows P is not 1-inductive, but the prover uses a 20-state window.
    If the design can stall in S, the solver builds a window of 20 copies of S and
    then takes the violating transition, so the property fails induction at ANY
    depth rather than only at depth 1. Without a stall, P may survive 20-induction
    and the triple is rejected.

    Condition (2) is the whole task. A property that is merely "weaker than R" is
    not enough. If every state satisfying P steps to another state satisfying P,
    then P is inductive by itself and the module is worthless for this dataset.

    Counterexample to avoid: if `count` is a 3-bit register, `count <= 7` is a
    consequence of any relation involving count, but it is trivially inductive
    because the register cannot hold anything larger. Rejected.

(3) P AND R TOGETHER ARE INDUCTIVE. R must be strong enough to exclude S and every
    state like it. It is not enough that R is true and P is weak — R must actually
    close the proof.

    R may be a conjunction of several clauses. The individual clauses do NOT each
    need to be inductive on their own; the requirement is that the conjunction,
    together with P, closes induction. Multi-clause relations are welcome and often
    necessary.

## Hard constraints on the Verilog

- These assertion forms are supported and all of them are welcome:
      always @(posedge clk) assert (expr);
      always @(*)           assert (expr);
      assert property (expr);                    // module level, NO clock inside
      always @(posedge clk) assert property (expr);

  Gate any `$past` check with a past-valid register so cycle zero is not judged:
      reg pv = 0;
      always @(posedge clk) pv <= 1;
      always @(posedge clk) if (pv) assert (out == $past(in));
- Do NOT put a clock inside the property: `assert property (@(posedge clk) ...)`,
  `disable iff`, `|->`, `|=>`, `##N`, `property ... endproperty`, `s_eventually`,
  sequences and `bind` are REJECTED by the toolchain — the module fails to parse
  and is never graded. Do not nest these functions either: `$past($rose(x))`
  fails to elaborate.
- Give every state register an `initial` value, so counterexamples are genuine
  from-reset traces rather than artifacts of an unconstrained start state.
- The design MUST have an enable or idle condition — an input that, when low, leaves
  all state unchanged (e.g. `i_ce`, `step`, or push and pop both low). Condition (2)
  depends on it: the state S must be one the design can sit in indefinitely.

- Never write `assume`. Assumptions are not checked and would let a false premise
  carry the proof.
- Never write `->` as logical implication in an expression — the toolchain rejects
  it. Write `!a || b` instead.
- If a register's declared width admits values it can never reach (e.g. a counter
  that saturates at 8 in a 4-bit reg), include an invariant bounding it — induction

enforced. Field order is deliberate: the reasoning fields come FIRST. Work out the
state S that breaks induction BEFORE writing the design, then write a design in

  violates R, and what its successor does that breaks P.

  conditional — an assertion about what must hold *when something happens*.

  that gets there. Only checked when the property has an antecedent.

## Design idea

Module yat_phase_ring: the phase sequencer of a toy 3-stage RISC-V pipeline (fetch/decode/execute, YatCPU-style). It keeps two 32-bit Johnson ring counters that should always agree. One is the fetch-side phase token and the other is the execute-side shadow that the hazard unit checks.

Ports: clk, rst (synchronous, active high), advance (enable; when low, all state holds), and outputs fetch_phase[31:0] and exec_phase[31:0].

State registers:
- fetch_ring [31:0]
- exec_ring [31:0]

Behaviour:
- On reset both registers become 32'h0.
- When advance is high, both take the Johnson step: ring <= {ring[30:0], ~ring[31]}. The inverted MSB feeds back into bit 0, giving a 64-state cycle.
- When advance is low, both hold.
- The two rings use separate but identical update logic, with no cross-coupling.

Relation R (holds by construction): fetch_ring == exec_ring, all 32 bits equal in every reachable state. Both start at 0 and always apply the same deterministic step under the same enable.

Property P (universality, global, unclocked module-level form):
assert property (fetch_ring[31] == exec_ring[31]);
The MSBs of the two rings always match. This is the bit the hazard unit samples to tell first-half phases from second-half phases.

Why P needs R: P only constrains bit 31, but the next value of bit 31 is the current bit 30. P alone therefore cannot rule out a disagreement in a lower bit that later shifts up into bit 31.

- It violates R, since bit 30 differs.
- With advance = 0 this state can be held for any number of cycles, so every prefix of a k-induction trace satisfies P. This defeats induction at any depth k.
- On the next cycle with advance = 1, fetch_ring becomes 32'h00000001 and exec_ring becomes 32'h80000001. Now fetch_ring[31] = 0 and exec_ring[31] = 1, which violates P.

With R supplied as a strengthening invariant, P follows immediately, and R itself is 1-inductive: equal rings under the same update stay equal.

Make the design's counters and data words 32-bit (wider only where a count needs more); if it stores several items, give that storage 64 entries.

constant to match.

You write SystemVerilog modules for a formal verification dataset.

Each module is a "planted triple": a design containing an internal structural
relation R that holds by construction, plus a property P that is true of the design
but CANNOT be proven by k-induction unless the prover is also given R.

## The criterion

Three conditions, all required.

(1) P is true of the design.

(2) P is NOT inductive on its own. Concretely, there exists a state S such that:
      - S satisfies P
      - S violates R  (so S is unreachable in real operation, but a solver
        performing induction may start there)
      - S transitions in ONE step to a state that VIOLATES P

    S must also be a state the design can IDLE IN — one it can remain in for
    arbitrarily many cycles by holding the enable low. This matters: a one-step
    CTI only shows P is not 1-inductive, but the prover uses a 20-state window.
    If the design can stall in S, the solver builds a window of 20 copies of S and
    then takes the violating transition, so the property fails induction at ANY
    depth rather than only at depth 1. Without a stall, P may survive 20-induction
    and the triple is rejected.

    Condition (2) is the whole task. A property that is merely "weaker than R" is
    not enough. If every state satisfying P steps to another state satisfying P,
    then P is inductive by itself and the module is worthless for this dataset.

    Counterexample to avoid: if `count` is a 3-bit register, `count <= 7` is a
    consequence of any relation involving count, but it is trivially inductive
    because the register cannot hold anything larger. Rejected.

(3) P AND R TOGETHER ARE INDUCTIVE. R must be strong enough to exclude S and every
    state like it. It is not enough that R is true and P is weak — R must actually
    close the proof.

    R may be a conjunction of several clauses. The individual clauses do NOT each
    need to be inductive on their own; the requirement is that the conjunction,
    together with P, closes induction. Multi-clause relations are welcome and often
    necessary.

## Hard constraints on the Verilog

- These assertion forms are supported and all of them are welcome:
      always @(posedge clk) assert (expr);
      always @(*)           assert (expr);
      assert property (expr);                    // module level, NO clock inside
      always @(posedge clk) assert property (expr);
  `$past`, `$rose`, `$fell` and `$stable` work inside a clocked always block.
  Gate any `$past` check with a past-valid register so cycle zero is not judged:
      reg pv = 0;
      always @(posedge clk) pv <= 1;
      always @(posedge clk) if (pv) assert (out == $past(in));
- Do NOT put a clock inside the property: `assert property (@(posedge clk) ...)`,
  `disable iff`, `|->`, `|=>`, `##N`, `property ... endproperty`, `s_eventually`,
  sequences and `bind` are REJECTED by the toolchain — the module fails to parse
  and is never graded. Do not nest these functions either: `$past($rose(x))`
  fails to elaborate.
- Give every state register an `initial` value, so counterexamples are genuine
  from-reset traces rather than artifacts of an unconstrained start state.
- The design MUST have an enable or idle condition — an input that, when low, leaves
  all state unchanged (e.g. `i_ce`, `step`, or push and pop both low). Condition (2)
  depends on it: the state S must be one the design can sit in indefinitely.
- One property per module, unless the property style below asks for two.
- Never write `assume`. Assumptions are not checked and would let a false premise
  carry the proof.
- Never write `->` as logical implication in an expression — the toolchain rejects
  it. Write `!a || b` instead.
- If a register's declared width admits values it can never reach (e.g. a counter
  that saturates at 8 in a 4-bit reg), include an invariant bounding it — induction
  otherwise starts from an impossible value and fails on a phantom CTI.

## Output format

Your output is emitted through the API's structured-output mode — the schema is
enforced. Field order is deliberate: the reasoning fields come FIRST. Work out the
state S that breaks induction BEFORE writing the design, then write a design in
which that state is reachable-under-induction and the transition is real.

Field notes:

- `cti_reasoning`: one or two sentences: why this state satisfies P, why it
  violates R, and what its successor does that breaks P.

- `cti_state`: the state S from condition (2), as a list of {signal, value}
  pairs with concrete values. Every signal needed to evaluate both P and R must
  appear. Vague answers are rejected: "pointers disagree" is not acceptable;
  [{"signal": "count", "value": "3'd1"}, {"signal": "wptr", "value": "2'd2"},
  {"signal": "rptr", "value": "2'd0"}] is.

  Self-check before you answer: evaluate R at cti_state. It MUST come out false.
  If your named state does not violate your own invariant, you have contradicted
  yourself — fix one or the other.

- `invariants` is R. Supplied SEPARATELY from the Verilog — it must NOT appear as
  an assertion in the source. One string per clause.

- `verilog` is the full module source with the property assertion inline.

- `top_module` must match `module <name>` in the source. `clock` is the clock
  signal name.

- `antecedents` is the guard of P. If P is `if (count == 3'd0) assert (wptr == rptr);`
  the antecedent is `"count == 3'd0"`. If P is unconditional, use [].
  Prefer writing P with a guard, because real hardware properties are overwhelmingly
  conditional — an assertion about what must hold *when something happens*.

- `sanity_covers` must be genuinely reachable, e.g. `"count == 3'd2"` for a counter
  that gets there. Only checked when the property has an antecedent.

## Design idea

Module hadesv_mie_jk: a HaDes-V-style CSR interrupt-enable bit (mstatus.MIE) built as a JK flip-flop, with a 32-bit history counter and a trap window. Inputs: clk, rst_n, en (idle input; when low ALL state holds), j (csrrs sets MIE), k (csrrc clears MIE), trap_enter, mret. On a clock edge with en=1, the JK rules apply: j&~k sets, ~j&k resets, j&k toggles, ~j&~k holds.

State registers:
- q (1 bit): the MIE JK flop, reset 0.
- tcnt (32 bits): shadow history counter, reset 0. It increments, wrapping at 2^32, whenever en=1 and the next q differs from the current q. It records how many past changes of MIE occurred.
- in_trap (1 bit): window register, reset 0. With en=1 it is set by trap_enter and cleared by mret (mret wins if both). The window can open and close repeatedly.

Relation R, which holds by construction: q == tcnt[0]. MIE starts at 0, and every change of q flips tcnt's LSB. The wrap at 2^32 is even, so parity is preserved.

Property P (precedence, scope, edge style):
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) (in_trap && $rose(q)) |-> tcnt[0] == 1'b1);
Meaning: inside a trap window, whenever MIE rises, an odd number of MIE changes must already be on record in the shadow counter, counting the change that just happened. The shadow register thus witnesses that an earlier set event occurred.

Why P needs R: P alone is not k-inductive.
- Counterexample-to-induction state: q=0, tcnt=32'h0000_0001, in_trap=1.
- This state satisfies P, because q is not rising.
- It violates R, because q != tcnt[0].
- With en=0 it can be held for any number of cycles, so every finite k-step induction trace is consistent.
- Next apply en=1, j=1, k=0. Then q becomes 1, tcnt becomes 2, and tcnt[0] becomes 0.
- That cycle has in_trap=1 and $rose(q), but tcnt[0]==0, so P is violated.

Given R as a lemma, P follows in one step. If q rose, it is now 1, so R forces tcnt[0]=1.

## Size

Make the design's counters and data words 32-bit (wider only where a count needs more); if it stores several items, give that storage 12 entries.

Declare the design's registers and storage at this size, and size every
constant to match.

    }

  "invariants": [
    "state == 4'b0001 || state == 4'b0010 || state == 4'b0100 || state == 4'b1000"
  ],
  "verilog": "module onehot_fsm (\n    input wire clk,\n    input wire rst,\n    input wire step,\n    output reg [3:0] state\n);\n    initial state = 4'b0001;\n\n    always @(posedge clk) begin\n        if (rst)\n            state <= 4'b0001;\n        else if (step)\n            state <= {state[2:0], state[3]};\n    end\n\n    always @(posedge clk)\n        assert (!(state[0] && state[2]));\nendmodule",
  "top_module": "onehot_fsm",
  "clock": "clk",
  "antecedents": [],
  "sanity_covers": [
    "state == 4'b0100"
  ]
}

Three conditions, all required.

(1) P is true of the design.

      - S satisfies P

    then takes the violating transition, so the property fails induction at ANY
    depth rather than only at depth 1. Without a stall, P may survive 20-induction
    and the triple is rejected.

    not enough. If every state satisfying P steps to another state satisfying P,
    then P is inductive by itself and the module is worthless for this dataset.

    Counterexample to avoid: if `count` is a 3-bit register, `count <= 7` is a
    consequence of any relation involving count, but it is trivially inductive
    because the register cannot hold anything larger. Rejected.

    state like it. It is not enough that R is true and P is weak — R must actually
    close the proof.

    R may be a conjunction of several clauses. The individual clauses do NOT each
    need to be inductive on their own; the requirement is that the conjunction,
    together with P, closes induction. Multi-clause relations are welcome and often
    necessary.

      always @(posedge clk) assert (expr);

You write SystemVerilog modules for a formal verification dataset.

Each module is a "planted triple": a design containing an internal structural
relation R that holds by construction, plus a property P that is true of the design
but CANNOT be proven by k-induction unless the prover is also given R.

## The criterion

Three conditions, all required.

(1) P is true of the design.

(2) P is NOT inductive on its own. Concretely, there exists a state S such that:
      - S satisfies P
      - S violates R  (so S is unreachable in real operation, but a solver
        performing induction may start there)
      - S transitions in ONE step to a state that VIOLATES P

    S must also be a state the design can IDLE IN — one it can remain in for
    arbitrarily many cycles by holding the enable low. This matters: a one-step
    CTI only shows P is not 1-inductive, but the prover uses a 20-state window.
    If the design can stall in S, the solver builds a window of 20 copies of S and
    then takes the violating transition, so the property fails induction at ANY
    depth rather than only at depth 1. Without a stall, P may survive 20-induction
    and the triple is rejected.

    Condition (2) is the whole task. A property that is merely "weaker than R" is
    not enough. If every state satisfying P steps to another state satisfying P,
    then P is inductive by itself and the module is worthless for this dataset.

    Counterexample to avoid: if `count` is a 3-bit register, `count <= 7` is a
    consequence of any relation involving count, but it is trivially inductive
    because the register cannot hold anything larger. Rejected.

(3) P AND R TOGETHER ARE INDUCTIVE. R must be strong enough to exclude S and every
    state like it. It is not enough that R is true and P is weak — R must actually
    close the proof.

    R may be a conjunction of several clauses. The individual clauses do NOT each
    need to be inductive on their own; the requirement is that the conjunction,
    together with P, closes induction. Multi-clause relations are welcome and often
    necessary.

## Hard constraints on the Verilog

- These assertion forms are supported and all of them are welcome:
      always @(posedge clk) assert (expr);
      always @(*)           assert (expr);
      assert property (expr);                    // module level, NO clock inside
      always @(posedge clk) assert property (expr);
  `$past`, `$rose`, `$fell` and `$stable` work inside a clocked always block.
  Gate any `$past` check with a past-valid register so cycle zero is not judged:
      reg pv = 0;
      always @(posedge clk) pv <= 1;
      always @(posedge clk) if (pv) assert (out == $past(in));
- Do NOT put a clock inside the property: `assert property (@(posedge clk) ...)`,
  `disable iff`, `|->`, `|=>`, `##N`, `property ... endproperty`, `s_eventually`,
  sequences and `bind` are REJECTED by the toolchain — the module fails to parse
  and is never graded. Do not nest these functions either: `$past($rose(x))`
  fails to elaborate.
- Give every state register an `initial` value, so counterexamples are genuine
  from-reset traces rather than artifacts of an unconstrained start state.
- The design MUST have an enable or idle condition — an input that, when low, leaves
  all state unchanged (e.g. `i_ce`, `step`, or push and pop both low). Condition (2)
  depends on it: the state S must be one the design can sit in indefinitely.
- One property per module, unless the property style below asks for two.
- Never write `assume`. Assumptions are not checked and would let a false premise
  carry the proof.
- Never write `->` as logical implication in an expression — the toolchain rejects
  it. Write `!a || b` instead.
- If a register's declared width admits values it can never reach (e.g. a counter
  that saturates at 8 in a 4-bit reg), include an invariant bounding it — induction
  otherwise starts from an impossible value and fails on a phantom CTI.

## Output format

Your output is emitted through the API's structured-output mode — the schema is
enforced. Field order is deliberate: the reasoning fields come FIRST. Work out the
state S that breaks induction BEFORE writing the design, then write a design in
which that state is reachable-under-induction and the transition is real.

Field notes:

- `cti_reasoning`: one or two sentences: why this state satisfies P, why it
  violates R, and what its successor does that breaks P.

- `cti_state`: the state S from condition (2), as a list of {signal, value}
  pairs with concrete values. Every signal needed to evaluate both P and R must
  appear. Vague answers are rejected: "pointers disagree" is not acceptable;
  [{"signal": "count", "value": "3'd1"}, {"signal": "wptr", "value": "2'd2"},
  {"signal": "rptr", "value": "2'd0"}] is.

  Self-check before you answer: evaluate R at cti_state. It MUST come out false.
  If your named state does not violate your own invariant, you have contradicted
  yourself — fix one or the other.

- `invariants` is R. Supplied SEPARATELY from the Verilog — it must NOT appear as
  an assertion in the source. One string per clause.

- `verilog` is the full module source with the property assertion inline.

- `top_module` must match `module <name>` in the source. `clock` is the clock
  signal name.

- `antecedents` is the guard of P. If P is `if (count == 3'd0) assert (wptr == rptr);`
  the antecedent is `"count == 3'd0"`. If P is unconditional, use [].
  Prefer writing P with a guard, because real hardware properties are overwhelmingly
  conditional — an assertion about what must hold *when something happens*.

- `sanity_covers` must be genuinely reachable, e.g. `"count == 3'd2"` for a counter
  that gets there. Only checked when the property has an antecedent.

## Design idea

Module tile_rf_led: a matrix tile register file in the style of a hobby FPGA gateware block (think ice40 demo). Storage mem[0:15] holds 64-bit rows. Row-wise stores fill rows; a matrix engine 'consume' reads the whole tile as one operand; a per-tile shape config limits how many rows may be filled.

Inputs: clk, rst, en (idle/enable: when low, every state register holds its value), ld, ld_data[63:0], consume, reshape, new_rows[4:0].

State registers:
- mem[16][63:0]: tile data.
- wptr[4:0]: next row index.
- fill_cnt[63:0]: rows loaded since the last consume.
- shape_rows[4:0]: configured row count. Resets to 12.
- pristine (1 bit): resets to 1.

Behavior when en is high:
- ld with wptr != shape_rows: write mem[wptr] = ld_data, then wptr++ and fill_cnt++. Saturation is decided only by wptr.
- consume: wptr = 0 and fill_cnt = 0. The engine reads mem as the operand.
- reshape (only accepted when wptr == 0): shape_rows = min(new_rows, 16) and pristine = 0. The scope event R_evt is the first reshape.
- Reset: wptr = 0, fill_cnt = 0, shape_rows = 12, pristine = 1.

Relation R (holds by construction):
- fill_cnt == {59'b0, wptr}
- wptr <= shape_rows
- pristine -> (shape_rows == 12)

Property P (pattern: bounded existence, at most 12; scope: before the first reshape; pristine is listed in the antecedents):
always @(posedge clk) assert (!pristine || fill_cnt <= 64'd12);
The bound 12 is far below the 2^64 range of fill_cnt, so it is a genuine reachability fact. It also holds only before reshape, since afterwards shape_rows may be 16.

Why k-induction fails without R: P constrains only fill_cnt, while the saturation guard uses wptr. Counterexample-to-induction state:
- pristine = 1, shape_rows = 12, wptr = 5, fill_cnt = 12.
- It satisfies P (12 <= 12) but violates R (fill_cnt != wptr).
- It can be held indefinitely with en = 0, so any length of P-satisfying prefix exists.
- Then en = 1, ld = 1: wptr = 5 != 12, so the store is accepted. fill_cnt becomes 13 while pristine is still 1, which violates P.

With R supplied, fill_cnt equals wptr, which is at most shape_rows = 12 while pristine, so P is 1-inductive.

## Size

Make the design's counters and data words 64-bit (wider only where a count needs more); if it stores several items, give that storage 16 entries.

Declare the design's registers and storage at this size, and size every
constant to match.

With tick low the design idles here indefinitely; one tick then takes remaining to 0 while elapsed becomes 6, so the property fails in the next state.",

    },
    {
      "signal": "remaining",
      "value": "64'd1"
    }
  ],
  "invariants": [
    "elapsed + remaining == 64'd48"
  ],
  "verilog": "module timer64 (\n    input wire clk,\n    input wire rst,\n    input wire tick,\n    output wire expired,\n    output wire [63:0] o_elapsed\n);\n    localparam [63:0] PERIOD = 64'd48;\n    reg [63:0] elapsed, remaining;\n    initial begin elapsed = 64'd0; remaining = PERIOD; end\n\n    always @(posedge clk) begin\n        if (rst) begin\n            elapsed <= 64'd0;\n            remaining <= PERIOD;\n        end else if (tick && remaining != 64'd0) begin\n            elapsed <= elapsed + 64'd1;\n            remaining <= remaining - 64'd1;\n        end\n    end\n\n    assign expired = (remaining == 64'd0);\n    assign o_elapsed = elapsed;\n\n    always @(posedge clk)\n        if (expired)\n            assert (elapsed == PERIOD);\nendmodule\n",
  "top_module": "timer64",
  "clock": "clk",
  "antecedents": [
    "remaining == 64'd0"
  ],
  "sanity_covers": [
    "remaining == 64'd40"
  ]
}

# Verilog-Adders
Implementing Different Adder Structures in Verilog

The Aim of this project is to describe and differentiate different types of adders in verilog and distinguish them at simulation level.
All adders have been defined for **8, 16, 32 and 64 bit** addition along with test benches for each type of adder.
This project implements the following adders :

## Carry Lookaheaed Adder

       
4-bit Carry Lookahead Adder

A carry-look ahead adder improves speed by reducing the amount of time required to determine carry bits. It can be contrasted with the simpler, but usually slower, ripple-carry adder (RCA), for which the carry bit is calculated alongside the sum bit, and each stage must wait until the previous carry bit has been calculated to begin calculating its own sum bit and carry bit. The carry-lookahead adder calculates one or more carry bits before the sum, which reduces the wait time to calculate the result of the larger-value bits of the adder. The Kogge–Stone adder (KSA) and Brent–Kung adder (BKA) are examples of this type of adder.
Carry-lookahead depends on two things:
* Calculating for each digit position whether that position is going to propagate a carry if one comes in from the right.
* Combining these calculated values to be able to deduce quickly whether, for each group of digits, that group is going to propagate a carry that comes in from the right.

{"idea":"Module orbit_mrs_unit: a DRAM mode-register programming unit, framed as an Orbit-style 'package installer' that installs one configuration word (CAS latency, burst length, ODT, drive strength, etc.) into one of 8 mode registers at a time.

Inputs: clk, rst_n, en, req_valid, req_idx[2:0], req_data[15:0], cfg_lock. When en is low, every state register holds its value.

State registers:
- shadow[0:7], each 16 bits: shadow copies of the mode registers.
- pend[7:0]: pending-update flags.
- cur_idx[2:0]: index of the register being updated.
- cur_data[15:0]: data being written.
- cnt[15:0]: tMRD/tMOD countdown.
- win (1 bit): observation window.

Output: busy = |pend.

Behavior on each clock edge with en=1:
- Accept: if req_valid && !busy, the unit accepts the request. It sets pend[req_idx], latches cur_idx and cur_data, loads cnt=16'd8, and drives mrs_cmd_valid with {req_idx, req_data}.
- Count down: else if busy && cnt>1, cnt decrements.
- Complete: else if busy && cnt==1, then shadow[cur_idx]<=cur_data, pend[cur_idx]<=0 and cnt<=0.
- Window: win is set on an accept (Q). It is cleared when cfg_lock is asserted (R). cfg_lock may never arrive.
- Reset clears all registers.

Relation R (holds by construction):
- pend is either zero or exactly the one-hot vector (8'b1 << cur_idx).
- (pend != 0) == (cnt != 0).
- cnt <= 8.

- State: win=1, pend=8'b0000_0011, cur_idx=0, cnt=16'd1, other registers arbitrary.
- P holds: busy=1 and cnt!=0.
- R is violated: two pending bits are set, which is not one-hot.
- With en=0 the state is frozen indefinitely, so it can be held while idle.
- Next step with en=1 and cfg_lock=0: completion fires because cnt==1. It clears only pend[0] and sets cnt=0. pend becomes 8'b0000_0010, so busy is still 1 while cnt=0 and win=1. P fails.

Why R is needed: from reachable states, only one bit of pend is ever set, so completion always drops busy in the same cycle cnt reaches 0. k-induction on P alone cannot exclude the multi-pending CTI, because the en=0 stall lets it persist for any k. prompt.content:
You write SystemVerilog modules for a formal verification dataset.

Each module is a "planted triple": a design containing an internal structural
relation R that holds by construction, plus a property P that is true of the design
but CANNOT be proven by k-induction unless the prover is also given R.

## The criterion

Three conditions, all required.

(1) P is true of the design.

(2) P is NOT inductive on its own. Concretely, there exists a state S such that:
      - S satisfies P
      - S violates R  (so S is unreachable in real operation, but a solver
        performing induction may start there)
      - S transitions in ONE step to a state that VIOLATES P

    S must also be a state the design can IDLE IN — one it can remain in for
    arbitrarily many cycles by holding the enable low. This matters: a one-step
    CTI only shows P is not 1-inductive, but the prover uses a 20-state window.
    If the design can stall in S, the solver builds a window of 20 copies of S and
    then takes the violating transition, so the property fails induction at ANY
    depth rather than only at depth 1. Without a stall, P may survive 20-induction
    and the triple is rejected.

    Condition (2) is the whole task. A property that is merely "weaker than R" is
    not enough. If every state satisfying P steps to another state satisfying P,
    then P is inductive by itself and the module is worthless for this dataset.

    Counterexample to avoid: if `count` is a 3-bit register, `count <= 7` is a
    consequence of any relation involving count, but it is trivially inductive
    because the register cannot hold anything larger. Rejected.

(3) P AND R TOGETHER ARE INDUCTIVE. R must be strong enough to exclude S and every
    state like it. It is not enough that R is true and P is weak — R must actually
    close the proof.

    R may be a conjunction of several clauses. The individual clauses do NOT each
    need to be inductive on their own; the requirement is that the conjunction,
    together with P, closes induction. Multi-clause relations are welcome and often
    necessary.

## Hard constraints on the Verilog

- These assertion forms are supported and all of them are welcome:
      always @(posedge clk) assert (expr);
      always @(*)           assert (expr);
      assert property (expr);                    // module level, NO clock inside
      always @(posedge clk) assert property (expr);
  `$past`, `$rose`, `$fell` and `$stable` work inside a clocked always block.
  Gate any `$past` check with a past-valid register so cycle zero is not judged:
      reg pv = 0;
      always @(posedge clk) pv <= 1;
      always @(posedge clk) if (pv) assert (out == $past(in));
- Do NOT put a clock inside the property: `assert property (@(posedge clk) ...)`,
  `disable iff`, `|->`, `|=>`, `##N`, `property ... endproperty`, `s_eventually`,
  sequences and `bind` are REJECTED by the toolchain — the module fails to parse
  and is never graded. Do not nest these functions either: `$past($rose(x))`
  fails to elaborate.
- Give every state register an `initial` value, so counterexamples are genuine
  from-reset traces rather than artifacts of an unconstrained start state.
- The design MUST have an enable or idle condition — an input that, when low, leaves
  all state unchanged (e.g. `i_ce`, `step`, or push and pop both low). Condition (2)
  depends on it: the state S must be one the design can sit in indefinitely.
- One property per module, unless the property style below asks for two.
- Never write `assume`. Assumptions are not checked and would let a false premise
  carry the proof.
- Never write `->` as logical implication in an expression — the toolchain rejects
  it. Write `!a || b` instead.
- If a register's declared width admits values it can never reach (e.g. a counter
  that saturates at 8 in a 4-bit reg), include an invariant bounding it — induction
  otherwise starts from an impossible value and fails on a phantom CTI.

## Output format

Your output is emitted through the API's structured-output mode — the schema is
enforced. Field order is deliberate: the reasoning fields come FIRST. Work out the
state S that breaks induction BEFORE writing the design, then write a design in
which that state is reachable-under-induction and the transition is real.

Field notes:

- `cti_reasoning`: one or two sentences: why this state satisfies P, why it
  violates R, and what its successor does that breaks P.

- `cti_state`: the state S from condition (2), as a list of {signal, value}
  pairs with concrete values. Every signal needed to evaluate both P and R must
  appear. Vague answers are rejected: "pointers disagree" is not acceptable;
  [{"signal": "count", "value": "3'd1"}, {"signal": "wptr", "value": "2'd2"},
  {"signal": "rptr", "value": "2'd0"}] is.

  Self-check before you answer: evaluate R at cti_state. It MUST come out false.
  If your named state does not violate your own invariant, you have contradicted
  yourself — fix one or the other.

- `invariants` is R. Supplied SEPARATELY from the Verilog — it must NOT appear as
  an assertion in the source. One string per clause.

- `verilog` is the full module source with the property assertion inline.

- `top_module` must match `module <name>` in the source. `clock` is the clock
  signal name.

- `antecedents` is the guard of P. If P is `if (count == 3'd0) assert (wptr == rptr);`
  the antecedent is `"count == 3'd0"`. If P is unconditional, use [].
  Prefer writing P with a guard, because real hardware properties are overwhelmingly
  conditional — an assertion about what must hold *when something happens*.

- `sanity_covers` must be genuinely reachable, e.g. `"count == 3'd2"` for a counter
  that gets there. Only checked when the property has an antecedent.

DRAM retention-time estimator, a bipartite table unit themed on DRAM Bender. A 4-bit temperature code x selects entries in two tables: x[3:2] indexes a coarse table-of-initial-values (TIV) and x[1:0] indexes a table-of-offsets (TO). Ports: clk, rst, en (idle input: when en=0 every register holds), x[3:0], and output est[7:0]=sum_q.

Constants: TIVc={200,150,100,60} and TOc={0,12,24,36}.

State:
- tiv[0:3] (8b each) and to[0:3] (8b each): table registers loaded with TIVc/TOc at reset and never written.
- Stage 1: idx1 (4b), the shadow of the accepted input; tiv_r (8b); to_r (8b).
- Stage 2: idx2 (4b), the shadow carried from idx1; sum_q (8b), the sum register.
- arm (1b): sticky; set on the first en-high cycle after reset (Q = first lookup accepted) and never cleared.

Reset values: idx1=0, tiv_r=200, to_r=0, idx2=0, sum_q=200, arm=0.

On an en-high cycle:
- idx1<=x; tiv_r<=tiv[x[3:2]]; to_r<=to[x[1:0]].
- idx2<=idx1; sum_q<=tiv_r+to_r.
- arm<=1.

Relation R (holds by construction), with i ranging over 0..3:
arm -> (tiv[i]==TIVc[i] && to[i]==TOc[i] && tiv_r==TIVc[idx1[3:2]] && to_r==TOc[idx1[1:0]]).

Counterexample-to-induction state:
- arm=1; tables correct.
- idx2=4'b0000, sum_q=200, so P holds.
- idx1=4'b0101, which requires tiv_r=150 and to_r=12.
- But tiv_r=0, so R is violated.

With en=0 the state is held for any number of cycles while P keeps holding. On the next en=1 cycle, idx2 becomes 0101 and sum_q becomes 0+12=12, whereas P requires 150+12=162. P is violated.

What a strengthened proof uses: given R, stage 1 always holds the correct table values for idx1. Its sum therefore always moves into sum_q together with idx1 moving into idx2, so P is preserved.

## Size

Make the design's counters and data words 8-bit (wider only where a count needs more); if it stores several items, give that storage 4 entries.

Declare the design's registers and storage at this size, and size every
constant to match.

## Worked example

{
  "cti_reasoning": "This state satisfies the property because count is not zero, so the guard does not fire. It violates the invariant because count[1:0] is 1 while wptr - rptr is 2. With push and pop both low the design idles here indefinitely; one pop then takes count to 0 while the pointers still disagree, so the property fails in the next state.",
  "cti_state": [
    {
      "signal": "count",
      "value": "3'd1"
    },
    {
      "signal": "wptr",
      "value": "2'd2"
    },
    {
      "signal": "rptr",
      "value": "2'd0"
    }
  ],
  "invariants": [
    "count <= 3'd4",
    "count[1:0] == wptr - rptr"
  ],
  "verilog": "module fifo (\n    input wire clk,\n    input wire rst,\n    input wire push,\n    input wire pop,\n    output reg [2:0] count\n);\n    reg [1:0] wptr, rptr;\n    initial begin wptr = 0; rptr = 0; count = 0; end\n\n    wire do_push = push && count != 3'd4;\n    wire do_pop  = pop  && count != 3'd0;\n\n    always @(posedge clk) begin\n        if (rst) begin\n            wptr <= 0; rptr <= 0; count <= 0;\n        end else begin\n            if (do_push) wptr <= wptr + 1;\n            if (do_pop)  rptr <= rptr + 1;\n            case ({do_push, do_pop})\n                2'b10:   count <= count + 1;\n                2'b01:   count <= count - 1;\n                default: count <= count;\n            endcase\n        end\n    end\n\n    always @(posedge clk)\n        if (count == 3'd0)\n            assert (wptr == rptr);\nendmodule",
  "top_module": "fifo",
  "clock": "clk",
  "antecedents": [
    "count == 3'd0"
  ],
  "sanity_covers": [
    "count == 3'd2"
  ]
}

different from the worked example. Fill in every field of the schema.

You write SystemVerilog modules for a formal verification dataset.

Each module is a "planted triple": a design containing an internal structural
relation R that holds by construction, plus a property P that is true of the design
but CANNOT be proven by k-induction unless the prover is also given R.

## The criterion

Three conditions, all required.

(1) P is true of the design.

(2) P is NOT inductive on its own. Concretely, there exists a state S such that:
      - S satisfies P
      - S violates R  (so S is unreachable in real operation, but a solver
        performing induction may start there)
      - S transitions in ONE step to a state that VIOLATES P

    S must also be a state the design can IDLE IN — one it can remain in for
    arbitrarily many cycles by holding the enable low. This matters: a one-step
    CTI only shows P is not 1-inductive, but the prover uses a 20-state window.
    If the design can stall in S, the solver builds a window of 20 copies of S and
    then takes the violating transition, so the property fails induction at ANY
    depth rather than only at depth 1. Without a stall, P may survive 20-induction
    and the triple is rejected.

    Condition (2) is the whole task. A property that is merely "weaker than R" is
    not enough. If every state satisfying P steps to another state satisfying P,
    then P is inductive by itself and the module is worthless for this dataset.

    Counterexample to avoid: if `count` is a 3-bit register, `count <= 7` is a
    consequence of any relation involving count, but it is trivially inductive
    because the register cannot hold anything larger. Rejected.

(3) P AND R TOGETHER ARE INDUCTIVE. R must be strong enough to exclude S and every
    state like it. It is not enough that R is true and P is weak — R must actually
    close the proof.

    R may be a conjunction of several clauses. The individual clauses do NOT each
    need to be inductive on their own; the requirement is that the conjunction,
    together with P, closes induction. Multi-clause relations are welcome and often
    necessary.

## Hard constraints on the Verilog

- These assertion forms are supported and all of them are welcome:
      always @(posedge clk) assert (expr);
      always @(*)           assert (expr);
      assert property (expr);                    // module level, NO clock inside
      always @(posedge clk) assert property (expr);
  `$past`, `$rose`, `$fell` and `$stable` work inside a clocked always block.
  Gate any `$past` check with a past-valid register so cycle zero is not judged:
      reg pv = 0;
      always @(posedge clk) pv <= 1;
      always @(posedge clk) if (pv) assert (out == $past(in));
- Do NOT put a clock inside the property: `assert property (@(posedge clk) ...)`,
  `disable iff`, `|->`, `|=>`, `##N`, `property ... endproperty`, `s_eventually`,
  sequences and `bind` are REJECTED by the toolchain — the module fails to parse
  and is never graded. Do not nest these functions either: `$past($rose(x))`
  fails to elaborate.
- Give every state register an `initial` value, so counterexamples are genuine
  from-reset traces rather than artifacts of an unconstrained start state.
- The design MUST have an enable or idle condition — an input that, when low, leaves
  all state unchanged (e.g. `i_ce`, `step`, or push and pop both low). Condition (2)
  depends on it: the state S must be one the design can sit in indefinitely.
- One property per module, unless the property style below asks for two.
- Never write `assume`. Assumptions are not checked and would let a false premise
  carry the proof.
- Never write `->` as logical implication in an expression — the toolchain rejects
  it. Write `!a || b` instead.
- If a register's declared width admits values it can never reach (e.g. a counter
  that saturates at 8 in a 4-bit reg), include an invariant bounding it — induction
  otherwise starts from an impossible value and fails on a phantom CTI.

## Output format

Your output is emitted through the API's structured-output mode — the schema is
enforced. Field order is deliberate: the reasoning fields come FIRST. Work out the
state S that breaks induction BEFORE writing the design, then write a design in
which that state is reachable-under-induction and the transition is real.

Field notes:

- `cti_reasoning`: one or two sentences: why this state satisfies P, why it
  violates R, and what its successor does that breaks P.

- `cti_state`: the state S from condition (2), as a list of {signal, value}
  pairs with concrete values. Every signal needed to evaluate both P and R must
  appear. Vague answers are rejected: "pointers disagree" is not acceptable;
  [{"signal": "count", "value": "3'd1"}, {"signal": "wptr", "value": "2'd2"},
  {"signal": "rptr", "value": "2'd0"}] is.

  Self-check before you answer: evaluate R at cti_state. It MUST come out false.
  If your named state does not violate your own invariant, you have contradicted
  yourself — fix one or the other.

- `invariants` is R. Supplied SEPARATELY from the Verilog — it must NOT appear as
  an assertion in the source. One string per clause.

- `verilog` is the full module source with the property assertion inline.

- `top_module` must match `module <name>` in the source. `clock` is the clock
  signal name.

- `antecedents` is the guard of P. If P is `if (count == 3'd0) assert (wptr == rptr);`
  the antecedent is `"count == 3'd0"`. If P is unconditional, use [].
  Prefer writing P with a guard, because real hardware properties are overwhelmingly
  conditional — an assertion about what must hold *when something happens*.

- `sanity_covers` must be genuinely reachable, e.g. `"count == 3'd2"` for a counter
  that gets there. Only checked when the property has an antecedent.

## Design idea

Module perfect_id_rom: a PERFECT-themed device identification ROM that auto-scans six hardwired 32-bit ID words. Each word is presented on a registered read-data output, like a Chisel ID-chain walker.

Constants (localparam, 6 entries x 32 bits):
- ROM[0] VENDOR = 0x49424D00 ("IBM")
- ROM[1] PART = 0x50455246 ("PERF")
- ROM[2] REVISION = 0x00000003
- ROM[3] FEAT0 = 0x0000C3A5
- ROM[4] FEAT1 = 0x00000011
- ROM[5] SIGNATURE = 0x43484933 ("CHI3")

Ports: clk, rst (synchronous), en (scan enable / idle when low), rdata[31:0], last.

State registers:
- ptr [31:0]: current ROM index.
- remaining [31:0]: words left before wrap.
- rdata_q [31:0]: read-data output register.

Reset values: ptr = 0, remaining = 5, rdata_q = 0.

When en is low, all three registers hold. When en is high, the update is deliberately cross-coupled:
- rdata_q <= ROM[ptr], or 0 if ptr > 5.
- ptr <= (remaining == 0) ? 0 : ptr + 1. The pointer wraps on the other counter.
- remaining <= (ptr == 5) ? 5 : remaining - 1. The countdown reloads on the pointer.
- last = (remaining == 0).

Relation R (holds by construction): ptr <= 5 && remaining == 5 - ptr. The two counters always sum to 5, so ptr hits 5 exactly when remaining hits 0, and both branches fire together.

Property P (Bounded Existence, at most k, global, two assertions, no arming register):
- A1: assert property (ptr <= 5). The index never exceeds 5 even though 32 bits allow about 4e9.
- A2: assert property (remaining <= 5). The countdown never exceeds 5.

Why neither is inductive alone:
- A1 alone, state ptr=5, remaining=3: remaining != 0, so ptr steps to 6.
- A2 alone, state ptr=2, remaining=0: ptr != 5, so remaining underflows to 0xFFFFFFFF.
- Even A1 && A2 together are not inductive; the counterexample to induction (CTI) below satisfies both.
- Adding R closes both: the wrap and the reload are then simultaneous, so ptr stays in 0..5 and remaining = 5 - ptr stays in 0..5.

CTI (satisfies P, violates R, holdable while idle, steps to a P violation):
- State: ptr = 5, remaining = 3, rdata_q = 0.
- P holds: 5 <= 5 and 3 <= 5.
- R is violated: 5 - 5 = 0, not 3.
- With en = 0 the state is held indefinitely, so it survives any induction depth k.
- With en = 1, remaining != 0 so ptr becomes 6, violating A1. Meanwhile ptr == 5 reloads remaining to 5.

The mirror state ptr = 3, remaining = 0 is also held while idle. It steps to remaining = 0xFFFFFFFF, violating A2.

So k-induction on A1 and A2 fails for every k without R and succeeds at k = 1 once R is supplied as a strengthening invariant.

## Size

Make the design's counters and data words 32-bit (wider only where a count needs more); if it stores several items, give that storage 6 entries.

Declare the design's registers and storage at this size, and size every
constant to match.

You write SystemVerilog modules for a formal verification dataset.

Each module is a "planted triple": a design containing an internal structural
relation R that holds by construction, plus a property P that is true of the design
but CANNOT be proven by k-induction unless the prover is also given R.

## The criterion

Three conditions, all required.

(1) P is true of the design.

(2) P is NOT inductive on its own. Concretely, there exists a state S such that:
      - S satisfies P
      - S violates R  (so S is unreachable in real operation, but a solver
        performing induction may start there)
      - S transitions in ONE step to a state that VIOLATES P

    S must also be a state the design can IDLE IN — one it can remain in for
    arbitrarily many cycles by holding the enable low. This matters: a one-step
    CTI only shows P is not 1-inductive, but the prover uses a 20-state window.
    If the design can stall in S, the solver builds a window of 20 copies of S and
    then takes the violating transition, so the property fails induction at ANY
    depth rather than only at depth 1. Without a stall, P may survive 20-induction
    and the triple is rejected.

    Condition (2) is the whole task. A property that is merely "weaker than R" is
    not enough. If every state satisfying P steps to another state satisfying P,
    then P is inductive by itself and the module is worthless for this dataset.

    Counterexample to avoid: if `count` is a 3-bit register, `count <= 7` is a
    consequence of any relation involving count, but it is trivially inductive
    because the register cannot hold anything larger. Rejected.

(3) P AND R TOGETHER ARE INDUCTIVE. R must be strong enough to exclude S and every
    state like it. It is not enough that R is true and P is weak — R must actually
    close the proof.

    R may be a conjunction of several clauses. The individual clauses do NOT each
    need to be inductive on their own; the requirement is that the conjunction,
    together with P, closes induction. Multi-clause relations are welcome and often
    necessary.

## Hard constraints on the Verilog

- These assertion forms are supported and all of them are welcome:
      always @(posedge clk) assert (expr);
      always @(*)           assert (expr);
      assert property (expr);                    // module level, NO clock inside
      always @(posedge clk) assert property (expr);
  `$past`, `$rose`, `$fell` and `$stable` work inside a clocked always block.
  Gate any `$past` check with a past-valid register so cycle zero is not judged:
      reg pv = 0;
      always @(posedge clk) pv <= 1;
      always @(posedge clk) if (pv) assert (out == $past(in));

  `disable iff`, `|->`, `|=>`, `##N`, `property ... endproperty`, `s_eventually`,
  sequences and `bind` are REJECTED by the toolchain — the module fails to parse
  and is never graded. Do not nest these functions either: `$past($rose(x))`
  fails to elaborate.
- Give every state register an `initial` value, so counterexamples are genuine
  from-reset traces rather than artifacts of an unconstrained start state.
- The design MUST have an enable or idle condition — an input that, when low, leaves
  all state unchanged (e.g. `i_ce`, `step`, or push and pop both low). Condition (2)
  depends on it: the state S must be one the design can sit in indefinitely.
- One property per module, unless the property style below asks for two.
- Never write `assume`. Assumptions are not checked and would let a false premise
  carry the proof.
- Never write `->` as logical implication in an expression — the toolchain rejects
  it. Write `!a || b` instead.
- If a register's declared width admits values it can never reach (e.g. a counter
  that saturates at 8 in a 4-bit reg), include an invariant bounding it — induction
  otherwise starts from an impossible value and fails on a phantom CTI.
