Your output is emitted through the API's structured-output mode — the schema is
enforced. Field order is deliberate: the reasoning fields come FIRST. Work out the
state S that breaks induction BEFORE writing the design, then write a design in
which that state is reachable-under-induction and the transition is real.

Field notes:

- `cti_reasoning`: one or two sentences: why this state satisfies P, why it
  violates R, and what its successor does that breaks P.

- `cti_state`: the state S from condition (2), as a list of {signal, value}
  pairs with concrete values. Every signal needed to evaluate both P and R must
  appear. Vague answers are rejected: "pointers disagree" is not acceptable;
  [{"signal": "count", "value": "3'd1"}, {"signal": "wptr", "value": "2'd2"},
  {"signal": "rptr", "value": "2'd0"}] is.

  Self-check before you answer: evaluate R at cti_state. It MUST come out false.
  If your named state does not violate your own invariant, you have contradicted
  yourself — fix one or the other.

- `invariants` is R. Supplied SEPARATELY from the Verilog — it must NOT appear as
  an assertion in the source. One string per clause.

- `verilog` is the full module source with the property assertion inline.

- `top_module` must match `module <name>` in the source. `clock` is the clock
  signal name.

- `antecedents` is the guard of P. If P is `if (count == 3'd0) assert (wptr == rptr);`
  the antecedent is `"count == 3'd0"`. If P is unconditional, use [].
  Prefer writing P with a guard, because real hardware properties are overwhelmingly
  conditional — an assertion about what must hold *when something happens*.

- `sanity_covers` must be genuinely reachable, e.g. `"count == 3'd2"` for a counter
  that gets there. Only checked when the property has an antecedent.

Clio-style memory-node Golay scrubber (golay_scrub). A 16-entry store mem[0:15] holds 24-bit extended Golay codewords; host writes encode 12-bit data via the generator matrix. A scrub engine walks entries, computes a 12-bit syndrome, and corrects up to 3 errors through a decode lookup table.

Behavior when en=1: inj XORs inj_mask into mem[inj_addr], sets err_flag[inj_addr], increments inj_cnt and sets inj_seen. wr stores encode(wr_data) and clears err_flag[wr_addr]. - P holds because win=0.
- R is violated because corr_cnt!=0 and err_flag!=0 while inj_seen=0.
- With en=0, all state is frozen, so the state persists for any k.
- Then en=1 with scrub_start=1 sets win=1 while corr_cnt stays 5 and inj_seen stays 0, so P fails.

Given R as an invariant, any state with inj_seen=0 has corr_cnt=0 and no flags. corr_cnt therefore cannot become nonzero without a prior inj, and P becomes inductive.

Make the design's counters and data words 32-bit (wider only where a count needs more); if it stores several items, give that storage 16 entries.

Declare the design's registers and storage at this size, and size every
constant to match.

Three conditions, all required.

(1) P is true of the design.

(2) P is NOT inductive on its own. Concretely, there exists a state S such that:
      - S satisfies P

        performing induction may start there)
      - S transitions in ONE step to a state that VIOLATES P

    arbitrarily many cycles by holding the enable low. This matters: a one-step
    CTI only shows P is not 1-inductive, but the prover uses a 20-state window.
    If the design can stall in S, the solver builds a window of 20 copies of S and
    then takes the violating transition, so the property fails induction at ANY
    depth rather than only at depth 1. Without a stall, P may survive 20-induction
    and the triple is rejected.

    Condition (2) is the whole task. A property that is merely "weaker than R" is
    not enough. If every state satisfying P steps to another state satisfying P,
    then P is inductive by itself and the module is worthless for this dataset.

    Counterexample to avoid: if `count` is a 3-bit register, `count <= 7` is a
    consequence of any relation involving count, but it is trivially inductive
    because the register cannot hold anything larger. Rejected.

(3) P AND R TOGETHER ARE INDUCTIVE. R must be strong enough to exclude S and every
    state like it. It is not enough that R is true and P is weak — R must actually
    close the proof.

    R may be a conjunction of several clauses. The individual clauses do NOT each
    need to be inductive on their own; the requirement is that the conjunction,
    together with P, closes induction. Multi-clause relations are welcome and often
    necessary.

# Counting until the heat death of the universe

ASIC with a large enough counter to theoretically count until the heat death of the universe. 
Counter value is incremented ever 20ns and every second the ASIC will broadcasts an ethernet frame over 100Mbps ethernet
with the current counters value, not that anyone is going to be listening for long anyways. 

Assuming the universe dies in approximately $10^{100}$ years. If you are patient enough to wait until then there is 
a hidden easter egg when we eventually overflow.  

Quickstart can be found [in the documentation](/docs/info.md).

## Tapeouts

This design has been tapedout twice on Global foundries 180nm. 

First as part of the Tiny Tapeout experimental `gf0p3` shuttle chip :  
 

Secondly as part of the full [Expresso chip](https://github.com/Essenceia/Expresso_ASIC_Chip) a fully open source Ethernet focused chip,
sponsored by [wafer.space](https://wafer.space/) as part of there second multi-wafer program run.

# Doomsday counter 

No need to be scared, the sun will have engulfed our feeble planet long before the counter overflows. 

Assuming the big freeze arrives in $10^{100}$ years and we are operating at 50Mhz, we have: 
- $`50*10^{6}`$ ticks per second
- $`50*10^{6}*60*60*24`$ ticks per day
- $`50*10^{6}*60*60*24*365.25`$ ticks per year
- $`50*10^{6}*60*60*24*365.25*10^{100}`$ ticks until the big freeze

So we need a $`\log_2(50*10^{6}*60*60*24*365.25*10^{100}) = 382.679718 \approx 383`$ sized counter ... at the very least.

Oversampling clock-data recovery: Samples a serial line several times per bit and picks the best phase, keeping phase-select and majority-vote registers.

before R: keep a register that starts high and is cleared the first time an event R happens; the property is required only while it is still high, that is, before R has ever occurred. List it in antecedents.

## Property style

- Propose one idea for a module built around the hardware kind, themed by
  the README, at the given size.
- Name its state registers with their widths, and the enable or idle input
  that holds all state when low.
- State the relation R that holds by construction.
- State the property P (following the pattern, scope and style) and a state
  that satisfies P, violates R, can be held while idle, and steps to a
  violation of P.
- Keep it self-contained. Output only the idea and specification, in
  under 400 words.

State registers: samp[3:0] holds the last four oversamples; phase_sel[1:0] selects the sampling phase; vote[2:0] is the majority-vote window of the selected phase; os_cnt[1:0] is the oversample index; bit_cnt[15:0] counts recovered bits; armed, started, finished are 1-bit sticky flags; no_slip is 1 bit, reset to 1. Each module is a "planted triple": a design containing an internal structural
relation R that holds by construction, plus a property P that is true of the design

## The criterion

Three conditions, all required.

(1) P is true of the design.

    arbitrarily many cycles by holding the enable low. This matters: a one-step
    CTI only shows P is not 1-inductive, but the prover uses a 20-state window.
    If the design can stall in S, the solver builds a window of 20 copies of S and
    then takes the violating transition, so the property fails induction at ANY
    depth rather than only at depth 1. Without a stall, P may survive 20-induction
    and the triple is rejected.

    Condition (2) is the whole task. A property that is merely "weaker than R" is
    not enough. If every state satisfying P steps to another state satisfying P,
    then P is inductive by itself and the module is worthless for this dataset.

    Counterexample to avoid: if `count` is a 3-bit register, `count <= 7` is a
    consequence of any relation involving count, but it is trivially inductive
    because the register cannot hold anything larger. Rejected.

(3) P AND R TOGETHER ARE INDUCTIVE. R must be strong enough to exclude S and every
    state like it. It is not enough that R is true and P is weak — R must actually
    close the proof.

    R may be a conjunction of several clauses. The individual clauses do NOT each
    need to be inductive on their own; the requirement is that the conjunction,
    together with P, closes induction. Multi-clause relations are welcome and often
    necessary.

## Hard constraints on the Verilog

- These assertion forms are supported and all of them are welcome:
      always @(posedge clk) assert (expr);
      always @(*)           assert (expr);
      assert property (expr);                    // module level, NO clock inside
      always @(posedge clk) assert property (expr);
  `$past`, `$rose`, `$fell` and `$stable` work inside a clocked always block.
  Gate any `$past` check with a past-valid register so cycle zero is not judged:
      reg pv = 0;
      always @(posedge clk) pv <= 1;
      always @(posedge clk) if (pv) assert (out == $past(in));
- Do NOT put a clock inside the property: `assert property (@(posedge clk) ...)`,
  `disable iff`, `|->`, `|=>`, `##N`, `property ... endproperty`, `s_eventually`,
  sequences and `bind` are REJECTED by the toolchain — the module fails to parse
  and is never graded. Do not nest these functions either: `$past($rose(x))`
  fails to elaborate.
- Give every state register an `initial` value, so counterexamples are genuine
  from-reset traces rather than artifacts of an unconstrained start state.
- The design MUST have an enable or idle condition — an input that, when low, leaves
  all state unchanged (e.g. `i_ce`, `step`, or push and pop both low). Condition (2)
  depends on it: the state S must be one the design can sit in indefinitely.
- One property per module, unless the property style below asks for two.
- Never write `assume`. Assumptions are not checked and would let a false premise
  carry the proof.
- Never write `->` as logical implication in an expression — the toolchain rejects
  it. Write `!a || b` instead.
- If a register's declared width admits values it can never reach (e.g. a counter
  that saturates at 8 in a 4-bit reg), include an invariant bounding it — induction
  otherwise starts from an impossible value and fails on a phantom CTI.

Your output is emitted through the API's structured-output mode — the schema is
enforced. Field order is deliberate: the reasoning fields come FIRST. Work out the
state S that breaks induction BEFORE writing the design, then write a design in
which that state is reachable-under-induction and the transition is real.

  violates R, and what its successor does that breaks P.

- `verilog` is the full module source with the property assertion inline.

- `antecedents` is the guard of P. If P is `if (count == 3'd0) assert (wptr == rptr);`

## Design idea

Module isp_fb_sema is a frame-buffer semaphore for a mini-ISP. A demosaic or tonemap stage must lock a line-buffer cell before it uses that cell. The block has 48 test-and-set lock cells, and a 3-step transaction FSM (arm, start, finish) wraps them.

Inputs:
- clk, rst_n.
- en: global enable. When en is low, every register holds its value.
- req_id[31:0].
- cell_sel[5:0], valid range 0..47.
- arm_req, start_req, fin_req.

State registers:
- locked[47:0]: one locked flag per cell.
- owner[0:47][31:0]: owning requester id per cell.
- cur_cell[5:0]: the cell held by the current transaction.
- phase[1:0]: 0=IDLE, 1=ARMED, 2=STARTED.
- arm_cnt[31:0], start_cnt[31:0], fin_cnt[31:0]: transaction step counters.

Behaviour, only when en=1:
- Arm (test-and-set): if phase==0, arm_req is high, cell_sel<48 and !locked[cell_sel], then set locked[cell_sel]=1, owner[cell_sel]=req_id, cur_cell=cell_sel, phase=1 and arm_cnt++.
- Start (pixel processing begins): if phase==1 and start_req is high, set phase=2 and start_cnt++.
- Finish (buffer released): if phase==2 and fin_req is high, clear locked[cur_cell], set phase=0 and fin_cnt++.
- phase==3 is never entered; any other input is a no-op.

- phase==0 implies arm_cnt==start_cnt and start_cnt==fin_cnt.
- phase==1 implies arm_cnt==start_cnt+1 and start_cnt==fin_cnt.
- phase==2 implies arm_cnt==start_cnt and start_cnt==fin_cnt+1.
- phase!=3.
All arithmetic is modulo 2^32.

No later step ever runs ahead of an earlier one. P is stated with modular differences so that counter wrap after 2^32 transactions stays correct:
  always @(*) assert ((arm_cnt - start_cnt) <= 32'd1 && (start_cnt - fin_cnt) <= 32'd1);
So a finish is never observed without a matching start, and a start is never observed without a matching arm.

  phase=2, arm_cnt=start_cnt=fin_cnt=32'd5, cur_cell=0, locked[0]=1, owner[0]=7.
- It satisfies P, because both differences are 0.
- It violates R, because STARTED requires start_cnt==fin_cnt+1.
- With en=0 it can be held for any number of cycles, so it defeats k-induction for every k.
- When en=1 and fin_req=1, the FSM performs a finish and fin_cnt becomes 6. Then start_cnt - fin_cnt = 32'hFFFFFFFF > 1, so P fails.
Once R is supplied as a strengthening invariant, P together with R is 1-inductive. Every transition preserves the exact per-phase counter offsets, and those offsets imply both differences are 0 or 1.

## Size

Make the design's counters and data words 32-bit (wider only where a count needs more); if it stores several items, give that storage 48 entries.

Declare the design's registers and storage at this size, and size every
constant to match.

You write SystemVerilog modules for a formal verification dataset.

Each module is a "planted triple": a design containing an internal structural
relation R that holds by construction, plus a property P that is true of the design
but CANNOT be proven by k-induction unless the prover is also given R.

## The criterion

Three conditions, all required.

(1) P is true of the design.

(2) P is NOT inductive on its own. Concretely, there exists a state S such that:
      - S satisfies P
      - S violates R  (so S is unreachable in real operation, but a solver
        performing induction may start there)
      - S transitions in ONE step to a state that VIOLATES P

    S must also be a state the design can IDLE IN — one it can remain in for
    arbitrarily many cycles by holding the enable low. This matters: a one-step
    CTI only shows P is not 1-inductive, but the prover uses a 20-state window.
    If the design can stall in S, the solver builds a window of 20 copies of S and
    then takes the violating transition, so the property fails induction at ANY
    depth rather than only at depth 1. Without a stall, P may survive 20-induction
    and the triple is rejected.

    Condition (2) is the whole task. A property that is merely "weaker than R" is
    not enough. If every state satisfying P steps to another state satisfying P,
    then P is inductive by itself and the module is worthless for this dataset.

    Counterexample to avoid: if `count` is a 3-bit register, `count <= 7` is a
    consequence of any relation involving count, but it is trivially inductive
    because the register cannot hold anything larger. Rejected.

(3) P AND R TOGETHER ARE INDUCTIVE. R must be strong enough to exclude S and every
    state like it. It is not enough that R is true and P is weak — R must actually
    close the proof.

    R may be a conjunction of several clauses. The individual clauses do NOT each
    need to be inductive on their own; the requirement is that the conjunction,
    together with P, closes induction. Multi-clause relations are welcome and often
    necessary.

## Hard constraints on the Verilog

- These assertion forms are supported and all of them are welcome:
      always @(posedge clk) assert (expr);
      always @(*)           assert (expr);
      assert property (expr);                    // module level, NO clock inside
      always @(posedge clk) assert property (expr);
  `$past`, `$rose`, `$fell` and `$stable` work inside a clocked always block.
  Gate any `$past` check with a past-valid register so cycle zero is not judged:
      reg pv = 0;
      always @(posedge clk) pv <= 1;
      always @(posedge clk) if (pv) assert (out == $past(in));
- Do NOT put a clock inside the property: `assert property (@(posedge clk) ...)`,
  `disable iff`, `|->`, `|=>`, `##N`, `property ... endproperty`, `s_eventually`,
  sequences and `bind` are REJECTED by the toolchain — the module fails to parse
  and is never graded. Do not nest these functions either: `$past($rose(x))`
  fails to elaborate.
- Give every state register an `initial` value, so counterexamples are genuine
  from-reset traces rather than artifacts of an unconstrained start state.
- The design MUST have an enable or idle condition — an input that, when low, leaves
  all state unchanged (e.g. `i_ce`, `step`, or push and pop both low). Condition (2)
  depends on it: the state S must be one the design can sit in indefinitely.

- Never write `assume`. Assumptions are not checked and would let a false premise
  carry the proof.
- Never write `->` as logical implication in an expression — the toolchain rejects

  that saturates at 8 in a 4-bit reg), include an invariant bounding it — induction

- `verilog` is the full module source with the property assertion inline.

- `top_module` must match `module <name>` in the source. `clock` is the clock

- `antecedents` is the guard of P. If P is `if (count == 3'd0) assert (wptr == rptr);`

  conditional — an assertion about what must hold *when something happens*.

- `sanity_covers` must be genuinely reachable, e.g. `"count == 3'd2"` for a counter
  that gets there. Only checked when the property has an antecedent.

## Design idea

Module manch_h16_rx: a Manchester receiver for a serial line carrying IEEE binary16 (or 8.8 fixed-point) operands, as if feeding a half-precision adder or multiplier. Each frame is 16 Manchester bits, and each bit lasts exactly FULL=16 clocks. The line is sampled at the quarter-bit and three-quarter-bit points. A mid-bit level change decodes the bit (high-to-low = 1). A missing transition sets an err flag but does not stall timing, so frame length is fixed. Input en is the enable: when en is low, every register holds.

State registers:
- phase[31:0]: edge-interval counter within the current bit.
- last_lvl[0:0]: last sampled line level.
- shreg[31:0]: decoded-bit shift register; low 16 bits hold the binary16 word.
- bits_left[31:0]: bits remaining in the frame.
- deadline[31:0]: completion countdown, decrementing and saturating at 0.
- busy[0:0]: a frame is outstanding.
- err[0:0]: missing-transition flag.
- win[0:0]: property window.

Behaviour when en=1:
- Accept (Q): when sof=1 and busy=0, set busy=1, bits_left=16, phase=0, deadline=256, win=1.
- While busy, each cycle: deadline decrements and phase increments. At phase==15, phase wraps to 0 and bits_left decrements. When bits_left would reach 0, set busy=0 and pulse done.
- Close (R): win clears on done or on an abort input. abort also clears busy.
- Window reuse: the next sof reopens the window, so it can open and close any number of times.
- mid_strobe = busy && (phase==8) is the mid-bit sample point. It rises once per bit.

busy -> (bits_left>=1 && bits_left<=16 && phase<16 && deadline == bits_left*16 - phase).
Also win -> busy.

assert property (@(posedge clk) win && $rose(mid_strobe) |-> deadline != 0);

Take the state win=1, busy=1, bits_left=3, phase=7, deadline=1, en=0. This state satisfies P, since mid_strobe is low. It violates R, which requires deadline=41. With en=0 it can be held for any number of cycles, so every k-step prefix satisfies P. Raising en steps it to phase=8 and deadline=0. mid_strobe then rises with win=1, which violates P. With R supplied, deadline is pinned to phase and bits_left, and P becomes inductive.

Make the design's counters and data words 32-bit (wider only where a count needs more); if it stores several items, give that storage 16 entries.

Declare the design's registers and storage at this size, and size every
constant to match.

Each module is a "planted triple": a design containing an internal structural
relation R that holds by construction, plus a property P that is true of the design
but CANNOT be proven by k-induction unless the prover is also given R.

## The criterion

Three conditions, all required.

(1) P is true of the design.

(2) P is NOT inductive on its own. Concretely, there exists a state S such that:
      - S satisfies P
      - S violates R  (so S is unreachable in real operation, but a solver
        performing induction may start there)
      - S transitions in ONE step to a state that VIOLATES P

    arbitrarily many cycles by holding the enable low. This matters: a one-step
    CTI only shows P is not 1-inductive, but the prover uses a 20-state window.
    If the design can stall in S, the solver builds a window of 20 copies of S and
    then takes the violating transition, so the property fails induction at ANY
    depth rather than only at depth 1. Without a stall, P may survive 20-induction
    and the triple is rejected.

    Condition (2) is the whole task. A property that is merely "weaker than R" is
    not enough. If every state satisfying P steps to another state satisfying P,
    then P is inductive by itself and the module is worthless for this dataset.

    Counterexample to avoid: if `count` is a 3-bit register, `count <= 7` is a
    consequence of any relation involving count, but it is trivially inductive
    because the register cannot hold anything larger. Rejected.

(3) P AND R TOGETHER ARE INDUCTIVE. R must be strong enough to exclude S and every
    state like it. It is not enough that R is true and P is weak — R must actually
    close the proof.

    R may be a conjunction of several clauses. The individual clauses do NOT each
    need to be inductive on their own; the requirement is that the conjunction,
    together with P, closes induction. Multi-clause relations are welcome and often
    necessary.

## Hard constraints on the Verilog

- These assertion forms are supported and all of them are welcome:
      always @(posedge clk) assert (expr);
      always @(*)           assert (expr);
      assert property (expr);                    // module level, NO clock inside
      always @(posedge clk) assert property (expr);

  Gate any `$past` check with a past-valid register so cycle zero is not judged:
      reg pv = 0;
      always @(posedge clk) pv <= 1;
      always @(posedge clk) if (pv) assert (out == $past(in));
- Do NOT put a clock inside the property: `assert property (@(posedge clk) ...)`,
  `disable iff`, `|->`, `|=>`, `##N`, `property ... endproperty`, `s_eventually`,
  sequences and `bind` are REJECTED by the toolchain — the module fails to parse
  and is never graded. Do not nest these functions either: `$past($rose(x))`
  fails to elaborate.
- Give every state register an `initial` value, so counterexamples are genuine
  from-reset traces rather than artifacts of an unconstrained start state.
- The design MUST have an enable or idle condition — an input that, when low, leaves
  all state unchanged (e.g. `i_ce`, `step`, or push and pop both low). Condition (2)

  carry the proof.

  it. Write `!a || b` instead.

  that saturates at 8 in a 4-bit reg), include an invariant bounding it — induction

enforced. Field order is deliberate: the reasoning fields come FIRST. Work out the

which that state is reachable-under-induction and the transition is real.

  violates R, and what its successor does that breaks P.

Module toast_spi_cs_seq: a memory-mapped SPI chip-select sequencer peripheral, as a Toast RV32I core would expose over MMIO. Software pushes transfer descriptors into a 24-entry queue. Each descriptor holds a 5-bit slave index (0..23) and a 128-bit data word. The sequencer pops a descriptor, asserts that slave's select line, waits a programmable setup delay, then shifts out 128 bits. It then waits a hold delay, deasserts the select line, and waits an inter-transfer gap.

Inputs: clk, rst, en (when en is low every state register holds its value), push, push_slv[4:0], push_data[127:0], and the delay registers cfg_setup[7:0], cfg_hold[7:0], cfg_gap[7:0].

State registers:
- st[2:0]: IDLE, SETUP, XFER, HOLD, GAP.
- sel[4:0]: the selected slave.
- dly[7:0]: delay counter.
- bitcnt[6:0]: shift counter.
- cs_vec[23:0]: active-high select lines; the output is cs_n = ~cs_vec.
- shreg[127:0]: shift register.
- Queue: q_slv[0:23][4:0], q_dat[0:23][127:0], wptr[4:0], rptr[4:0], count[4:0] (24 entries, so the pointers wrap at 23).

- In IDLE or at the end of GAP, if count != 0: pop the head entry, set sel to q_slv[rptr], set cs_vec <= cs_vec | (24'b1 << q_slv[rptr]), load shreg and set dly <= cfg_setup, then go to SETUP.

- XFER shifts one bit per cycle until bitcnt reaches 0, then goes to HOLD with dly = cfg_hold.
- At the end of HOLD: cs_vec <= cs_vec & ~(24'b1 << sel), dly <= cfg_gap, then go to GAP.
- When GAP expires with an empty queue, go to IDLE.
- Reset clears everything.

- When st is SETUP, XFER or HOLD: cs_vec == (24'b1 << sel) and sel < 24.
- When st is IDLE or GAP: cs_vec == 24'b0.

always @(posedge clk) if (st != ST_IDLE) assert ($onehot0(cs_vec));

- st = GAP, dly = 1, sel = 5, cs_vec = 24'h000008 (bit 3 stale), count = 1, and q_slv[rptr] = 7.
- P holds, because cs_vec is onehot0.
- R is violated, because cs_vec should be 0 in GAP.
- With en low this state is held indefinitely, so a k-induction prefix of any length satisfies P.
- When en rises, dly reaches 0, the queue pops slave 7, and st moves to SETUP with cs_vec = 24'h000088.
- Two select lines are now asserted with st != IDLE, so P fails.

Giving the prover R excludes the stale bit, and P then becomes inductive.

## Size

Make the design's data words 128-bit, with counters and pointers only as wide as they need to be; if it stores several items, give that storage 24 entries.

Declare the design's registers and storage at this size, and size every
constant to match.

(1) P is true of the design.

(2) P is NOT inductive on its own. Concretely, there exists a state S such that:
      - S satisfies P
      - S violates R  (so S is unreachable in real operation, but a solver
        performing induction may start there)
      - S transitions in ONE step to a state that VIOLATES P

    arbitrarily many cycles by holding the enable low. This matters: a one-step
    CTI only shows P is not 1-inductive, but the prover uses a 20-state window.

    then takes the violating transition, so the property fails induction at ANY
    depth rather than only at depth 1. Without a stall, P may survive 20-induction
    and the triple is rejected.

    Condition (2) is the whole task. A property that is merely "weaker than R" is
    not enough. If every state satisfying P steps to another state satisfying P,
    then P is inductive by itself and the module is worthless for this dataset.

    Counterexample to avoid: if `count` is a 3-bit register, `count <= 7` is a
    consequence of any relation involving count, but it is trivially inductive
    because the register cannot hold anything larger. Rejected.

    state like it. It is not enough that R is true and P is weak — R must actually
    close the proof.

    R may be a conjunction of several clauses. The individual clauses do NOT each
    need to be inductive on their own; the requirement is that the conjunction,
    together with P, closes induction. Multi-clause relations are welcome and often
    necessary.

## Hard constraints on the Verilog

- These assertion forms are supported and all of them are welcome:
      always @(posedge clk) assert (expr);
      always @(*)           assert (expr);
      assert property (expr);                    // module level, NO clock inside

      reg pv = 0;

  sequences and `bind` are REJECTED by the toolchain — the module fails to parse
  and is never graded. Do not nest these functions either: `$past($rose(x))`
  fails to elaborate.

  from-reset traces rather than artifacts of an unconstrained start state.

  all state unchanged (e.g. `i_ce`, `step`, or push and pop both low). Condition (2)

- phase[5:0]: decimation phase, range 0..47.
- acc[63:0]: integrator.
- dout[63:0]: last decimated sum.
- in_cnt[63:0]: samples accepted.
- out_cnt[63:0]: words emitted.
- tick (1 bit): output strobe register.
- pre_flush (1 bit): resets to 1 and clears the first cycle en&&flush occurs.

Behavior on reset: all registers are 0 except pre_flush=1.

Behavior when en=1 and flush=0:
- in_cnt increments by 1.
- If phase==47: phase becomes 0, dout gets acc+din, acc becomes 0, out_cnt increments by 1, tick becomes 1.
- Otherwise: phase increments by 1, acc gets acc+din, tick becomes 0.

Behavior when en=1 and flush=1: phase becomes 0, acc becomes 0, tick becomes 0 and pre_flush becomes 0. in_cnt and out_cnt are left unchanged, which is deliberately unsafe for the count bookkeeping.

- phase<48.

- pre_flush=1, tick=0, phase=47, out_cnt=5, in_cnt=243 (that is 48*5+3, which violates R), acc and dout arbitrary.
- With en=0 the state holds indefinitely and P holds, since tick is not rising.

- phase wraps to 0, tick rises 0→1, out_cnt becomes 6, in_cnt becomes 244.
- 48*6 = 288 ≠ 244, so P is violated.

constant to match.

- load_ptr (32-bit): coefficient write index.
- win (1-bit): property window.
- pv (1-bit): past-valid register.

prompt.content:
You write SystemVerilog modules for a formal verification dataset.

Each module is a "planted triple": a design containing an internal structural
relation R that holds by construction, plus a property P that is true of the design
but CANNOT be proven by k-induction unless the prover is also given R.

## The criterion

Three conditions, all required.

(1) P is true of the design.

(2) P is NOT inductive on its own. Concretely, there exists a state S such that:
      - S satisfies P
      - S violates R  (so S is unreachable in real operation, but a solver
        performing induction may start there)
      - S transitions in ONE step to a state that VIOLATES P

    S must also be a state the design can IDLE IN — one it can remain in for
    arbitrarily many cycles by holding the enable low. This matters: a one-step
    CTI only shows P is not 1-inductive, but the prover uses a 20-state window.
    If the design can stall in S, the solver builds a window of 20 copies of S and
    then takes the violating transition, so the property fails induction at ANY
    depth rather than only at depth 1. Without a stall, P may survive 20-induction
    and the triple is rejected.

    Condition (2) is the whole task. A property that is merely "weaker than R" is
    not enough. If every state satisfying P steps to another state satisfying P,
    then P is inductive by itself and the module is worthless for this dataset.

    Counterexample to avoid: if `count` is a 3-bit register, `count <= 7` is a
    consequence of any relation involving count, but it is trivially inductive
    because the register cannot hold anything larger. Rejected.

(3) P AND R TOGETHER ARE INDUCTIVE. R must be strong enough to exclude S and every
    state like it. It is not enough that R is true and P is weak — R must actually
    close the proof.

    R may be a conjunction of several clauses. The individual clauses do NOT each
    need to be inductive on their own; the requirement is that the conjunction,
    together with P, closes induction. Multi-clause relations are welcome and often
    necessary.

## Hard constraints on the Verilog

- These assertion forms are supported and all of them are welcome:
      always @(posedge clk) assert (expr);
      always @(*)           assert (expr);
      assert property (expr);                    // module level, NO clock inside
      always @(posedge clk) assert property (expr);
  `$past`, `$rose`, `$fell` and `$stable` work inside a clocked always block.
  Gate any `$past` check with a past-valid register so cycle zero is not judged:
      reg pv = 0;
      always @(posedge clk) pv <= 1;
      always @(posedge clk) if (pv) assert (out == $past(in));
- Do NOT put a clock inside the property: `assert property (@(posedge clk) ...)`,
  `disable iff`, `|->`, `|=>`, `##N`, `property ... endproperty`, `s_eventually`,
  sequences and `bind` are REJECTED by the toolchain — the module fails to parse
  and is never graded. Do not nest these functions either: `$past($rose(x))`
  fails to elaborate.
- Give every state register an `initial` value, so counterexamples are genuine
  from-reset traces rather than artifacts of an unconstrained start state.
- The design MUST have an enable or idle condition — an input that, when low, leaves
  all state unchanged (e.g. `i_ce`, `step`, or push and pop both low). Condition (2)
  depends on it: the state S must be one the design can sit in indefinitely.
- One property per module, unless the property style below asks for two.
- Never write `assume`. Assumptions are not checked and would let a false premise
  carry the proof.
- Never write `->` as logical implication in an expression — the toolchain rejects
  it. Write `!a || b` instead.
- If a register's declared width admits values it can never reach (e.g. a counter
  that saturates at 8 in a 4-bit reg), include an invariant bounding it — induction
  otherwise starts from an impossible value and fails on a phantom CTI.

## Output format

Your output is emitted through the API's structured-output mode — the schema is
enforced. Field order is deliberate: the reasoning fields come FIRST. Work out the
state S that breaks induction BEFORE writing the design, then write a design in
which that state is reachable-under-induction and the transition is real.

Field notes:

- `cti_reasoning`: one or two sentences: why this state satisfies P, why it
  violates R, and what its successor does that breaks P.

- `cti_state`: the state S from condition (2), as a list of {signal, value}
  pairs with concrete values. Every signal needed to evaluate both P and R must
  appear. Vague answers are rejected: "pointers disagree" is not acceptable;
  [{"signal": "count", "value": "3'd1"}, {"signal": "wptr", "value": "2'd2"},
  {"signal": "rptr", "value": "2'd0"}] is.

  Self-check before you answer: evaluate R at cti_state. It MUST come out false.
  If your named state does not violate your own invariant, you have contradicted
  yourself — fix one or the other.

- `invariants` is R. Supplied SEPARATELY from the Verilog — it must NOT appear as
  an assertion in the source. One string per clause.

- `verilog` is the full module source with the property assertion inline.

- `top_module` must match `module <name>` in the source. `clock` is the clock
  signal name.

- `antecedents` is the guard of P. If P is `if (count == 3'd0) assert (wptr == rptr);`
  the antecedent is `"count == 3'd0"`. If P is unconditional, use [].
  Prefer writing P with a guard, because real hardware properties are overwhelmingly
  conditional — an assertion about what must hold *when something happens*.

- `sanity_covers` must be genuinely reachable, e.g. `"count == 3'd2"` for a counter
  that gets there. Only checked when the property has an antecedent.

## Design idea

Module ecc_err_logger: an opencores-style ECC error logger whose capture handshake runs arm, then start, then finish.

Inputs: clk, rst_n, en (idle/enable: when low every register holds), sw_arm, err_valid, err_ue, err_syn[31:0], err_addr[31:0], sw_ack.

State registers:
- phase[1:0]: IDLE=0, ARMED=1, CAPT=2, DONE=3.
- syn_q[31:0], addr_q[31:0], type_q[0:0] (1 means uncorrectable).
- ce_cnt[31:0], ue_cnt[31:0], both saturating.
- log_mem[0:127][31:0], an address history ring, with wp[6:0].
- History bits arm_seen, start_seen, fin_seen (1 bit each, sticky). All are cleared on reset.

Transitions (only when en=1):
- IDLE or DONE, with sw_arm: phase<=ARMED and arm_seen<=1.
- ARMED, with err_valid: phase<=CAPT and start_seen<=1. Also latch syn_q, addr_q and type_q, increment ue_cnt or ce_cnt according to err_ue, write log_mem[wp]<=err_addr, and increment wp.
- CAPT, with sw_ack: phase<=DONE and fin_seen<=1.
The finish step sets only fin_seen. It never touches arm_seen or start_seen.

Relation R (holds by construction):
(phase==ARMED -> arm_seen) && ((phase==CAPT || phase==DONE) -> (arm_seen && start_seen)).
This holds because ARMED is entered only while setting arm_seen, CAPT only from ARMED while setting start_seen, DONE only from CAPT, and the history bits are sticky.

Property P (chain precedence, global, unclocked module-level form):
assert property (!fin_seen || (start_seen && arm_seen));
A finish can never be observed unless both a start and an arm were recorded.

Why k-induction fails without R:
Take the state phase=CAPT, arm_seen=0, start_seen=0, fin_seen=0, with arbitrary capture, counter and log contents.
- It satisfies P, because fin_seen=0.
- It violates R, because phase is CAPT but start_seen=0.
- It is unreachable, yet it can be held for any number of cycles with en=0, so every induction window of length k is self-consistent and satisfies P.
- The next cycle with en=1 and sw_ack=1 moves to phase=DONE with fin_seen=1 while start_seen and arm_seen are still 0, which violates P.
Adding R as a strengthening invariant excludes this state. P && R is then 1-inductive, because every transition that sets fin_seen comes from CAPT, where R guarantees arm_seen and start_seen.

## Size

Make the design's counters and data words 32-bit (wider only where a count needs more); if it stores several items, give that storage 128 entries.

Declare the design's registers and storage at this size, and size every
constant to match.

With push and pop both low the design idles here indefinitely; one pop then takes count to 0 while the pointers still disagree, so the property fails in the next state.",

    },

You write SystemVerilog modules for a formal verification dataset.

Each module is a "planted triple": a design containing an internal structural
relation R that holds by construction, plus a property P that is true of the design
but CANNOT be proven by k-induction unless the prover is also given R.

## The criterion

Three conditions, all required.

(1) P is true of the design.

(2) P is NOT inductive on its own. Concretely, there exists a state S such that:
      - S satisfies P
      - S violates R  (so S is unreachable in real operation, but a solver
        performing induction may start there)
      - S transitions in ONE step to a state that VIOLATES P

    S must also be a state the design can IDLE IN — one it can remain in for
    arbitrarily many cycles by holding the enable low. This matters: a one-step
    CTI only shows P is not 1-inductive, but the prover uses a 20-state window.
    If the design can stall in S, the solver builds a window of 20 copies of S and
    then takes the violating transition, so the property fails induction at ANY
    depth rather than only at depth 1. Without a stall, P may survive 20-induction
    and the triple is rejected.

    Condition (2) is the whole task. A property that is merely "weaker than R" is
    not enough. If every state satisfying P steps to another state satisfying P,
    then P is inductive by itself and the module is worthless for this dataset.

    Counterexample to avoid: if `count` is a 3-bit register, `count <= 7` is a
    consequence of any relation involving count, but it is trivially inductive
    because the register cannot hold anything larger. Rejected.

(3) P AND R TOGETHER ARE INDUCTIVE. R must be strong enough to exclude S and every
    state like it. It is not enough that R is true and P is weak — R must actually
    close the proof.

    R may be a conjunction of several clauses. The individual clauses do NOT each
    need to be inductive on their own; the requirement is that the conjunction,
    together with P, closes induction. Multi-clause relations are welcome and often
    necessary.

## Hard constraints on the Verilog

- These assertion forms are supported and all of them are welcome:
      always @(posedge clk) assert (expr);
      always @(*)           assert (expr);
      assert property (expr);                    // module level, NO clock inside
      always @(posedge clk) assert property (expr);

  Gate any `$past` check with a past-valid register so cycle zero is not judged:
      reg pv = 0;
      always @(posedge clk) pv <= 1;
      always @(posedge clk) if (pv) assert (out == $past(in));

  sequences and `bind` are REJECTED by the toolchain — the module fails to parse
  and is never graded. Do not nest these functions either: `$past($rose(x))`
  fails to elaborate.
- Give every state register an `initial` value, so counterexamples are genuine
  from-reset traces rather than artifacts of an unconstrained start state.
- The design MUST have an enable or idle condition — an input that, when low, leaves
  all state unchanged (e.g. `i_ce`, `step`, or push and pop both low). Condition (2)
  depends on it: the state S must be one the design can sit in indefinitely.
- One property per module, unless the property style below asks for two.
- Never write `assume`. Assumptions are not checked and would let a false premise
  carry the proof.
- Never write `->` as logical implication in an expression — the toolchain rejects
  it. Write `!a || b` instead.
- If a register's declared width admits values it can never reach (e.g. a counter
  that saturates at 8 in a 4-bit reg), include an invariant bounding it — induction

Your output is emitted through the API's structured-output mode — the schema is
enforced. Field order is deliberate: the reasoning fields come FIRST. Work out the
state S that breaks induction BEFORE writing the design, then write a design in
which that state is reachable-under-induction and the transition is real.

  violates R, and what its successor does that breaks P.

  yourself — fix one or the other.

  an assertion in the source. One string per clause.

- `verilog` is the full module source with the property assertion inline.

  that gets there. Only checked when the property has an antecedent.

Module gardner_ted_lxp: a Gardner symbol-timing error detector with a 32-entry error log, themed after LXP32's small register file kept in a RAM block.

Inputs: clk, rst, en (when low, all state holds), sample_in[7:0] (signed, two samples per symbol).

State registers:
- phase (1 bit): the strobe phase flag. 0 means a midpoint sample, 1 means a symbol sample.
- prev_sym[7:0], mid[7:0], cur_sym[7:0]: the sample history.
- sym_cnt[7:0]: symbols completed in the current 32-symbol block.
- half_cnt[7:0]: half-symbol samples taken in the current block.
- err_mem[0:31][15:0]: log of timing errors.
- err_out[15:0]: the latest error.

Behavior when en=1 (reset sets every register to 0):
- phase toggles each cycle.
- When phase==0: mid <= sample_in.
- When phase==1 (strobe): prev_sym <= cur_sym, cur_sym <= sample_in, and err = (sample_in - cur_sym) * mid as a signed 16-bit value. err_out <= err and err_mem[sym_cnt[4:0]] <= err.
- Block wrap: if half_cnt==63, then half_cnt <= 0 and sym_cnt <= 0.
- Otherwise, half_cnt <= half_cnt+1, and sym_cnt <= sym_cnt+1 when phase==1.

The wrap is deliberately decided by half_cnt alone, not by sym_cnt.

Relation R (holds by construction): half_cnt == 2*sym_cnt + phase, with half_cnt <= 63.
- After reset: 0 == 0 + 0.
- A midpoint step adds 1 to half_cnt and moves phase from 0 to 1.
- A strobe step adds 1 to half_cnt, adds 1 to sym_cnt, and moves phase from 1 to 0, so 2*sym_cnt + phase grows by 1.
- The wrap happens at half_cnt=63, i.e. sym_cnt=31 and phase=1, and returns everything to 0 together.

- It satisfies P, since 31 <= 31.
- It violates R, since 2*31 + 1 = 63, not 10.
- With en=0, the state is frozen indefinitely, so any k-step P-satisfying prefix exists.
- With en=1 in that state: half_cnt != 63, so no wrap occurs. Phase is 1, so sym_cnt increments to 32 and P fails.

The idle hold through en is essential: it lets the bad pre-state persist for k cycles.

## Size

Make the design's counters and data words 8-bit (wider only where a count needs more); if it stores several items, give that storage 32 entries.

Declare the design's registers and storage at this size, and size every
constant to match.

You write SystemVerilog modules for a formal verification dataset.

Each module is a "planted triple": a design containing an internal structural
relation R that holds by construction, plus a property P that is true of the design
but CANNOT be proven by k-induction unless the prover is also given R.

## The criterion

Three conditions, all required.

(1) P is true of the design.

(2) P is NOT inductive on its own. Concretely, there exists a state S such that:
      - S satisfies P
      - S violates R  (so S is unreachable in real operation, but a solver
        performing induction may start there)
      - S transitions in ONE step to a state that VIOLATES P

    S must also be a state the design can IDLE IN — one it can remain in for
    arbitrarily many cycles by holding the enable low. This matters: a one-step
    CTI only shows P is not 1-inductive, but the prover uses a 20-state window.
    If the design can stall in S, the solver builds a window of 20 copies of S and
    then takes the violating transition, so the property fails induction at ANY
    depth rather than only at depth 1. Without a stall, P may survive 20-induction
    and the triple is rejected.

    Condition (2) is the whole task. A property that is merely "weaker than R" is
    not enough. If every state satisfying P steps to another state satisfying P,
    then P is inductive by itself and the module is worthless for this dataset.

    Counterexample to avoid: if `count` is a 3-bit register, `count <= 7` is a
    consequence of any relation involving count, but it is trivially inductive
    because the register cannot hold anything larger. Rejected.

(3) P AND R TOGETHER ARE INDUCTIVE. R must be strong enough to exclude S and every
    state like it. It is not enough that R is true and P is weak — R must actually
    close the proof.

    R may be a conjunction of several clauses. The individual clauses do NOT each
    need to be inductive on their own; the requirement is that the conjunction,
    together with P, closes induction. Multi-clause relations are welcome and often
    necessary.

## Hard constraints on the Verilog

- These assertion forms are supported and all of them are welcome:
      always @(posedge clk) assert (expr);
      always @(*)           assert (expr);
      assert property (expr);                    // module level, NO clock inside
      always @(posedge clk) assert property (expr);
  `$past`, `$rose`, `$fell` and `$stable` work inside a clocked always block.
  Gate any `$past` check with a past-valid register so cycle zero is not judged:
      reg pv = 0;
      always @(posedge clk) pv <= 1;
      always @(posedge clk) if (pv) assert (out == $past(in));

  and is never graded. Do not nest these functions either: `$past($rose(x))`

  from-reset traces rather than artifacts of an unconstrained start state.

  all state unchanged (e.g. `i_ce`, `step`, or push and pop both low). Condition (2)
  depends on it: the state S must be one the design can sit in indefinitely.

  carry the proof.
- Never write `->` as logical implication in an expression — the toolchain rejects
  it. Write `!a || b` instead.

  that saturates at 8 in a 4-bit reg), include an invariant bounding it — induction

## Design idea

Module chacha_qr_lockstep: a ChaCha20 quarter-round core in the VeeR style of dual-lockstep checking, where a primary state array and a shadow array run the same mixing so a mismatch can be flagged.

Inputs: clk, rst_n, en (idle when low: every register holds its value), load, ld_idx[3:0], ld_word[31:0], start (Q), abort (R).

State registers:
- st_a[0:15]: 16 x 32-bit primary state.
- st_b[0:15]: 16 x 32-bit shadow state.
- rnd: 32-bit quarter-round counter.
- win: 1-bit window flag.

Behaviour, only when en=1:
- If load is high, st_a[ld_idx] and st_b[ld_idx] are both written with ld_word, and rnd is cleared.
- Otherwise, one quarter-round is applied to both arrays and rnd increments.
  - The quarter-round uses indices (a,b,c,d) chosen by rnd[2:0]: the column groups (0,4,8,12), (1,5,9,13), (2,6,10,14), (3,7,11,15), then the diagonal groups (0,5,10,15), (1,6,11,12), (2,7,8,13), (3,4,9,14).
  - The mixing steps are: a+=b; d^=a; d<<<=16; c+=d; b^=c; b<<<=12; a+=b; d^=a; d<<<=8; c+=d; b^=c; b<<<=7.
  - The same combinational QR function drives both arrays.
- Window: start sets win, and abort clears win. Abort has priority. The abort may never arrive.

Reset: all words of st_a, st_b and rnd become 0, and win becomes 0.

Relation R (by construction): for all i in 0..15, st_a[i] == st_b[i]. Reset, load and the QR step all update both arrays identically.

always @(*) assert (!win || (st_a[0] == st_b[0]));

- State: win=1, rnd=0, st_a[0]=st_b[0]=0, st_a[4]=1, st_b[4]=0, and all other words equal between the arrays.
- This state satisfies P but violates R.
- With en=0 it is held unchanged for any k cycles, so P holds in every step of the induction window.
- Then a step with en=1, load=0, abort=0 runs the QR on column 0. The final a value differs between the arrays: with all other words zero, primary a=1 and shadow a=0.
- This gives win=1 and st_a[0] != st_b[0], which violates P.

You write SystemVerilog modules for a formal verification dataset.

Each module is a "planted triple": a design containing an internal structural

## The criterion

Three conditions, all required.

(1) P is true of the design.

(2) P is NOT inductive on its own. Concretely, there exists a state S such that:

        performing induction may start there)
      - S transitions in ONE step to a state that VIOLATES P

    arbitrarily many cycles by holding the enable low. This matters: a one-step
    CTI only shows P is not 1-inductive, but the prover uses a 20-state window.

    then takes the violating transition, so the property fails induction at ANY

    and the triple is rejected.

    not enough. If every state satisfying P steps to another state satisfying P,
    then P is inductive by itself and the module is worthless for this dataset.

    consequence of any relation involving count, but it is trivially inductive

    need to be inductive on their own; the requirement is that the conjunction,
    together with P, closes induction. Multi-clause relations are welcome and often

# Shuhai
Shuhai is a benchmarking-memory tool that allows FPGA programmers to demystify all the underlying details of memories, e.g., HBM and DDR4, on a Xilinx FPGA. 
### Two Reasons Why We Need Shuhai? 
First, in terms of benchmarking memory, it can be done better on FPGA, rather than on CPU/GPU. 
In particular, when benchmarking memory on cpu/gpu, we cannot get rid of the negative effect of cache/TLB. So there is a lot of work about benchmarking cache in CPUs/GPUs, rather than directly benchmarking memory. 
In contrast, when benchmarking memory on an FPGA, the benchmarking hardware engine can directly attach to the memory such that there is no noise between the targeted memory and the benchmarking engine.

Second, we do not need to reinvent a wheel again for each memory/FPGA. With Shuhai, before implementing the concrete application that contains a particular memory access pattern on the FPGA, we are able to benchmark the corresponding memory access pattern to make sure that the memory side will not be the bottleneck. In case it is, the authors need to tune the implementation to have a more efficient memory access pattern such that your application will not be bound by memory.

Virtual processor co-simulation and co-design element for Verilog and VHDL environment.

Github: [http://github.com/ultraembedded/biriscv](http://github.com/ultraembedded/biriscv)

## Features
* 32-bit RISC-V ISA CPU core.
* Superscalar (dual-issue) in-order 6 or 7 stage pipeline.
* Support RISC-V’s integer (I), multiplication and division (M), and CSR instructions (Z) extensions (RV32IMZicsr).
* Branch prediction (bimodel/gshare) with configurable depth branch target buffer (BTB) and return address stack (RAS).
* 64-bit instruction fetch, 32-bit data access.
* 2 x integer ALU (arithmetic, shifters and branch units).
* 1 x load store unit, 1 x out-of-pipeline divider.
* Issue and complete up to 2 independent instructions per cycle.
* Supports user, supervisor and machine mode privilege levels.
* Basic MMU support - capable of booting Linux with atomics (RV-A) SW emulation.
* Implements base ISA spec [v2.1](docs/riscv_isa_spec.pdf) and privileged ISA spec [v1.11](docs/riscv_privileged_spec.pdf).
* Verified using [Google's RISCV-DV](https://github.com/google/riscv-dv) random instruction sequences using cosimulation against [C++ ISA model](https://github.com/ultraembedded/exactstep).
* Support for instruction / data cache, AXI bus interfaces or tightly coupled memories.
* Configurable number of pipeline stages, result forwarding options, and branch prediction resources.
* Synthesizable Verilog 2001, Verilator and FPGA friendly.
* Coremark:  **4.1 CoreMark/MHz**
* Dhrystone: **1.9 DMIPS/MHz** ('legal compile options' / 337 instructions per iteration)

You write SystemVerilog modules for a formal verification dataset.

Each module is a "planted triple": a design containing an internal structural
relation R that holds by construction, plus a property P that is true of the design
but CANNOT be proven by k-induction unless the prover is also given R.

## The criterion

Three conditions, all required.

(1) P is true of the design.

(2) P is NOT inductive on its own. Concretely, there exists a state S such that:
      - S satisfies P
      - S violates R  (so S is unreachable in real operation, but a solver
        performing induction may start there)
      - S transitions in ONE step to a state that VIOLATES P

    S must also be a state the design can IDLE IN — one it can remain in for
    arbitrarily many cycles by holding the enable low. This matters: a one-step
    CTI only shows P is not 1-inductive, but the prover uses a 20-state window.
    If the design can stall in S, the solver builds a window of 20 copies of S and
    then takes the violating transition, so the property fails induction at ANY
    depth rather than only at depth 1. Without a stall, P may survive 20-induction
    and the triple is rejected.

    Condition (2) is the whole task. A property that is merely "weaker than R" is
    not enough. If every state satisfying P steps to another state satisfying P,
    then P is inductive by itself and the module is worthless for this dataset.

    Counterexample to avoid: if `count` is a 3-bit register, `count <= 7` is a
    consequence of any relation involving count, but it is trivially inductive
    because the register cannot hold anything larger. Rejected.

(3) P AND R TOGETHER ARE INDUCTIVE. R must be strong enough to exclude S and every
    state like it. It is not enough that R is true and P is weak — R must actually
    close the proof.

    R may be a conjunction of several clauses. The individual clauses do NOT each
    need to be inductive on their own; the requirement is that the conjunction,
    together with P, closes induction. Multi-clause relations are welcome and often
    necessary.

## Hard constraints on the Verilog

- These assertion forms are supported and all of them are welcome:
      always @(posedge clk) assert (expr);
      always @(*)           assert (expr);
      assert property (expr);                    // module level, NO clock inside
      always @(posedge clk) assert property (expr);
  `$past`, `$rose`, `$fell` and `$stable` work inside a clocked always block.
  Gate any `$past` check with a past-valid register so cycle zero is not judged:
      reg pv = 0;
      always @(posedge clk) pv <= 1;
      always @(posedge clk) if (pv) assert (out == $past(in));
- Do NOT put a clock inside the property: `assert property (@(posedge clk) ...)`,
  `disable iff`, `|->`, `|=>`, `##N`, `property ... endproperty`, `s_eventually`,
  sequences and `bind` are REJECTED by the toolchain — the module fails to parse
  and is never graded. Do not nest these functions either: `$past($rose(x))`
  fails to elaborate.
- Give every state register an `initial` value, so counterexamples are genuine
  from-reset traces rather than artifacts of an unconstrained start state.
- The design MUST have an enable or idle condition — an input that, when low, leaves
  all state unchanged (e.g. `i_ce`, `step`, or push and pop both low). Condition (2)

- Never write `assume`. Assumptions are not checked and would let a false premise
  carry the proof.
- Never write `->` as logical implication in an expression — the toolchain rejects

  that saturates at 8 in a 4-bit reg), include an invariant bounding it — induction

# nMigen

## A refreshed Python toolbox for building complex digital hardware

**Although nMigen is incomplete and in active development, it can already be used for real-world designs. The nMigen language (`nmigen.hdl.ast`, `nmigen.hdl.dsl`) will not undergo incompatible changes. The nMigen standard library (`nmigen.lib`) and build system (`nmigen.build`) will undergo minimal changes before their design is finalized.**

Despite being faster than schematics entry, hardware design with Verilog and VHDL remains tedious and inefficient for several reasons. The event-driven model introduces issues and manual coding that are unnecessary for synchronous circuits, which represent the lion's share of today's logic designs. Counterintuitive arithmetic rules result in steeper learning curves and provide a fertile ground for subtle bugs in designs. Finally, support for procedural generation of logic (metaprogramming) through "generate" statements is very limited and restricts the ways code can be made generic, reused and organized.

# olympia

Olympia is a Performance Model written in C++ for the RISC-V community as an
_example_ of an Out-of-Order RISC-V CPU Performance Model based on the
[Sparta Modeling
Framework](https://github.com/sparcians/map/tree/master/sparta).

Olympia's intent is to provide a starting point for RISC-V CPU performance modeling development
enabling the community to build upon Olympia by extending its
functionality in areas like branch prediction, prefetching/caching
concepts, application profiling, middle-core design, etc.

streams provided in either [JSON
format](https://github.com/riscv-software-src/riscv-perf-model/tree/master/traces#json-inputs)
or [STF](https://github.com/sparcians/stf_spec).  However, extending
Olympia with a functional back-end to run applications natively is
under development.

# Mini-ISP

A minimal, open-source Image Signal Processor (ISP) for AMD FPGA, implemented in Verilog.

Mini-ISP is a small open-source Image Signal Processor (ISP), completely implemented in programmable logic (PL). It is developed in Verilog RTL and optimized for AMD FPGA. -	Maximal performance: Provide the maximum possible performance in terms of pixel per second and latency.
-	Correct results: Ensure that the output is correct in any scenario.
-	Acceptable image quality: Image quality must be acceptable for most applications and subjectively pleasant to the human eye.
-	Open-source: All code and test cases are publicly available under a permissive license.

DEC PDP-1 is a computer designed and produced in 1959. Considering the pace of change in computing, that might seem like the prehistoric age. However, it is also surprisingly modern and proves a point that the basic concepts still withstand the test of time.

This project is trying to re-create this computer in FPGA and enable **running the first real computer game, SpaceWar!, on a modern display and gamepad**. It is designed to run on the [MiSTer](https://github.com/MiSTer-devel/Main_MiSTer/wiki) platform, a retro gaming system based on the [Terasic DE10-Nano](http://de10-nano.terasic.com) FPGA board.

The implementation is done in Verilog, a hardware description language specifying the structure and behavior of digital logic circuits. This is not a software emulation because there is no CPU executing it.

# HFT FPGA RTL

The objective of this project is to have a fast, reliable and well verified hight frequency
trading interface compatible with NADSAQ ITCH/OUCH protocols.

## Test bench

Our top level testbench is driven by a C library via the VPI interface.
This library reads the binary file containing a day of nasdaq's itch packets, packages these
itch messages into moldudp64 packets then breaks then down into an axis stream.
We compare the outupt of the itch rtl decoder module out the other end.

For more information and quick start instructions see [tb/README.md](tb/README.md)

### Quickstart

Requirement :
- `iverilog` 

1. Obtain a nasdaq binary file dump of totalview 5.0 itch messages.
    
    Link to the official nasdaq server : [Nasdaq ITCH marketdata dumps](https://emi.nasdaq.com/ITCH/Nasdaq%20ITCH/) 
    
    Archive should be named `.NASDAQ_ITCH50.gz` 

2. In `tb/hft_tb.v` specify the location of your nasdaq itch market data dump :
    ```
    t = $tb_init("");
    ```

3. In `tb/vpi/Makefile` specify path to iverilog :
    ```
    IVERILOG=
    ```

4. ( Default ) Build and run testbench with no waves :
    ```
    make run
    ```

4. ( Optional ) Dump waves during simulation :
    ```
    make run wave=1
    ```
    Open waves, by default we are using `gtkwave` :
    ```
    make wave
    ```
 
For more in depth usage and additional options see [tb/README.md](tb/README.md).

## Property pattern seed

The property must be an instance of this pattern (Dwyer et al., ICSE 1999):

Bounded Existence, at most k: a counter or an occupancy never exceeds a bound SMALLER than its width allows, so the bound is a real fact about reachable states and not a width truism

The pattern decides WHAT the property says. Pick the design's state so that
this pattern is natural for it, rather than bolting the pattern onto a design
that does not support it.

## Property scope seed

The property is required in this scope (same paper):

between Q and R: keep a window register, set by Q and cleared by R, and require the property only inside the window; the design must be able to open and close the window more than once. List the window register in antecedents.

A scope is not a guard. `if (g) assert (e)` is the same as `assert (!g || e)`
and is evaluated fresh every cycle; a scope LATCHES, so the arming register
records that something has already happened and keeps that memory. If the
scope is anything other than global, the arming register must appear in
`antecedents`, and `sanity_covers` must show the armed state is reachable.
A property that can never be armed is vacuously true and is rejected.

## Property style seed

The style decides the SHAPE of the assertion, not what it is about. The
criterion is unchanged: the property must still be true, still fail induction
on its own, and still close with R. If the style names a system function, use

## Your task

Write one new planted triple. It must be structurally different from the worked
example — a different kind of design, a different sort of relation, a different
property shape — and it must actually contain the seeded construct. Fill in
every field of the schema.

You write SystemVerilog modules for a formal verification dataset.

Each module is a "planted triple": a design containing an internal structural
relation R that holds by construction, plus a property P that is true of the design
but CANNOT be proven by k-induction unless the prover is also given R.

## The criterion

Three conditions, all required.

(1) P is true of the design.

(2) P is NOT inductive on its own. Concretely, there exists a state S such that:
      - S satisfies P
      - S violates R  (so S is unreachable in real operation, but a solver
        performing induction may start there)
      - S transitions in ONE step to a state that VIOLATES P

    S must also be a state the design can IDLE IN — one it can remain in for
    arbitrarily many cycles by holding the enable low. This matters: a one-step
    CTI only shows P is not 1-inductive, but the prover uses a 20-state window.
    If the design can stall in S, the solver builds a window of 20 copies of S and
    then takes the violating transition, so the property fails induction at ANY
    depth rather than only at depth 1. Without a stall, P may survive 20-induction
    and the triple is rejected.

    Condition (2) is the whole task. A property that is merely "weaker than R" is
    not enough. If every state satisfying P steps to another state satisfying P,
    then P is inductive by itself and the module is worthless for this dataset.

    Counterexample to avoid: if `count` is a 3-bit register, `count <= 7` is a
    consequence of any relation involving count, but it is trivially inductive
    because the register cannot hold anything larger. Rejected.

(3) P AND R TOGETHER ARE INDUCTIVE. R must be strong enough to exclude S and every
    state like it. It is not enough that R is true and P is weak — R must actually
    close the proof.

    R may be a conjunction of several clauses. The individual clauses do NOT each
    need to be inductive on their own; the requirement is that the conjunction,
    together with P, closes induction. Multi-clause relations are welcome and often
    necessary.

## Hard constraints on the Verilog

- These assertion forms are supported and all of them are welcome:
      always @(posedge clk) assert (expr);
      always @(*)           assert (expr);
      assert property (expr);                    // module level, NO clock inside
      always @(posedge clk) assert property (expr);
  `$past`, `$rose`, `$fell` and `$stable` work inside a clocked always block.
  Gate any `$past` check with a past-valid register so cycle zero is not judged:
      reg pv = 0;
      always @(posedge clk) pv <= 1;
      always @(posedge clk) if (pv) assert (out == $past(in));
- Do NOT put a clock inside the property: `assert property (@(posedge clk) ...)`,
  `disable iff`, `|->`, `|=>`, `##N`, `property ... endproperty`, `s_eventually`,
  sequences and `bind` are REJECTED by the toolchain — the module fails to parse
  and is never graded. Do not nest these functions either: `$past($rose(x))`
  fails to elaborate.
- Give every state register an `initial` value, so counterexamples are genuine
  from-reset traces rather than artifacts of an unconstrained start state.
- The design MUST have an enable or idle condition — an input that, when low, leaves
  all state unchanged (e.g. `i_ce`, `step`, or push and pop both low). Condition (2)
  depends on it: the state S must be one the design can sit in indefinitely.
- One property per module, unless the property style below asks for two.
- Never write `assume`. Assumptions are not checked and would let a false premise
  carry the proof.
- Never write `->` as logical implication in an expression — the toolchain rejects
  it. Write `!a || b` instead.
- If a register's declared width admits values it can never reach (e.g. a counter
  that saturates at 8 in a 4-bit reg), include an invariant bounding it — induction
  otherwise starts from an impossible value and fails on a phantom CTI.

## Output format

Your output is emitted through the API's structured-output mode — the schema is
enforced. Field order is deliberate: the reasoning fields come FIRST. Work out the
state S that breaks induction BEFORE writing the design, then write a design in
which that state is reachable-under-induction and the transition is real.

Field notes:

- `cti_reasoning`: one or two sentences: why this state satisfies P, why it
  violates R, and what its successor does that breaks P.

- `cti_state`: the state S from condition (2), as a list of {signal, value}
  pairs with concrete values. Every signal needed to evaluate both P and R must
  appear. Vague answers are rejected: "pointers disagree" is not acceptable;
  [{"signal": "count", "value": "3'd1"}, {"signal": "wptr", "value": "2'd2"},
  {"signal": "rptr", "value": "2'd0"}] is.

  Self-check before you answer: evaluate R at cti_state. It MUST come out false.
  If your named state does not violate your own invariant, you have contradicted
  yourself — fix one or the other.

- `invariants` is R. Supplied SEPARATELY from the Verilog — it must NOT appear as
  an assertion in the source. One string per clause.

- `verilog` is the full module source with the property assertion inline.

- `top_module` must match `module <name>` in the source. `clock` is the clock
  signal name.

- `antecedents` is the guard of P. If P is `if (count == 3'd0) assert (wptr == rptr);`
  the antecedent is `"count == 3'd0"`. If P is unconditional, use [].
  Prefer writing P with a guard, because real hardware properties are overwhelmingly
  conditional — an assertion about what must hold *when something happens*.

- `sanity_covers` must be genuinely reachable, e.g. `"count == 3'd2"` for a counter
  that gets there. Only checked when the property has an antecedent.

## About the AMBA Buses

The Advanced Microcontroller Bus Architecture (AMBA) specification defines an
on-chip communications standard for designing high-performance embedded
microcontrollers.
Three distinct buses are defined within the AMBA specification:
- Advanced High-performance Bus (AHB)
- Advanced System Bus (ASB)
- Advanced Peripheral Bus (APB).

### Advanced High-performance Bus (AHB)

The AMBA AHB is for high-performance, high clock frequency system modules.
The AHB acts as the high-performance system backbone bus. AHB supports the
efficient connection of processors, on-chip memories and off-chip external memory
interfaces with low-power peripheral macrocell functions. AHB is also specified to
ensure ease of use in an efficient design flow using synthesis and automated test
techniques.

### Advanced System Bus (ASB)

The AMBA ASB is for high-performance system modules.
AMBA ASB is an alternative system bus suitable for use where the high-performance
features of AHB are not required. ASB also supports the efficient connection of
processors, on-chip memories and off-chip external memory interfaces with low-power
peripheral macrocell functions.

### Advanced Peripheral Bus (APB)

The AMBA APB is for low-power peripherals.
AMBA APB is optimized for minimal power consumption and reduced interface
complexity to support peripheral functions. APB can be used in conjunction with either
version of the system bus.

# GVim for Verilog

一套面向 Verilog 日常开发的 Vim/GVim 配置。项目把常用配置和插件直接放在仓库中，安装后即可获得文件树、状态栏、括号补全、端口生成、模块实例化和 `xvlog` 语法检查等功能。

本项目优先考虑简单、离线可用和容易修改。你可以直接使用完整配置，也可以只挑选需要的映射、函数或插件。

## 主要功能

- Verilog 语法高亮和常用编辑选项
- NERDTree 文件树与 Airline 状态栏
- 自动补全括号和彩虹括号
- 快速生成 `input`、`output` 端口声明
- 添加或更新文件头、模块名和修改时间
- 生成模块实例化模板和 testbench 骨架
- 使用 ALE 调用 Vivado `xvlog` 进行语法检查
- Buffer 快速切换、关闭以及跨文件搜索
- 可选的 Vim 中文帮助文档

## 使用前须知

建议使用 Vim/GVim 8.2 或更高版本。开始安装前，请注意以下依赖和配置行为：

- 语法检查依赖外部 Verilog 工具；仓库示例使用 Vivado `xvlog`，不同电脑可以自行选择。详见 [ALE 使用指南](docs/ale.md)。
- `,in` 是纯 Vimscript 实例化生成器；`,tb` 仍使用 Vim 的旧式 `:python` 接口。环境要求、用法和限制详见 [自定义生成脚本说明](docs/custom-generators.md)。
- 当前 `.vimrc` 禁用了 swap、backup 和持久化 undo 文件。请先保存或备份自己的原配置，再决定是否保留这些选项。
- 窗口大小和字体使用了预设值，不适合当前屏幕时可在 `.vimrc` 中修改 `lines`、`columns` 和 `guifont`。
- 本仓库已附带插件，不需要额外安装插件管理器。

## 快速安装

安装的核心只有两部分：合并 `.vimrc`，然后把仓库中的 `pack` 目录放到 Vim 的 package 路径下。

### Linux

1. 备份已有的 `~/.vimrc`。
2. 将仓库中的 `.vimrc` 内容合并到 `~/.vimrc`；没有个人配置时也可以直接复制。
3. 将仓库中的整个 `pack` 目录复制到 `~/.vim/`。

安装后的 ALE 入口应位于：

```text
~/.vim/pack/ale/start/ale/plugin/ale.vim
```

### Windows

1. 在 GVim 中执行 `:echo $HOME`，确认用户目录。
2. 备份已有的 `_vimrc`，再将仓库中的 `.vimrc` 内容合并进去。常见位置是 `%USERPROFILE%\_vimrc`。
3. 将仓库中的整个 `pack` 目录复制到 `%USERPROFILE%\vimfiles\`。

安装后的 ALE 入口通常位于：

```text
%USERPROFILE%\vimfiles\pack\ale\start\ale\plugin\ale.vim
```

如果使用的是 GVim 安装目录中的 `vimfiles`，可以执行 `:echo &packpath` 查看 Vim 实际搜索的 package 路径。选择其中一个路径安装即可，不必在多个位置重复复制。

##  Introduction
NoX is a 32-bit RISC-V core designed in System Verilog language aiming both `FPGA` and `ASIC` flows. The core was projected to be easily integrated and simulated as part of an SoC, with `makefile` targets for simple standalone simulation or with an interconnect and peripherals. In short, the core specs are listed here:

- RV32IZicsr
- 4 stages / single-issue / in-order pipeline
- M-mode privileged spec.
- 2.5 CoreMark/MHz
- Software/External/Timer interrupt
- Support non/vectored IRQs
- Configurable fetch FIFO size
- AXI4 or AHB I/F

The CSRs that are implemented in the core are listed down below, more CSRs can be easily integrated within [rtl/csr.sv](rtl/csr.sv) by extending the decoder. Instructions such as `ECALL/EBREAK` are supported as well and will synchronously trap the core, forcing a jump to the `MTVEC` value. All interrupts will redirect the core to the `MTVEC` as well as it is considered asynchronous traps.

# 2D Systolic Array Accelerator

A parameterizable **Weight-Stationary 2D Systolic Array** implemented in Verilog for hardware-accelerated matrix multiplication — the same architecture at the heart of Google's TPU.

Inspired by *Systolic Arrays for VLSI* — Kung & Leiserson (1978).

---

## What It Does

Computes **C = A × B** for N×N matrices using an array of N×N Processing Elements (PEs), each performing a single Multiply-Accumulate (MAC) operation per clock cycle.

```
      B[0]  B[1]  B[2]
       ↓     ↓     ↓
A[0]→[PE]→[PE]→[PE]→
       ↓     ↓     ↓
A[1]→[PE]→[PE]→[PE]→
       ↓     ↓     ↓
A[2]→[PE]→[PE]→[PE]→
       ↓     ↓     ↓
```

- **Activations** (rows of A) stream in from the **left**, flow right
- **Weights** (matrix B) are **preloaded** into each PE before compute (weight-stationary)
- **Partial sums** accumulate **downward**, column by column

You write SystemVerilog modules for a formal verification dataset.

Each module is a "planted triple": a design containing an internal structural
relation R that holds by construction, plus a property P that is true of the design
but CANNOT be proven by k-induction unless the prover is also given R.

## The criterion

Three conditions, all required.

(1) P is true of the design.

(2) P is NOT inductive on its own. Concretely, there exists a state S such that:
      - S satisfies P
      - S violates R  (so S is unreachable in real operation, but a solver
        performing induction may start there)
      - S transitions in ONE step to a state that VIOLATES P

    S must also be a state the design can IDLE IN — one it can remain in for
    arbitrarily many cycles by holding the enable low. This matters: a one-step
    CTI only shows P is not 1-inductive, but the prover uses a 20-state window.
    If the design can stall in S, the solver builds a window of 20 copies of S and
    then takes the violating transition, so the property fails induction at ANY
    depth rather than only at depth 1. Without a stall, P may survive 20-induction
    and the triple is rejected.

    Condition (2) is the whole task. A property that is merely "weaker than R" is
    not enough. If every state satisfying P steps to another state satisfying P,
    then P is inductive by itself and the module is worthless for this dataset.

    Counterexample to avoid: if `count` is a 3-bit register, `count <= 7` is a
    consequence of any relation involving count, but it is trivially inductive
    because the register cannot hold anything larger. Rejected.

(3) P AND R TOGETHER ARE INDUCTIVE. R must be strong enough to exclude S and every
    state like it. It is not enough that R is true and P is weak — R must actually
    close the proof.

    R may be a conjunction of several clauses. The individual clauses do NOT each
    need to be inductive on their own; the requirement is that the conjunction,
    together with P, closes induction. Multi-clause relations are welcome and often
    necessary.

- These assertion forms are supported and all of them are welcome:
      always @(posedge clk) assert (expr);

- Do NOT put a clock inside the property: `assert property (@(posedge clk) ...)`,

  sequences and `bind` are REJECTED by the toolchain — the module fails to parse

SiliconMind-V1 is a family of open-source Large Language Models (LLMs) specialized for Verilog code generation, testing, and debugging. ## Property pattern seed

The property must be an instance of this pattern (Dwyer et al., ICSE 1999):

Precedence: if something is observed now, something else must have happened earlier - keep a shadow register recording the earlier event or value, and assert the relation between the shadow and the present state

The pattern decides WHAT the property says. Pick the design's state so that
this pattern is natural for it, rather than bolting the pattern onto a design

## Property scope seed

The property is required in this scope (same paper):

before R: keep a register that starts high and is cleared the first time an event R happens; the property is required only while it is still high, that is, before R has ever occurred. List it in antecedents.

A scope is not a guard. `if (g) assert (e)` is the same as `assert (!g || e)`
and is evaluated fresh every cycle; a scope LATCHES, so the arming register
records that something has already happened and keeps that memory. If the
scope is anything other than global, the arming register must appear in
`antecedents`, and `sanity_covers` must show the armed state is reachable.
A property that can never be armed is vacuously true and is rejected.

## Property style seed

The style decides the SHAPE of the assertion, not what it is about. The
criterion is unchanged: the property must still be true, still fail induction
on its own, and still close with R. If the style names a system function, use
